source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XI (Montreuil)

1.title: De perfectione evangelicæ legis
1.title_en: On the perfection of the Gospel law
1.note: A general introduction to the commentary on Luke: Denis expounds no verse of the Gospel here (the prologue, 1:1–4, begins in Art. II), so the article is placed at the head of chapter 1.

paras.t: Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus. Job xxxvi, 22. Quemadmodum in Prima Secundæ Thomas ostendit, lex est regula atque mensura actuum, per quam quis ad agendum vel non agendum bene se habet sive inducitur. Legis enim est, actus hominum regulare debito ordine secundum exigentiam finis a legislatore intenti.
paras.en: [[Job 36:22|Behold, God is high in his strength, and none is like him among the lawgivers.|Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus]] As Thomas shows in the Prima Secundæ [the first part of the second part of his *Summa theologiae*], law is a rule and measure of acts, by which one is well disposed, or led, to act or not to act. For it belongs to law to regulate the acts of men in due order, according to what is required by the end intended by the lawgiver.

paras.t: Multiplex autem lex ponitur, videlicet: lex æterna, quæ est dictamen et ratio divinæ sapientiæ, in quantum est directiva actionum ac motuum omnium creaturarum. De qua lege Deo Sapiens ait: Quum sis justus, juste omnia disponis; virtus enim tua justitiæ initium est. Hæc itaque lex realiter idem est quod summa et increata Sapientia, attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponens cuncta suaviter: quæ lex, secundum Anselmum in libro de Veritate, omnis rectitudinis et virtutis, omnis veritatis ac legis origo est, et fontale atque causale principium. — Alia est ergo lex naturalis, quæ est participatio legis æternæ, naturis rerum creatarum naturaliter indita, per quam quælibet tendit in proprium finem sibi a divina sapientia præstitutum, et operatur proprias actiones. Porro lex ista naturalis in homine est dictamen seu ordinatio vel censura practicæ rationis, per quam homo ad aliquid agendum vel omittendum inducitur. Istaque lex sufficeret homini, si homo non ordinaretur nisi ad naturalem felicitatem ac finem; sed quia ad supernaturalem beatitudinem (quæ est visio Dei per speciem, seu facie ad faciem, secundum Apostolum) creatus et ordinatus est, ideo supernaturali indiget lege, quæ dicitur lex divina, per quam de vera ac supernaturali beatitudine instruatur, atque de præceptis et actibus perveniendi ad illam illuminetur. Quæ lex est mensura ac regula actuum humanorum in ordine ad felicitatem supernaturalem æternam. Siquidem per hanc legem ratio cognoscit et dictat quid de Deo sentiendum, quomodo ei obsequendum, ad quem finem sit omne nostrum exercitium referendum. De qua ait Psalmista: Lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas.
paras.en: Now law is spoken of in several ways. There is the eternal law, which is the dictate and reason of the divine wisdom, inasmuch as it directs the actions and movements of all creatures. Of this law the Wise man says to God: [[Wis 12:15|thou art just, thou orderest all things justly|Quum sis justus, juste omnia disponis]]; for [[Wis 12:16|thy power is the beginning of justice|virtus enim tua justitiæ initium est]]. This law, then, is in reality the same as the supreme and uncreated Wisdom, reaching from end to end mightily and ordering all things sweetly[[Wis 8:1||]]; and this law, according to Anselm in his book *On Truth*, is the origin of all rightness and virtue, of all truth and law, their fountain and causal principle. — Next, then, there is the natural law, which is a participation of the eternal law, implanted by nature in the natures of created things, by which each thing tends to its own end, appointed for it by the divine wisdom, and performs its proper actions. In man this natural law is the dictate, ordering or judgment of the practical reason, by which man is led to do or to leave undone some thing. And this law would suffice for man if he were ordered only to a natural happiness and end; but because he has been created and ordered to a supernatural beatitude (which is the vision of God by sight, or face to face, according to the Apostle[[1 Cor 13:12||]][[2 Cor 3:18||]]), he needs a supernatural law, which is called the divine law, by which he may be instructed about true and supernatural beatitude, and enlightened about the precepts and acts by which it is reached. This law is the measure and rule of human acts in their ordering to eternal, supernatural happiness. For by this law reason knows and dictates what is to be believed of God, how he is to be served, and to what end all our activity is to be referred. Of it the Psalmist says: [[Ps 18:8|The law of the Lord is unspotted, converting souls|Lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas]].

paras.t: Insuper, præter legem æternam et naturalem ac divinam, ponitur lex humana, quæ est quoddam rationis dictamen, quo diriguntur actus humani in ordine ad finem boni communis in vita præsenti ad convivendum pacifice: quæ lex ex naturali lege progreditur, estque determinatio et explicatio ejus circa particularia hominum opera. Quemadmodum enim ratio speculativa ex primis ac indemonstrabilibus principiis elicit varias diversarum scientiarum conclusiones: sic ratio practica ex primis principiis operativis, seu agendorum, quæ ad naturalem pertinent legem, procedit ad particulariora, inquirendo et discutiendo quid in certis negotiis sit agendum; et hujusmodi particulares dispositiones per rationem inventæ, dicuntur leges humanæ, observatis aliis conditionibus quæ ad legem concurrere debent. Lex enim concernit bonum commune. Dicit quoque Isidorus, quod lex humana, quantum possibile est, debet esse honesta, ut religioni conveniat; justa, ut secundum rationem procedat; possibilis, ut a subditis portari valeat et impleri. Erit demum secundum consuetudinem patriæ, et loco ac tempori debet congruere.
paras.en: Besides the eternal, the natural and the divine law, there is also human law, which is a certain dictate of reason by which human acts are directed to the end of the common good in the present life, so that men may live together in peace. This law proceeds from the natural law, and is its determination and application to the particular works of men. For as the speculative reason draws from first and indemonstrable principles the various conclusions of the different sciences, so the practical reason proceeds from the first principles of action, or of things to be done, which belong to the natural law, to more particular things, inquiring and discussing what is to be done in given affairs; and such particular dispositions, found out by reason, are called human laws, provided the other conditions that must go into a law are observed. For law concerns the common good. Isidore also says that human law, as far as possible, ought to be honest, so as to accord with religion; just, so as to proceed according to reason; possible, so that subjects may be able to bear it and fulfil it. It will be, finally, in keeping with the custom of the country, and ought to suit the place and the time.

paras.t: Denique lex divina dividitur in legem veterem seu Mosaicam, et novam seu evangelicam. Quæ divisio non est per diversas seu oppositas species, quum utriusque sit unus finis, scilicet Christus, seu Deo conjungi ac frui; in utraque etiam principalia præcepta, puta moralia, sunt eadem: sed est sicut dividitur aliquid per perfectum et imperfectum, quæ tamen unius sunt speciei, ut homo per virum et puerum.
paras.en: Lastly, the divine law is divided into the old or Mosaic law and the new or Gospel law. This division is not into different or opposed species, since both have one end, namely Christ[[Rom 10:4||]], that is, to be joined to God and to enjoy him; in both, too, the chief precepts, that is, the moral ones, are the same. It is rather as a thing is divided into perfect and imperfect, which are nevertheless of one species, as man is divided into grown man and boy.

paras.t: Nunc ergo ostendenda est legis evangelicæ super omnem aliam legem creatam excellentia atque perfectio. Porro, quod omnem legem humanam excedat, certum et clarum est, et infra probabitur. Quod vero legem Moysis perfectione dignitateque superet, primo ostenditur ex parte legislatoris. Vetus enim lex a Deo data est, non immediate, sed mediate, imo per gradum duplicem ministrorum, puta per angelum et per Moysen. Deo namque jubente ac destinante, locutus est angelus Moysi, jubenteque angelo ex parte Dei, Moyses legem ab angelo immediate acceptam proposuit populo. Imo non unius dumtaxat ministerio angeli, sed plurium angelorum, data est vetus lex, juxta illud Apostoli: Lex propter transgressores posita est, ordinata per angelos in manu mediatoris. Unde in Actibus Stephanus exprobrans ingratis Judæis: Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum, et non custodistis. Evangelica vero lex a vero Deo, videlicet Jesu Christo Unigenito Patris æterni (de quo Christo in sua Canonica scribit Joannes: Hic est verus Deus et vita æterna) immediate collata est.
paras.en: Now, then, the excellence and perfection of the Gospel law above every other created law must be shown. That it surpasses every human law is certain and clear, and will be proved below. That it surpasses the law of Moses in perfection and dignity is shown, first, on the part of the lawgiver. For the old law was given by God not immediately but mediately, indeed through a double rank of ministers, namely through an angel and through Moses. At God's command and appointment the angel spoke to Moses[[Ex 19:3||]], and at the angel's command, on God's behalf, Moses set before the people the law he had received immediately from the angel. Indeed, the old law was given by the ministry not of one angel only but of many, according to the Apostle's words: The law [[Gal 3:19|was set because of transgressions|propter transgressores posita est]] [Denis's text reads *transgressores*, "transgressors", where the Vulgate has *transgressiones*], [[Gal 3:19|being ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator|ordinata per angelos in manu mediatoris]]. Hence in the Acts Stephen, reproaching the ungrateful Jews, says: You [[Acts 7:53|have received the law by the disposition of angels and have not kept it|Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum, et non custodistis]]. But the Gospel law was bestowed immediately by the true God, that is, by Jesus Christ, the Only-begotten of the eternal Father (of which Christ John writes in his canonical Epistle: [[1 John 5:20|This is the true God and life eternal|Hic est verus Deus et vita æterna]]).

paras.t: Secundo ostenditur idem, quia vetus lex comparatur ad novam sicut imperfectum ad perfectum, sicut medium ad finem, sicut dispositio ad formam seu habitum; imo lex evangelica se habet ad veterem legem sicut meridies ad auroram, lumen ad umbram, veritas ad figuram, domina ad ancillam. Quum enim finis legis divinæ, videlicet veteris ac novæ, sit ad veram felicitatem perducere seu Deo uniri ac frui, illa lex divina vocatur perfecta, quæ ea includit per quæ beatitudo acquiritur, ad quam sine gratia gratum faciente nemo perducitur. Vetus autem lex gratiam non continuit, sed promisit. Evangelica vero lex gratiam includit et confert, quoniam sacramenta ejus gratiam non solum figurant, seu signant, sed etiam conferunt, et efficiunt quod designant. Ideo dicit Apostolus: Nihil ad perfectum adduxit lex, introductio vero melioris spei, per quam approximamus ad Deum; rursus: Lex pædagogus noster fuit in Christo Jesu; itemque: Si data esset lex quæ posset vivificare, vere ex lege esset justitia; sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato. Hujus autem ratio assignatur, quoniam sacramenta veteris legis gratiam non continebant nec conferebant; sed ipsa lex dispositiva fuit ad evangelicam legem, eam præfigurando, Christum prænuntiando, idololatriam reprobando, ideo Christi lege promulgata cessavit. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Priusquam veniret fides, sub lege custodiebamur, conclusi in eam fidem quæ revelanda erat; ubi autem venit fides, jam non sumus sub pædagogo. Similiter loquitur ad Hebræos: Reprobatio quidem fit præcedentis mandati propter infirmitatem et inutilitatem.
paras.en: Secondly, the same is shown because the old law is compared to the new as the imperfect to the perfect, as the means to the end, as a disposition to the form or habit; indeed, the Gospel law stands to the old law as midday to the dawn, light to shadow, truth to the figure, the mistress to the handmaid. For since the end of the divine law, both old and new, is to lead to true happiness, that is, to be united to God and to enjoy him, that divine law is called perfect which contains the things by which beatitude is gained; and to beatitude no one is brought without sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes a man pleasing to God]. But the old law did not contain grace; it promised it. The Gospel law contains and confers grace, since its sacraments not only figure or signify grace but also confer it, and effect what they signify. Therefore the Apostle says: [[Heb 7:19|the law brought nothing to perfection: but a bringing in of a better hope, by which we draw nigh to God|Nihil ad perfectum adduxit lex, introductio vero melioris spei, per quam approximamus ad Deum]]; and again: [[Gal 3:24|the law was our pedagogue in Christ|Lex pædagogus noster fuit in Christo]] Jesus [the *pædagogus* was the slave who led a boy to school and kept him in order until he came of age]; and also: [[Gal 3:21|if there had been a law given which could give life, verily justice should have been by the law|Si data esset lex quæ posset vivificare, vere ex lege esset justitia]]; [[Gal 3:22|But the scripture hath concluded all under sin|sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato]]. The reason given for this is that the sacraments of the old law did not contain or confer grace; but the law itself was a preparation for the Gospel law, prefiguring it, foretelling Christ, condemning idolatry; and so, once the law of Christ was promulgated, it ceased. That is why the Apostle says: [[Gal 3:23|before the faith came, we were kept under the law shut up, unto that faith which was to be revealed|Priusquam veniret fides, sub lege custodiebamur, conclusi in eam fidem quæ revelanda erat]]; [[Gal 3:25|But after the faith is come, we are no longer under a pedagogue|ubi autem venit fides, jam non sumus sub pædagogo]]. In the same way he speaks to the Hebrews: [[Heb 7:18|There is indeed a setting aside of the former commandment, because of the weakness and unprofitableness thereof|Reprobatio quidem fit præcedentis mandati propter infirmitatem et inutilitatem]].

paras.t: Tertio, idem probatur, quia lex evangelica bona cœlestia et futura in patria manifeste prænuntiat, figurat, promittit, atque ad ea immediate introducit. Horum autem bonorum lex vetus non habuit significationem expressam et propinquam, sed obscuram atque remotam, prout scriptum est: Umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum. Hinc, juxta divum Dionysium, status evangelicæ legis medius est inter statum Synagogæ seu veteris legis, ac patriæ: ita quod sacramenta et cærimonialia novæ legis habent imaginem perfectam et evidentem similitudinem bonorum cœlestium, quorum umbram gerebant sacramenta ac cærimonialia veteris Testamenti, quia in veteri lege bona illa ventura promittebantur, et figurabantur sub velamine et confuse. Denique dicitur lex evangelica gratiam continere et dare, per inclusionem sacramentorum suorum, hoc est, in quantum includit Christi sacramenta, quæ sunt spiritualiter medicinalia vasa. Et quoniam lex vetus talia sacramenta gratiæ contentiva non habuit, ideo propria virtute non justificavit, sed fide et gratia Christi tunc venturi, per cujus fidem opera hominum sub lege positorum meritoria erant. Hinc ab Apostolo dicitur lex illa subintrasse, ut abundaret delictum, et quod per eam peccatum revixit; itemque, quod fuit administratio mortis, non utique causaliter et directe, sed occasionaliter et consecutive, et quoniam gratiam non præstabat; rursusque, quia peccatum post legislationem gravius fuit quam ante, et quoniam talis est nostra perversitas, quod nitimur in vetitum, et ea quæ nobis prohibentur, magis optamus.
paras.en: Thirdly, the same is proved because the Gospel law openly foretells, figures and promises the heavenly goods to come in our true country, and leads straight into them. Of these goods the old law had no express and near signification, but only an obscure and remote one, as it is written: [[Heb 10:1|the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things|Umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum]]. Hence, according to the divine Dionysius, the state of the Gospel law is midway between the state of the Synagogue, or of the old law, and that of our heavenly country: so that the sacraments and ceremonies of the new law have a perfect image and evident likeness of the heavenly goods, of which the sacraments and ceremonies of the Old Testament bore the shadow; for in the old law those goods to come were promised and figured under a veil and confusedly. Further, the Gospel law is said to contain and give grace by its inclusion of its sacraments, that is, inasmuch as it includes the sacraments of Christ, which are vessels of spiritual medicine. And since the old law had no such sacraments containing grace, it did not justify by its own power, but by faith in Christ, then still to come, and by his grace; through faith in him the works of men placed under the law were meritorious. Hence the Apostle says that this law [[Rom 5:20|entered in that sin might abound|subintrasse, ut abundaret delictum]], and that through it [[Rom 7:9|sin revived|peccatum revixit]]; and also that it was [[2 Cor 3:7|the ministration of death|administratio mortis]] [the margin reference is read as II Cor. i, 4; the words are those of 2 Cor 3:7]: not, indeed, as its cause and directly, but as its occasion and consequently, and because it did not give grace; and again, because sin was graver after the giving of the law than before it, and because such is our perversity that we strive after what is forbidden, and long the more for the things that are forbidden us.

paras.t: Quarto declaratur id ipsum, videlicet excellentia et perfectio legis evangelicæ super omnem aliam legem divinam atque humanam, quoniam proprietates et actus legis eminentius ei conveniunt quam alicui alteri legi. — Quum enim legis officium sit homines facere virtuosos, et primo oporteat declinare a malo: ideo primo ad legem pertinet vitia exstirpare per comminationem seu inflictionem pœnarum, seu alio modo: quod propter vitiosos, protervos, et ad mala proclives, potissimum necessarium est; et quantum ad hoc dicit Apostolus: Justo non est lex posita, sed injustis, et non subditis, impiis et sceleratis. Hoc autem lex humana perfecte non efficit: nam quia communitati proponitur, in qua plures sunt imperfecti, vitiosi, ad malaque proni, quædam mala permittit ne deteriora contingant, videlicet meretrices et usurarios, quæ tamen divino relinquit judicio punienda, secundum quod asserit Augustinus: Lex quæ regendis civitatibus datur, multa concedit ac impunita relinquit, quæ per divinam providentiam vindicantur. Lex quoque Mosaica divinitus lata, quia populo rudi ad maxima mala proclivi dabatur, quædam mala permisit, ut dare libellum repudii et ad usuram extraneis accommodare, ut patet in Deuteronomio, ne majora mala incurrerentur, videlicet ne Judæi uxores suas occiderent, neque fratribus suis ad usuram concederent. Hinc Christus ait Judæis: Ad duritiam cordis vestri, Moyses permisit vobis dare libellum repudii. Lex autem evangelica tanquam perfecta, nullum prorsus malum permittit, sed omne peccatum excludit, et puniendum testatur, imo de omni verbo otioso rationem Deo reddendam fatetur.
paras.en: Fourthly, the same thing is made clear, namely the excellence and perfection of the Gospel law above every other law, divine and human, because the properties and acts of law belong to it more eminently than to any other law. — For since the office of law is to make men virtuous, and one must first decline from evil[[Ps 36:27||]], it belongs to law, first, to root out vices by threatening or inflicting punishments, or in some other way; and this is most of all necessary because of the vicious, the froward and those prone to evil. As to this the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 1:9|the law is not made for the just man but for the unjust and disobedient, for the ungodly|Justo non est lex posita, sed injustis, et non subditis, impiis]], and [[1 Tim 1:9|for the wicked|sceleratis]]. Human law does not do this perfectly: for since it is set before a community in which many are imperfect, vicious and prone to evil, it permits certain evils lest worse should happen, for instance harlots and usurers; these, however, it leaves to the judgment of God for punishment, as Augustine asserts: The law that is given for the governing of cities grants many things and leaves them unpunished, which are avenged by divine providence. The Mosaic law too, though given by God, because it was given to a rude people very prone to the greatest evils, permitted certain evils, such as giving a bill of divorce[[Deut 24:1||]] and lending at usury to strangers[[Deut 23:19||]], as is plain in Deuteronomy, lest greater evils be incurred, namely lest the Jews kill their wives, or lend at usury to their brethren. Hence Christ says to the Jews: [[Matt 19:8|Moses by reason of the hardness of your heart permitted you|Ad duritiam cordis vestri, Moyses permisit vobis]] [[Matt 19:7|to give a bill of divorce|dare libellum repudii]]. But the Gospel law, being perfect, permits no evil whatever, but excludes all sin and declares that it is to be punished; indeed, it professes that an account must be rendered to God for every idle word[[Matt 12:36||]].

paras.t: — Secundo, ad legem pertinet virtutes inducere, seu mores componere: quod lex humana non facit perfecte. Homo enim interiora aliorum non intuetur, idcirco de secretis cordium judicare non valet: ideo lex humana non nisi exteriores actus habet ordinare et judicare. Interiores vero affectus et cogitatus reformare et rectificare, ad legem spectat divinam; sed et lex Mosaica non facit hoc plene. Propter quod dicunt doctores, quod cohibet manum seu opus, non animum: quod intelligendum non est, quasi voluntatem malam nequaquam prohibeat, vel in cogitationibus vitium non consistat, quum Moyses dicat in Exodo, Non concupisces uxorem proximi tui, non bovem, non ancillam, non agrum, nec omnia quæ illius sunt; sed hoc ideo dicitur, quia lex Moysis non tam plene et evidenter prohibet inordinatum affectum et cogitatum, nec tantum versatur circa interiorem reformationem sicut lex nova. Verumtamen in multis ordinavit interiores affectus, nec solam respicit inordinatam affectionem in vitiis avaritiæ atque luxuriæ, ut aliqui dicunt, sed et in aliis multis. Unde in Levitico legitur: Ne oderis fratrem tuum in corde tuo, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum. Et in Deuteronomio habetur: Custodi te ipsum et animam tuam sollicite, ne obliviscaris verborum Domini Dei tui, et ne excidant de corde tuo cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ. Rursus in Deuteronomio præcipitur: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo et ex tota anima tua, et ex tota fortitudine tua. Nihilominus, si tota lex Moysis percurratur, patebit quod comparative loquendo, paucissima de interiorum directione et ordinatione loquatur, sed circa exteriora permaxime occupetur. Quod autem modicum est quasi pro nihilo computatur, sicque dici potuit, quod lex vetus manum non animum cohibebat.
paras.en: — Secondly, it belongs to law to bring in the virtues, or to set behaviour in order; and human law does not do this perfectly. For man does not see into the inward parts of others, and so cannot judge the secrets of hearts; therefore human law can only order and judge outward acts. To reform and set right the inward affections and thoughts belongs to the divine law; but the Mosaic law, too, does not do this fully. That is why the doctors say that it restrains the hand, or the deed, but not the mind. This is not to be understood as if it in no way forbade an evil will, or as if vice did not lie in the thoughts, since Moses says in Exodus[[Ex 20:17||]]: [[Deut 5:21|Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife|Non concupisces uxorem proximi tui]], not his ox, nor his handmaid, nor his field, [[Deut 5:21|nor any thing that is his|nec omnia quæ illius sunt]] [Denis names Exodus, but his wording is nearer that of Deuteronomy 5:21, which the margin also gives]. It is said rather because the law of Moses does not forbid inordinate affection and thought so fully and plainly as the new law, nor is it so much concerned with inward reform. Yet in many things it did order the inward affections; and it does not regard only inordinate affection in the vices of avarice and lust, as some say, but in many others too. Hence we read in Leviticus: [[Lev 19:17|Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart|Ne oderis fratrem tuum in corde tuo]], [[Lev 19:18|nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens|nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum]]. And in Deuteronomy we have: [[Deut 4:9|Keep thyself|Custodi te ipsum]], and [[Deut 4:9|thy soul carefully|animam tuam sollicite]]; [[Deut 4:9|Forget not the words|ne obliviscaris verborum]] of the Lord thy God, [[Deut 4:9|and let them not go out of thy heart all the days of thy life|et ne excidant de corde tuo cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ]]. Again, it is commanded in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 6:5|Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole strength.|Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo et ex tota anima tua, et ex tota fortitudine tua]] Nevertheless, if the whole law of Moses be gone through, it will be clear that, comparatively speaking, it says very little about the direction and ordering of inward things, and is taken up very largely with outward ones. And what is little is reckoned as nothing; and so it could be said that the old law restrained the hand and not the mind.

paras.t: — Præterea, quoniam virtus ad beatitudinem ordinatur, ideo ad legem tertio pertinet, ad felicitatem perducere. Vera autem hominis beatitudo est supernaturalis: ad quam lex humana seu naturalis nequit perducere, sed supernaturalis dumtaxat. Rursus, ad felicitatem supernaturalem non pertingitur, nisi per gratiam gratificantem, quam (ut patuit) lex Moysis non continebat, nec conferebat, idcirco nec ipsa ad felicitatem sua virtute perduxit: quod lex Christi per sua efficit sacramenta, quæ de latere Christi in cruce dormientis fluxerunt, efficaciamque sortita sunt, ita quod per ea virtus et meritum passionis Christi hominibus applicatur. Ideo in evangelio Joannis inducitur: Lex per Moysen data est, gratia et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est.
paras.en: — Further, since virtue is ordered to beatitude, it belongs to law, thirdly, to lead to happiness. But man's true beatitude is supernatural, and to it human or natural law cannot lead, but only supernatural law. Again, supernatural happiness is not reached except through sanctifying grace, which (as has been shown) the law of Moses did not contain or confer; and so neither did it lead to happiness by its own power. This the law of Christ does by its sacraments, which flowed from the side of Christ as he slept on the cross and drew their efficacy from it, so that through them the power and merit of Christ's passion are applied to men. Therefore it is set down in the Gospel of John: [[John 1:17|the law was given by Moses: grace and truth came by Jesus Christ|Lex per Moysen data est, gratia et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est]].

paras.t: — Insuper, quoniam lex pro communi datur utilitate, quarto spectat ad eam, ut omnibus promulgetur, et clare ac intelligibiliter proponatur, quia in communitate major pars grossa est, nec subtilia, difficilia, profundaque penetrat. Lex autem evangelica compendiosissime ac succincte datur atque proponitur. Mosaica vero lex multis velaminibus tegitur, et figuris involvitur; in qua etiam eadem sæpius repetuntur, et difficillimum fuit singula ejus præcepta memoriter continere, efficaciterque implere. Propter quod Petrus apostolus ait in Actibus de onere legis, Quod neque nos neque patres nostri portare potuimus.
paras.en: — Moreover, since law is given for the common good, it belongs to it, fourthly, to be promulgated to all and set forth clearly and intelligibly, because in a community the greater part is unlearned and does not penetrate subtle, difficult and deep things. Now the Gospel law is given and set forth most compendiously and briefly. But the Mosaic law is covered with many veils[[2 Cor 3:14||]] and wrapped in figures; in it, too, the same things are often repeated, and it was most difficult to hold each of its precepts in memory and to fulfil them effectively. That is why the apostle Peter says in the Acts, of the burden of the law: [[Acts 15:10|which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?|Quod neque nos neque patres nostri portare potuimus]].

paras.t: Adhuc autem evangelicæ legis eminentia constat ex hoc, quod vetus lex aperte atque communiter non promisit nisi bona terrena, de cœlesti præmio evidenter non loquens. Evangelica vero lex, cœlestia bona, spiritualem opulentiam, æternam ac deiformem beatitudinem apertissime et copiosissime pollicetur. Unde in principio prædicationis evangelicæ dicitur: Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cœlorum. — Postremo, lex Christi ad observantiam sui inducit amore boni; lex autem Moysis, timore pœnarum: ideo, secundum Augustinum, brevis differentia legis et Evangelii est amor et timor. Unde Apostolus: Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sobrietatis.
paras.en: The eminence of the Gospel law is further established by this: that the old law openly and generally promised nothing but earthly goods, and did not speak plainly of the heavenly reward; whereas the Gospel law most openly and most abundantly promises heavenly goods, spiritual riches, an eternal and godlike beatitude. Hence at the very beginning of the Gospel preaching it is said: [[Matt 3:2|Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand|Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cœlorum]][[Matt 4:17||]]. — Lastly, the law of Christ leads men to keep it by love of the good, but the law of Moses by fear of punishment; therefore, according to Augustine, the difference between the Law and the Gospel, in brief, is love and fear. Hence the Apostle: [[2 Tim 1:7|God hath not given us the spirit of fear: but of power and of love and of sobriety|Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sobrietatis]].

paras.t: Itaque de legislatore nostro unico Dei Filio vere accipitur, quod in principio hujus articuli dictum est: Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus. De quo Isaias ait: Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster, ipse veniet et salvabit nos. Interea, quo major est dignitas legiferi hujus, et quo major est caritas, beneficentia et dignatio ejus ad nos, in hoc quod pro nostra salute, in propria persona descendit ad nos, et proprio ore legem nobis deprompsit; quo etiam major est excellentia atque perfectio legis istius: eo gravior est nostra ingratitudo, perversitas et impietas, si legislatori huic inobedientes fuerimus. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Irritam quis faciens legem Moysis, sine ulla contradictione, duobus vel tribus testibus moritur: quanto magis putatis deteriora mereri supplicia, qui Filium Dei conculcaverit, et sanguinem testamenti pollutum duxerit, et Spiritui gratiæ contumeliam fecerit? Hinc ergo quo noster legifer exstat sublimior, et quo benignius se habuit circa nos, quo item præclariorem nobis contulit legem, eo diligentiores, ferventiores, efficacioresque simus in observatione suæ legis condigna, cum metu et reverentia servientes: scientes, quia cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo; et servus sciens voluntatem domini sui nec faciens, plagis vapulabit multis.
paras.en: Thus what was said at the beginning of this article is truly understood of our lawgiver, the only Son of God: [[Job 36:22|Behold, God is high in his strength, and none is like him among the lawgivers.|Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus]] Of him Isaias says: [[Is 33:22|the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king|Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster]]: he will come and [[Is 33:22|save us|salvabit nos]]. Meanwhile, the greater the dignity of this lawgiver, and the greater his charity, kindness and condescension towards us, in that for our salvation he came down to us in his own person and with his own mouth delivered the law to us, and the greater the excellence and perfection of this law, so much the graver is our ingratitude, perversity and impiety if we are disobedient to this lawgiver. That is why the Apostle says: [[Heb 10:28|A man making void the law of Moses dieth|Irritam quis faciens legem Moysis]] without any gainsaying [Denis's text reads *sine ulla contradictione*; the Vulgate has *miseratione*, "without any mercy"] [[Heb 10:28|under two or three witnesses|duobus vel tribus testibus moritur]]: [[Heb 10:29|How much more, do you think he deserveth worse punishments, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God and hath esteemed the blood of the testament unclean|quanto magis putatis deteriora mereri supplicia, qui Filium Dei conculcaverit, et sanguinem testamenti pollutum duxerit]], [[Heb 10:29|and hath offered an affront to the Spirit of grace?|et Spiritui gratiæ contumeliam fecerit?]] Hence, then, the more exalted our lawgiver is, and the more kindly he has dealt with us, and the more excellent the law he has given us, the more diligent, fervent and effective let us be in the worthy keeping of his law, serving with fear and reverence[[Phil 2:12||]] [the margin gives Phil. ii, 12, "with fear and trembling"; Denis's words are nearer Heb 12:28, "let us serve, pleasing God, with fear and reverence"]: knowing that [[Luke 12:48|unto whomsoever much is given, of him much shall be required|cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo]]; and that [[Luke 12:47|that servant, who knew the will of his lord|servus sciens voluntatem domini sui]] and doing it not [[Luke 12:47|shall be beaten with many stripes|plagis vapulabit multis]].

1.title: Elucidatio prologi sancti Lucæ in Evangelium suum, scilicet: Quoniam quidem multi conati sunt. Item et primi capituli: Fuit in diebus Herodis regis Judææ, sacerdos quidam nomine Zacharias
1.title_en: Explanation of St Luke's prologue to his Gospel, namely, “Forasmuch as many have taken in hand”; and also of the first chapter, “There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judea, a certain priest named Zachary”

paras.t: Præmittit libro suo brevem prologum S. Lucas, in quo causam se ad scribendum moventem insinuat, dicens: Quoniam quidem multi conati sunt ordinare narrationes, hoc est ordinate describere historias seu sermones, quæ in nobis completæ sunt rerum, id est operum, documentorum, mysteriorumque Christi, quæ inter nos ejus discipulos sunt peracta atque exhibita. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod et S. Lucas unus de discipulis Christi fuit, ejusque prædicationi et operibus miraculosis personaliter adfuit, saltem ad tempus, sicut prætactum est, et aliqui asserunt; vel dicit hæc in persona discipulorum qui adfuerunt, quibus ipse postea associatus sit. Aliqui autem ita exponunt: Quæ in nobis completæ sunt rerum, id est, quæ a nobis plene conscriptæ sunt: quia videlicet Lucas supplevit multa a Matthæo et Marco omissa. Isti multi qui conati sunt evangelium scribere, fuerunt quidam hæretici, sicut Basilides, et Apelles, ac alii quidam. Quidam enim evangelium scripsit, quod a duodecim Apostolis scriptum confinxit; alius, quod a Thoma editum affirmavit; alii, a Matthia. Sic et quidam sub nomine Pauli scripserunt epistolas, ut ipsemet in suis tangit epistolis. Hæc autem ex præsumptione fecerunt, et ut hæreses suas taliter persuaderent: qui recte conati fuisse dicuntur, quia non Spiritus Sancti illuminatione adjuti, sed propriis viribus confisi fuerunt, ideo habuerunt laborem, non fructum. Qui vero divinitus illustratur, prompte et faciliter scribit seu loquitur, et fructuose prosequitur: nempe, quo desuper plus illuminatur, dirigitur et juvatur, eo celerius, facilius et fructuosius operatur, et quod humiliter incipit, salubriter prosequitur atque consummat.
paras.en: St Luke sets a short prologue before his book, in which he hints at the cause that moves him to write, saying: [[1:1|Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a narration|Quoniam quidem multi conati sunt ordinare narrationes]], that is, to describe in order histories or discourses, [[1:1|of the things that have been accomplished among us|quæ in nobis completæ sunt rerum]], that is, of the works, teachings and mysteries of Christ, which were done and shown among us His disciples. From this it seems to follow that St Luke too was one of the disciples of Christ, and was personally present at His preaching and His miraculous works, at least for a time, as was touched on before and as some assert; or else he says this in the person of the disciples who were present, with whom he was afterwards associated. Some, however, expound it thus: *of the things that have been accomplished among us*, that is, which have been fully written down by us: since Luke, namely, supplied many things left out by Matthew and Mark. These many who took in hand to write a gospel were certain heretics, such as Basilides and Apelles, and certain others. For one wrote a gospel which he feigned to have been written by the twelve Apostles; another, one which he claimed was put out by Thomas; others, by Matthias. So too some wrote epistles under the name of Paul, as he himself touches on in his epistles[[2 Thess 2:2||]] [the margin reads II Thess. ii, 3; the epistle passed off as Paul's is mentioned at 2:2]. This they did out of presumption, and so as to win men to their heresies in this way: and they are rightly said to have *taken in hand* [*conati sunt*: literally, “attempted”], because they were not helped by the enlightenment of the Holy Ghost but trusted in their own strength, and so had labour, not fruit. But he who is enlightened by God writes or speaks readily and easily, and goes on fruitfully: for the more he is enlightened, directed and helped from above, the more quickly, easily and fruitfully he works, and what he begins humbly he carries on and completes to salvation.

paras.t: Denique ad componendos codices sacros, ad expositiones catholicas faciendas, necesse est hominem divinitus illuminari, luceque sapientiæ cum exuberantia quadam perfundi, loquendo de sapientia quæ inter dona gratiæ gratis datæ annumeratur: de qua protestatur Apostolus, Alii (inquiens) per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ. Quo igitur homo divinitus copiosius edocetur, eo in conscribendo, dictando, exponendo est promptior. Ibi namque in docendo nulla est mora, sed tetigisse est docuisse. Sic utique scripsit Jeremias, de quo ait Baruch ejus notarius: Ex ore suo loquebatur Jeremias, quasi legens omnes sermones istos, et ego scribebam in volumine atramento. Hinc ait Ambrosius: Sine conatu sunt donationes, et gratia Dei, quæ ubi se infuderit, rigare consuevit, ut non egeat sed redundet scriptoris ingenium. Non conati sunt quatuor Evangelistæ, sed divino Spiritu ubertatem dictorum factorumque ministrante, sine ullo molimine cœpta compleverunt.
paras.en: Lastly, to compose the sacred books and to make catholic expositions, a man must be enlightened by God and flooded, with a kind of abundance, by the light of wisdom: speaking of the wisdom that is counted among the gifts of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*: gifts given for the good of others, as distinct from the grace that makes the receiver himself pleasing to God], of which the Apostle declares: [[1 Cor 12:8|To one indeed, by the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom: and to another, the word of knowledge|Alii (inquiens) per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ]]. The more copiously, then, a man is taught by God, the readier he is in writing, dictating and expounding. For there, in teaching, there is no delay; to have touched is to have taught. Thus indeed did Jeremias write, of whom Baruch his scribe says: [[Jer 36:18|With his mouth he pronounced all these words as if he were reading to me: and I wrote in a volume with ink|Ex ore suo loquebatur Jeremias, quasi legens omnes sermones istos, et ego scribebam in volumine atramento]]. Hence Ambrose says: The gifts and grace of God are without effort [*sine conatu*]; where it has poured itself in, it is wont to water, so that the writer's mind does not lack but overflows. The four Evangelists did not *take in hand* [that is, strain at the work]; but with the divine Spirit supplying an abundance of words and deeds, they completed what they had begun without any toil.

paras.t: Insuper, secundum Origenem, Evangelista ait, Completæ sunt rerum, quia non phantastice, ut dixerunt hæretici, exercuit Christus corporalem suum adventum, sed quum veritas esset, revera negotium prosecutus est. Affectum autem suum indicat Lucas, dicendo: Quæ in nobis completa sunt rerum, hoc est, quæ in nobis manifestissime sunt ostensa. Certa enim fide et ratione cognoverat ista, nec in aliquo fluctuabat.
paras.en: Moreover, according to Origen, the Evangelist says *that have been accomplished*, because Christ did not carry out His bodily coming in mere appearance, as the heretics said, but, since He was the Truth, He truly went through with the business. And Luke shows his own disposition in saying *the things that have been accomplished among us*, that is, which have been shown most manifestly among us. For he had come to know these things by sure faith and reason, and wavered in nothing.

paras.t: Sicut tradiderunt nobis, id est, nobis dixerunt, nosque docuerunt, qui ab initio evangelicæ prædicationis Christi, ipsi viderunt corporalibus atque mentalibus oculis opera Christi magnifica, puta Apostoli, quibus loquitur Christus: Beati oculi qui vident quæ vos videtis. De quibus ait Joannes: Verbum caro factum est et habitavit in nobis, et vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre. Unde in exordio primæ suæ Canonicæ idem scribit: Quod fuit (inquit) ab initio, quod audivimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod perspeximus, et manus nostræ contrectaverunt de Verbo vitæ. — Sed huic obviare videtur, quod secundum Hieronymum, Lucas potissimum discipulus fuit Pauli, quemadmodum Marcus Petri; et in legenda Lucæ habetur, quod sicut Marcus ex informatione Petri, sic Lucas ex instructione Pauli, qui opera Christi non vidit, evangelium scripsit. Et respondendum, quod Lucas primo ab aliis Apostolis qui a principio prædicationis Christo adhæserunt, instructionem accepit; deinde Paulo exponente plenius est instructus. Hinc ait Theophilus: Veritatem, vel Paulo exponente, vel aliis Apostolis qui ab initio viderant, consecutus est. Insuper, juxta Bedam, non solum Lucas et Marcus, sed Matthæus quoque et Joannes, multa de infantia Salvatoris et pueritia ac genealogia ipsius aliis narrantibus didicerunt. — Rursus quæritur, si Lucas ex Apostolorum instructione evangelium scripsit, et similiter Marcus ex beati apostoli Petri informatione, quomodo ex inspiratione et eruditione Spiritus Sancti scripsisse feruntur? Et respondendum, quod Spiritus Sanctus infallibiliter eos in scribendo direxit, et adeptam eorum ab Apostolis aliis instructionem sua deifica illuminatione perfecit, certificavit et gubernavit, eosque ad scribendum induxit.
paras.en: [[1:2|According as they have delivered them unto us|Sicut tradiderunt nobis]], that is, told us and taught us, [[1:2|who from the beginning were eyewitnesses|qui ab initio ipsi viderunt]]: who from the beginning of Christ's gospel preaching themselves saw, with the eyes of the body and of the mind, the wonderful works of Christ; the Apostles, namely, to whom Christ says: [[Luke 10:23|Blessed are the eyes that see the things which you see|Beati oculi qui vident quæ vos videtis]]. Of whom John says: [[John 1:14|And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (and we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father|Verbum caro factum est et habitavit in nobis, et vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre]]. Hence at the opening of his first Canonical Epistle the same John writes: [[1 John 1:1|That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have handled, of the word of life|Quod fuit (inquit) ab initio, quod audivimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod perspeximus, et manus nostræ contrectaverunt de Verbo vitæ]]. — But against this there seems to be the fact that, according to Jerome, Luke was above all a disciple of Paul, as Mark was of Peter; and in the legend [that is, the account of his life read on his feast] of Luke we have it that, as Mark wrote his gospel from what Peter told him, so Luke wrote his from the instruction of Paul, who did not see the works of Christ. The answer is that Luke was first instructed by the other Apostles, who had cleaved to Christ from the beginning of His preaching; and afterwards was more fully instructed by Paul's exposition. Hence Theophilus [the edition's footnote reads *alias Theophylactus*: that is, Theophylact, whom Denis cites under this name] says: He attained the truth either by Paul's exposition or from the other Apostles, who had seen from the beginning. Moreover, according to Bede, not only Luke and Mark but Matthew and John also learned many things about the infancy, childhood and genealogy of the Saviour from what others told them. — Again it is asked: if Luke wrote his gospel from the Apostles' instruction, and Mark likewise from what blessed Peter the apostle told him, how are they said to have written by the inspiration and teaching of the Holy Ghost? The answer is that the Holy Ghost directed them infallibly in writing, and by His divine enlightenment perfected, made certain and governed the instruction they had received from the other Apostles, and moved them to write.

paras.t: Et ministri fuerunt sermonis, id est evangelicæ prædicationis, quam Christo jubente, et Spiritu Sancto implente, fideliter prædicaverunt: huicque prædicationi ministraverunt, in quantum ei subjecti fuerunt et ex Christi imperio eam prædicando aliis exhibuerunt. Hinc in Actibus Spiritus Sanctus effatur: Segregate (inquiens) mihi Paulum et Barnabam in opus ad quod assumpsi eos. Et Petrus testatur: Nobis præcepit Deus prædicare populo et testificari, quia Jesus Christus est qui constitutus est judex vivorum et mortuorum. Et Apostoli quoque dicunt: Nos vero orationi et ministerio verbi instantes erimus. Potest quoque de increato Dei Patris Verbo intelligi, cui ministraverunt Apostoli: de quo ad Hebræos Paulus, Vivus (inquit) est sermo Dei et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti; et non est ulla creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus.
paras.en: [[1:2|and ministers of the word|et ministri fuerunt sermonis]], that is, of the gospel preaching, which they preached faithfully at Christ's command and with the Holy Ghost filling them: and they ministered to this preaching inasmuch as they were subject to it, and by Christ's command set it forth to others in preaching it. Hence in the Acts the Holy Ghost speaks, saying: [[Acts 13:2|Separate me Saul and Barnabas, for the work whereunto I have taken them|Segregate … mihi Paulum … assumpsi eos]]. And Peter testifies: [[Acts 10:42|he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that it is he who was appointed by God to be judge of the living and of the dead|Nobis præcepit Deus prædicare populo et testificari, quia Jesus Christus est qui constitutus est judex vivorum et mortuorum]]. And the Apostles too say: [[Acts 6:4|But we will give ourselves continually to prayer and to the ministry of the word.|Nos vero orationi et ministerio verbi instantes erimus.]] It can also be understood of the uncreated Word of God the Father, to whom the Apostles ministered: of whom Paul says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 4:12|For the word of God is living and effectual and more piercing than any two edged sword|Vivus … est sermo … gladio ancipiti]]; [[Heb 4:13|Neither is there any creature invisible in his sight|et non est ulla creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus]].

paras.t: Visum est et mihi, id est, rationabile mihi apparuit tam ex inspiratione divina quam ex ratione humana. Consideravit etenim Lucas per propriam rationem, quod expediens esset a se evangelium scribi, in quo ab aliis prætermissa insererentur. Assecuto omnia a principio. Quod ait, Omnia a principio, referri potest ad participium, Assecuto; eritque sensus: Visum est mihi assecuto, id est, per cognitionem adepto omnia quæ Christus a principio suæ prædicationis fecit ac docuit, hoc est, universorum operum documentorumque Christi cognitionem adepto, tam per illuminationem divinam quam per Apostolorum informationem. Non quod simpliciter omnia in specie ac individuo facta et documenta Salvatoris aliquis Evangelistarum descripserit, sed omnia ad fidelium instructionem requisita, seu omnia in genere, vel quædam de omnibus, ut sit distributio pro generibus singulorum, non pro singulis generum: juxta quem modum ait Psalmista, Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo, narrabo omnia mirabilia tua; et in Actibus Lucas, Primum (inquit) quidem sermonem feci de omnibus, o Theophile, quæ cœpit Jesus facere et docere. Quod autem non simpliciter omnia, constat ex eo quod in Joanne legitur: Multa alia fecit Jesus, quæ si scribantur per singula, nec ipsum mundum arbitror posse capere eos qui scribendi sunt libros.
paras.en: [[1:3|It seemed good to me also|Visum est et mihi]], that is, it appeared reasonable to me, as much by divine inspiration as by human reason. For Luke considered by his own reason that it was expedient for a gospel to be written by him, in which things passed over by the others might be put in. [[1:3|having diligently attained to all things from the beginning|Assecuto omnia a principio]]. The words *all things from the beginning* can be referred to the participle *having attained*; and the sense will be: It seemed good to me, having attained, that is, having gained knowledge of, all that Christ did and taught from the beginning of His preaching; that is, having gained knowledge of all the works and teachings of Christ, as much by divine enlightenment as by what the Apostles told me. Not that any of the Evangelists described absolutely all the deeds and teachings of the Saviour, in every kind and every single instance, but all that is required for the instruction of the faithful; or all things by kind, or some things of every sort, so that the distribution is “for the kinds of individual things, not for the individuals of each kind” [a scholastic distinction: *all* here means something of every kind, not every single thing]: in the way in which the Psalmist says: [[Ps 9:2|I will give praise to thee, O Lord, with my whole heart: I will relate all thy wonders|Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo, narrabo omnia mirabilia tua]]; and Luke in the Acts: [[Acts 1:1|The former treatise I made, O Theophilus, of all things which Jesus began to do and to teach|Primum … quidem sermonem … facere et docere]]. That it is not absolutely all is clear from what we read in John: [[John 21:25|many other things which Jesus did which, if they were written every one, the world itself. I think, would not be able to contain the books that should be written|Multa alia fecit Jesus, quæ si scribantur per singula, nec ipsum mundum arbitror posse capere eos qui scribendi sunt libros]].

paras.t: Denique verba hæc, Omnia a principio, referri possunt ad id quod subditur, Diligenter ex ordine tibi scribere, ut sit sensus: Visum est et mihi assecuto, id est, Christum et Apostolos, potissimum Paulum, corporaliter ac spiritualiter imitato, vel saltem ipsos Apostolos, corporaliter etiam, non spiritualiter tantum, omnia Christi mysteria, verba et gesta, juxta sensum prætactum, a principio annuntiationis præcursoris Christi, vel a principio incarnationis Christi, diligenter: hoc enim exigit altitudo materiæ libri hujus et dignitas ejus de quo tractat volumen hoc, utpote excellentia Christi, de quo tanquam de vero Deo, non nisi circumspecte ac reverenter loquendum est; et ut Jeremias fatetur, Maledictus qui facit opus Dei negligenter: imo quanto diviniora, altiora ac salubriora sunt quæ scribuntur, tanto reverentialius diligentiusque scribenda sunt, non præcipitanter et intimorate, jactanter aut præsumptuose. Et ex ordine, id est ordinate, videlicet secundum ordinem seu processum rei gestæ: quod confert ad prolixitatem vitandam et ad intelligentiam clariorem habendam. Utque Apostolus loquitur, Quæ a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt. Sapientis enim est ordinare, atque in verbis, factis et scriptis se ordinate habere. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Omnia honeste et secundum ordinem fiant in vobis.
paras.en: Again, the words *all things from the beginning* can be referred to what follows, *diligently to write to thee in order*, so that the sense is: It seemed good to me also, having attained, that is, having followed Christ and the Apostles, above all Paul, bodily and spiritually, or at least the Apostles themselves bodily as well and not only spiritually, to write all the mysteries, words and deeds of Christ, in the sense touched on above, from the beginning of the annunciation of Christ's forerunner, or from the beginning of Christ's incarnation, [[1:3|diligently|diligenter]]: for this is demanded by the height of this book's matter and the dignity of Him of whom this volume treats, namely the excellence of Christ, of whom, as of the true God, one may speak only circumspectly and reverently; and as Jeremias declares, [[Jer 48:10|Cursed be he that doth the work of the Lord deceitfully|Maledictus qui facit opus Dei negligenter]] [Denis has *negligenter*, “negligently”, where the Vulgate has *fraudulenter*, “deceitfully”]. Nay, the more divine, lofty and saving the things written, the more reverently and diligently they must be written: not hastily and fearlessly, boastfully or presumptuously. [[1:3|in order|Et ex ordine]], that is, orderly, namely according to the order or course of what was done: which helps to avoid prolixity and to give a clearer understanding. And as the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:1|those that are ordained of God|Quæ a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt]]. For it belongs to the wise man to set in order, and to bear himself orderly in words, deeds and writings. Wherefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 14:40|let all things be done decently and according to order|Omnia honeste et secundum ordinem fiant]] among you.

paras.t: Tibi scribere, non solum ad tuam, sed ad omnium Christianorum utilitatem: sicut ait Dominus, Quod uni dico, omnibus dico; optime Theophile. Circa quod scribit Theophilus: Scribit autem ad Theophilum virum inclytum, fortassis et principem, quia quod dicit, Optime, dicebatur principibus atque præsidibus, sicut Paulus Festo præsidi dixit: Optime Feste. Contra quod arguit quidam, quia (ut dicit) talis modus loquendi proprius est ad prælatos, qui debent alios in bonitate excellere; iterum, non est verisimile quod omissis episcopis, quorum est alios informare, scripserit principi sæculari. Hæ autem instantiæ non procedunt. In Scripturis enim canonicis non invenitur, quod alicui prælato quis ita loquatur. Quod vero consuetudo fuerat Lucæ principibus sæcularibus taliter loqui, patet ex eo quod etiam in Actibus Lysias tribunus sic scribit principi tali: Optimo præsidi Felici, salutem. Præterea in primitiva Ecclesia sæculares principes erant communiter valde religiosi, ideo satis probabile est quod alicui tali scripserit ista. Eidem quoque Theophilo scripsit Actus Apostolorum. Porro Theophilus interpretatur amans Deum, vel amatus a Deo. Quisquis ergo amat Deum, vel ab eo amari se cupit, sibi putet hoc evangelium scriptum, et tanquam munus sibi a Deo donatum accipiat, sibique commendatum pignus conservet.
paras.en: [[1:3|to write to thee|tibi scribere]], not only for thy profit but for that of all Christians: as the Lord says, What I say to one, I say to all[[Mark 13:37||]]; [[1:3|most excellent Theophilus|optime Theophile]]. On which Theophilus [Theophylact] writes: He writes to Theophilus, a renowned man and perhaps also a prince, because the word he uses, *most excellent*, was said to princes and governors, as Paul said to Festus the governor: [[Acts 26:25|most excellent Festus|Optime Feste]]. Against this someone argues that (as he says) such a way of speaking is proper to prelates, who ought to excel others in goodness; and again, that it is not likely that, passing over the bishops, whose task it is to instruct others, he wrote to a secular prince. But these objections do not hold. For in the canonical Scriptures it is not found that anyone speaks so to a prelate. And that it was Luke's custom to speak in this way to secular princes is plain from the fact that in the Acts too Lysias the tribune writes thus to such a prince: [[Acts 23:26|to the most excellent governor, Felix, greeting|Optimo præsidi Felici, salutem]]. Besides, in the primitive Church secular princes were commonly very devout, so it is quite probable that he wrote these things to such a one. To the same Theophilus he also wrote the Acts of the Apostles[[Acts 1:1||]]. Now Theophilus is interpreted *loving God*, or *loved by God*. Whoever, then, loves God, or desires to be loved by Him, let him think this gospel written for himself, and receive it as a gift given him by God, and keep it as a pledge entrusted to him.

paras.t: Ut cognoscas eorum verborum, id est evangelicorum sermonum, de quibus eruditus es per Christi discipulos, vel sola instructione vocali, vel etiam per evangelia Matthæi et Marci jam scripta (quæ forsitan vidit, quamvis hoc certum non sit), veritatem, ut scilicet certius pleniusque instruaris de Christi verbis et factis atque mysteriis. Frequenter autem in Scripturis verbum pro facto seu re significata per verbum accipitur, ut dum in libris Regum loquitur Ezechias: Non fuit verbum in domo mea, quod non ostenderim eis.
paras.en: [[1:4|That thou mayest know the verity of those words|Ut cognoscas eorum verborum]], that is, of the gospel discourses, [[1:4|in which thou hast been instructed|de quibus eruditus es]] by the disciples of Christ, either by spoken instruction alone, or also through the gospels of Matthew and Mark already written (which perhaps he had seen, though this is not certain), [[1:4|the verity|veritatem]]: that is, so that thou mayest be more surely and more fully instructed about the words, deeds and mysteries of Christ. Now in the Scriptures *word* is often taken for the deed, or the thing signified by the word, as when Ezechias says in the books of Kings: There was not a *word* [that is, a thing] in my house which I have not shewn them[[Is 39:4||]] [the margin gives Is. xxxix, 2, 4, where Isaias has *verbum* in this sense at 39:2; in the books of Kings the passage is 4 Kings 20:15].

paras.t: Consequenter Lucas incipit narrationem. Fuit in diebus Herodis regis Judææ sacerdos quidam nomine Zacharias. Convenienter Lucas a præcursore Christi evangelium suum exorsus est: quia ex his quæ de Præcursore leguntur, fides non parum corroboratur, et ea quæ de Christi mirabilibus leguntur, credibiliora redduntur. Itaque tempore quo Herodes in Judæa regnabat, fuit hic Zacharias. Tres autem fuerunt Herodes de quibus fit mentio in Scripturis. Primus fuit Herodes de quo nunc sermo: qui dictus est Ascalonita, quia in Ascalone urbe Palæstinæ suum construxit palatium; qui necavit infantes. Secundus fuit filius ejus, dictus Herodes Antipas, qui Christum in passione derisit et decollavit Joannem. Tertius fuit Herodes Agrippa, qui Jacobum decapitavit, et Petrum incarceravit, atque ob suam superbiam ab angelo sancto percussus, vermibusque consumptus est. Tres quoque leguntur fuisse Zachariæ qui sancti fuerunt. Primus fuit Zacharias filius Joiadæ pontificis, de quo in libris Regum habetur. Secundus fuit Zacharias, unus duodecim Prophetarum, cujus liber sententiosissimus pulcherrimusque consistit. Tertius, de quo nunc agitur.
paras.en: Next, Luke begins the narrative. [[1:5|There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judea, a certain priest named Zachary|Fuit in diebus Herodis regis Judææ sacerdos quidam nomine Zacharias]]. Fittingly did Luke begin his Gospel with the Forerunner of Christ: for by what we read of the Forerunner faith is not a little strengthened, and what we read of the wonders of Christ is made the more credible. So this Zachary lived at the time when Herod reigned in Judea. Now there were three Herods of whom mention is made in the Scriptures. The first was the Herod spoken of here, who was called the Ascalonite, because he built his palace in Ascalon, a city of Palestine; it was he who slew the infants[[Matt 2:16||]]. The second was his son, called Herod Antipas, who mocked Christ in His passion[[Luke 23:11||]] and beheaded John[[Mark 6:27||]]. The third was Herod Agrippa[[Acts 12:1||]], who beheaded James[[Acts 12:2||]] and imprisoned Peter[[Acts 12:4||]], and for his pride was struck by a holy angel and consumed by worms[[Acts 12:23||]]. We read also of three Zacharies who were holy. The first was Zacharias the son of Joiada the high priest, of whom we read in the books of Kings[[2 Par 24:20||]] [the margin refers to 2 Paralipomenon 24, where his story is told]. The second was Zacharias, one of the twelve Prophets, whose book is most rich in weighty sayings and most beautiful. The third is the one now treated of.

paras.t: Apte autem de primo Herode jam verbum fit, ut tacite demonstretur, quod sub illius imperio Christus veraciter venit. Jacob enim in Genesi prophetavit, quod dominatu Judæorum ad alienigenam prorsus translato, nasceretur Messias: Non auferetur, inquit, sceptrum de Juda, et dux de femore ejus, donec veniat qui mittendus est, et ipse erit exspectatio gentium. Herodes autem de genere exstitit Idumæorum, et ab imperatore Romano factus est rex Judæorum. Qui quum ingressi fuissent terram promissionis, primo regebantur per judices usque ad Saul exclusive, seu Samuelem inclusive; deinde per reges usque ad captivitatem Babylonicam. Postea per pontifices regebantur usque ad Hyrcanum regem simul atque pontificem: quo ab Herode primo occiso, regnavit Herodes, et Judæi de cetero sub alienigenarum principatu fuerunt, sicut nunc usque sunt.
paras.en: Fittingly, too, mention is made here of the first Herod, to show tacitly that it was under his rule that Christ truly came. For Jacob prophesied in Genesis that the Messias would be born when the dominion of the Jews had passed wholly to a foreigner: [[Gen 49:10|The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda, nor a ruler from his thigh, till he come that is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of nations|Non auferetur, inquit, sceptrum de Juda, et dux de femore ejus, donec veniat qui mittendus est, et ipse erit exspectatio gentium]]. Now Herod was of the race of the Idumeans, and was made king of the Jews by the Roman emperor. The Jews, when they had entered the land of promise, were governed first by judges[[Judg 2:16||]], up to Saul exclusive, or Samuel inclusive[[1 Kings 10:24||]]; then by kings, up to the Babylonian captivity[[4 Kings 25:1||]]. Afterwards they were governed by high priests, up to Hyrcanus, who was at once king and high priest: and when he had been slain by the first Herod, Herod reigned, and from then on the Jews were under the rule of foreigners, as they are to this day.

paras.t: De vice Abia, id est de semine Abia sacerdotis, et loco ejus in templo ministrans, seu ei in ministerio templi succedens, prout tunc patribus sacerdotibus mortuis, filii loco illorum in templi ministerio successerunt. Porro, ut in libro Paralipomenon legitur, David rex cultum cupiens ampliare divinum, constituit viginti quatuor sacerdotes principales de totidem familiis sacerdotalibus ex semine Aaron natis. Tunc enim inventæ sunt sedecim familiæ de Eleazaro filio Aaron natæ, octo autem de Ithamar filio Aaron: de quarum qualibet ordinavit David unum summum sacerdotem, qui toti suæ præesset familiæ, atque in sua ministraret hebdomada; ceciditque sors octava super Abia, cui linealiter successit hic Zacharias. Verumtamen omnibus istis præfuit unus summus sacerdos, qui pontifex dicebatur, princepsque sacerdotum.
paras.en: [[1:5|of the course of Abia|De vice Abia]], that is, of the seed of Abia the priest, and ministering in his place in the temple, or succeeding him in the ministry of the temple; for at that time, when the fathers who were priests died, their sons succeeded in their place in the ministry of the temple. For, as we read in the book of Paralipomenon, King David, wishing to enlarge the worship of God, appointed twenty-four chief priests from as many priestly families born of the seed of Aaron[[1 Par 24:3||]]. For there were then found sixteen families descended from Eleazar the son of Aaron, and eight from Ithamar the son of Aaron[[1 Par 24:4||]]: and over each of them David set one chief priest, to be over his whole family and to minister in his own week; and the eighth lot fell upon Abia[[1 Par 24:10||]], to whom this Zachary succeeded in direct line. Over all of these, however, was one supreme priest, who was called the pontiff, and the prince of the priests.

paras.t: Et uxor illi de filiabus Aaron, et nomen ejus Elisabeth. Uterque itaque, scilicet Zacharias et Elisabeth, Aaronitæ fuerunt. Et quamvis in veteri fuerit Testamento præceptum, ut viri de suis tribubus acciperent conjuges, et econtra, ne sortium distributio seu hereditatum divisio confunderetur in jubilæo, id est quinquagenario anno, in quo omnis hereditas ad priorem ac proprium possessorem redibat; hoc tamen in tribu sacerdotali non servabatur, sed homines tribus illius aliarum tribuum hominibus poterant matrimonialiter copulari. Non enim ut ceteri hereditatem habebant, sed Dominus Deus fuit eorum hereditas, quia de ejus sacrificiis sustentabantur, nec certa loca hereditaria habuerunt, nisi ad habitandum, pecoraque alenda: sic nempe Jeremias propheta atque sacerdos, agrum se habuisse testatur. In hoc ergo dignitas Præcursoris ostenditur, quod utroque parente Aaroniticæ sacerdotalisque exstitit stirpis, imo filius sacerdotis principalis in sua familia. Sacerdotalis quippe et regia tribus tunc principales fuerunt, et matrimonialiter copulari consueverunt, quemadmodum a principio uxor Aaron fuit Elisabeth, filia Aminadab de tribu Juda. Verumtamen Thomas allegat Theophilum hic dicentem: Non permittebatur Zacharias de alia tribu accipere uxorem.
paras.en: [[1:5|and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name Elizabeth|Et uxor illi de filiabus Aaron, et nomen ejus Elisabeth]]. So both of them, Zachary and Elizabeth, were of the line of Aaron. And although it was commanded in the Old Testament that men should take wives from their own tribes, and the converse[[Num 36:7||]], lest the distribution of the lots, or the division of the inheritances, be confounded in the jubilee, that is, the fiftieth year, in which every inheritance returned to its former and proper owner[[Lev 25:10||]], this was nevertheless not observed in the priestly tribe: the men of that tribe could be joined in marriage with those of the other tribes. For they did not have an inheritance as the rest did, but the Lord God was their inheritance[[Deut 18:2||]][[Jos 13:14||]], since they lived on His sacrifices; nor did they have fixed places of inheritance, except for dwelling in and for feeding their cattle[[Jos 21:2||]]. So Jeremias, prophet and priest, testifies that he had a field[[Jer 32:9||]]. Herein, then, the dignity of the Forerunner is shown: that on both his parents' side he was of the priestly stock of Aaron, and was indeed the son of the chief priest of his family. For the priestly and the royal tribes were then the principal ones, and were accustomed to intermarry, as from the beginning the wife of Aaron was Elizabeth, the daughter of Aminadab, of the tribe of Juda[[Ex 6:23||]]. Yet Thomas cites Theophilus [that is, Theophylact] as saying here: Zachary was not permitted to take a wife from another tribe.

paras.t: Erant autem justi, triplici utique justitia, scilicet vitæ, et veritatis, ac virtutis, ambo: ita quod non solum carnis propagatione, sed et virtutum imitatione soboles Aaron erant, de quo fertur in Psalmo: Aaron sanctum Domini; ante Deum, id est, vere, non ficte, sed divino judicio tales erant: quales et nunc omnes sunt qui Deo in omnibus placere desiderant, ejusque jugiter in cunctis gloriam et honorem intendunt. Sunt autem quamplurimi ante homines justi, sicut hypocritæ, et omnes inanis gloriæ cupidi, simulatores et callidi, qui provocant iram Dei: de quibus ait Salvator, Receperunt mercedem suam.
paras.en: [[1:6|And they were both just|Erant autem justi]], with a threefold justice, namely of life, of truth and of virtue, both of them; so that they were the offspring of Aaron not only by descent in the flesh but also by imitation of his virtues, of whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 105:16|Aaron the holy one of the Lord|Aaron sanctum Domini]]. [[1:6|before God|ante Deum]], that is, truly, not feignedly: they were such by the judgment of God; as are all those now who desire to please God in all things, and continually seek His glory and honour in everything. But there are very many who are just before men, as hypocrites, and all who are [[Gal 5:26|desirous of vain glory|inanis gloriæ cupidi]], [[Job 36:13|dissemblers and crafty men|simulatores et callidi]], who provoke the wrath of God; of whom the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:2|they have received their reward|Receperunt mercedem suam]].

paras.t: Sed quum scriptum sit in libro Psalmorum, Non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens; et Job dicat, Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo; itemque Sapiens, Non te justifices ante Deum: quomodo quisquam mortalium justus dicitur ante Deum? Et respondendum, quod hominem viatorem ante Deum justificari, justumve esse aut dici, intelligi potest tripliciter: Primo, quod pura sit ejus justitia, nihil habens culpæ admixtum: et sic non justificatur ante Deum omnis vivens in carne mortali, quia in multis offendimus omnes, et quasi pannus menstruatæ sunt universæ justitiæ nostræ, ut dicit Isaias. Secundo, quod comparatione æquitatis divinæ justus dicatur: et hoc rursus stare non valet, juxta illud Job, Numquid homo Dei comparatione justificabitur? Tertio, quod a Deo justus judicetur, et coram eo justus sit, secundum modum humanæ conditioni proportionatum: sicque electi et omnes in gratia exsistentes, aliquo modo justi sunt ante Deum. Proprie tamen justi dicuntur notabiliter virtuosi, præsertim homines perfecti et sancti seu divini atque heroici, quorum corda in affectum bonitatis et æquitatis conversa, omni se custodia coram Deo custodiunt: de quibus loquitur Christus, Beati mundo corde.
paras.en: But since it is written in the book of Psalms, [[Ps 142:2|in thy sight no man living shall be justified|Non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens]], and Job says, [[Job 9:2|man cannot be justified, compared with God|Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo]], and likewise the Wise man, [[Ecclus 7:5|Justify not thyself before God|Non te justifices ante Deum]], how is any mortal called just before God? The answer is that for a man still on the way [*viator*: one still in this life, not yet in the homeland] to be justified before God, or to be just, or to be called just, can be understood in three ways. First, that his justice be pure, having no fault mixed in with it: and in this way no man living in mortal flesh is justified before God, because [[Jas 3:2|in many things we all offend|in multis offendimus omnes]], and [[Is 64:6|all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman|quasi pannus menstruatæ sunt universæ justitiæ nostræ]], as Isaias says. Secondly, that he be called just in comparison with the divine equity: and this again cannot stand, according to that word of Job, [[Job 4:17|Shall man be justified in comparison of God|Numquid homo Dei comparatione justificabitur]]? Thirdly, that he be judged just by God, and be just before Him in a measure proportioned to the human condition: and in this way the elect, and all who are in grace, are in some manner just before God. Properly, however, those are called just who are notably virtuous, above all men perfect and holy, or godlike and heroic, whose hearts, turned to the love of goodness and equity, keep themselves before God [[Prov 4:23|with all watchfulness|omni se custodia]]; of whom Christ says: [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart|Beati mundo corde]].

paras.t: Insuper, decuit valde Christi præcursorem de sanctis nasci parentibus, ut testificatio ejus de Christo, suæque sanctitatis conversatio, ex sanctitate parentum suorum credibiliores judicarentur. Proles namque frequenter parentum sequitur bonitatem. Unde et nunc parentum Joannis describitur sanctitas, ut ipse Joannes quasi hereditario jure videatur assecutus justitiam.
paras.en: Moreover, it was most fitting that the forerunner of Christ should be born of holy parents, so that his testimony to Christ, and the holy manner of his life, might be judged the more credible from the holiness of his parents. For children often follow the goodness of their parents. Hence the holiness of John's parents is described here, so that John himself may seem to have come into justice as by right of inheritance.

paras.t: Incedentes, id est, ad beatitudinem festinantes, propinquantes, seu spiritualiter transeuntes, in omnibus mandatis, observando præcepta Decalogi quæ vocantur moralia. Recte autem ait, In omnibus, quia non sufficit aliqua observare, si unum prætermittatur, secundum illud Jacobi: Quicumque totam legem impleverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus. Et justificationibus, id est in observantiis præceptorum judicialium, quæ erant quædam determinationes præceptorum moralium quoad modum servandi justitiam circa proximos, in observantiis quoque præceptorum cærimonialium, quæ erant determinationes præceptorum moralium quantum ad modum ac ritum colendi Deum. Sine querela, id est irreprehensibiliter: ita quod nullus contra eos movit, movereve potuit rationabiliter querelam seu accusationem, quia etsi quotidie venialiter peccaverunt, de hoc tamen quotidie satisfecerunt: implentes illud Apostoli, Nemini dantes ullam offensionem, ut non vituperetur ministerium nostrum. Unde ad Philippenses hortatur: Omnia (inquiens) facite sine murmurationibus, ut sitis sine querela et simplices filii Dei, in medio nationis pravæ atque perversæ. Sic de Judith in libro ejus scriptum est, quod erat in omnibus nominatissima, nec erat qui malum loqueretur de ea.
paras.en: [[1:6|walking|Incedentes]], that is, hastening towards beatitude, drawing near to it, or passing onward in spirit, [[1:6|in all the commandments|in omnibus mandatis]], by keeping the precepts of the Decalogue, which are called moral. And rightly he says *in all*, because it is not enough to keep some of them if one is left aside, according to that word of James: [[Jas 2:10|whosoever shall keep the whole law, but offend in one point, is become guilty of all|Quicumque totam legem impleverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus]]. [[1:6|and justifications|Et justificationibus]], that is, in the observance of the judicial precepts, which were certain determinations of the moral precepts as to the manner of keeping justice towards one's neighbours; and also in the observance of the ceremonial precepts, which were determinations of the moral precepts as to the manner and rite of worshipping God. [[1:6|without blame|Sine querela]], that is, irreprehensibly: so that no one raised, or could reasonably raise, a complaint or accusation against them; for though they sinned venially every day, yet every day they made satisfaction for it, fulfilling that word of the Apostle: [[2 Cor 6:3|Giving no offence to any man, that our ministry be not blamed|Nemini dantes ullam offensionem, ut non vituperetur ministerium nostrum]]. Hence he exhorts the Philippians: [[Phil 2:14|do ye all things without murmurings|Omnia facite sine murmurationibus]], he says, [[Phil 2:15|That you may be blameless and sincere children of God|ut sitis sine querela et simplices filii Dei]], [[Phil 2:15|in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation|in medio nationis pravæ atque perversæ]]. So it is written of Judith in her book that [[Jdt 8:8|she was greatly renowned among all|erat in omnibus nominatissima]], and [[Jdt 8:8|neither was there any one that spoke an ill word of her|nec erat qui malum loqueretur de ea]].

paras.t: Denique sunt quædam virtutes morales, quibus homo proximis suis acceptus redditur et suavis, videlicet: mansuetudo, humilitas, patientia, modestia, liberalitas, eutrapelia. Unde Augustinus ait in regula: In omnibus motibus vestris, nihil sit quod cujusquam offendat adspectum, sed quod vestram deceat sanctitatem. Itaque, qui inter alios conversatur, non per indiscretum rigorem se illis exhibeat onerosum, imo socialiter se gerat ac dulciter, salvo semper ordine æquitatis. Hinc Seneca loquitur: Sic te geras sapienter, ut nemo te habeat tanquam asperum, nec spernat ut vilem. Qui autem ita non agunt, ab Aristotele duri et agrestes vocantur. Siquidem durior hominum æquitas querimoniam provocat, secundum Ambrosium. Ad hanc pietatem specialiter dare se debent, qui ex naturali inclinatione in irascibili abundantes, semper ad æquitatis rigorem feruntur.
paras.en: Further, there are certain moral virtues by which a man is made acceptable and pleasant to his neighbours: namely meekness, humility, patience, modesty, liberality and *eutrapelia* [Aristotle's name for the virtue of pleasant and seemly playfulness in company]. Hence Augustine says in his Rule: In all your movements let there be nothing that may offend the eye of anyone, but only what befits your holiness. So let one who lives among others not make himself burdensome to them by indiscreet rigour, but let him bear himself sociably and gently, always saving the order of equity. Hence Seneca says: So bear yourself wisely that no one may think you harsh, nor despise you as mean. Those who do not act so are called hard and boorish by Aristotle. For the harsher equity of men provokes complaint, according to Ambrose. To this kindliness those especially should give themselves who, abounding by natural inclination in the irascible power, are always carried towards the rigour of equity.

paras.t: Porro, in verbis his paucis, Zacharias et Elisabeth magnifice commendantur, et in verbo abbreviato continetur sensus exuberans. Tanta namque fuit eorum justitia, ut jugum illud legis (quod adeo grave fuit, ut de ipso Petrus testetur, quia nec nos nec patres nostri illud portare potuimus: quibus verbis præcipua difficultas, non absoluta impossibilitas observandi insinuatur) plene portasse probentur; fueruntque similes Josue, de quo legitur: Non præteriit Josue de universis mandatis Domini, ne unum quidem verbum. Qui ergo Zachariam ejusque conjugem appetit imitari, impleat illud Apostoli: Providentes bona, non tantum coram Deo, sed coram omnibus hominibus. — Præterea, secundum Ambrosium: Quum mandatis cœlestibus obedimus, in eis incedimus; dum autem congrue judicamus, justificationes Domini tenere videmur.
