So from shame, or bashfulness, Elizabeth hid herself five months, that is, until the most blessed Virgin Mary should conceive, and Elizabeth's child, leaping for joy, should prophesy, as Origen explains.

paras.t: Porro, hoc loco ostendit Ambrosius, homines quosdam incontinentes, feminas impregnatas et gravidas cognoscere non erubescentes, esse pecoribus irrationabiliores ac turpiores. Sunt enim pecora, quæ muto quodam opere quasi loquuntur generandi sibi studium esse, non desiderium coeundi. Siquidem ubi semel gravem sibi senserint alvum, jam concubitum non admittunt, nec amantis lasciviam, sed curam parentis assumunt. Porro homines nec conceptis fetibus, nec Deo parcunt; illos contaminant, hunc exasperant. Ad cohibendam petulantiam tuam, manus tui Creatoris in utero fetum formantis adverte. Ille operatur ibidem, et tu uteri illius secretum incestas libidine: vel pecudem imitare, vel Deum verere. — Postremo, ex hoc loco Ambrosius et Beda eliciunt, quanta cura fuerit verecundiæ Sanctis: quia et ipsa Elisabeth de re bona ac licita in tantum erubuit, quod quinque se mensibus occultavit, eo quod res quæ sibi acciderat, apud ignorantes speciem habere potuit mali. Nempe, ut ait Ambrosius, unicuique officio præscripta est ætas, et quod uno tempore decet, alio tempore non decet: suntque tempora quædam præscripta conjugio, quando dare operam liberis procreandis decorum sit, dum anni vigent, et spes prolis exsistit; ubi vero matura senectus successerit, pudor est gestare indicia coitus, quamvis legitimi, gravarique onere alienæ ætatis, et tumescere alvum non sui temporis fructu.
paras.en: Further, Ambrose shows on this passage that certain incontinent men, who do not blush to know women who have conceived and are with child, are more unreasoning and more shameful than the beasts. For there are beasts which by a kind of mute action all but say that what they care for is begetting, not the desire of coupling. For once they have felt the womb grow heavy, they no longer admit intercourse, nor the wantonness of the lover, but take up the care of the parent. But men spare neither the offspring conceived nor God: they defile the one and provoke the other. To restrain thy wantonness, consider the hands of thy Creator forming the child in the womb. He is at work there, and thou defilest the secret of that womb with lust: either imitate the beast, or fear God. — Lastly, Ambrose and Bede draw from this passage how great a care the Saints had for modesty: for Elizabeth herself blushed so much over a thing good and lawful that she hid herself five months, because what had happened to her could have had the appearance of evil among those who did not know. For, as Ambrose says, to every duty its age is assigned, and what is fitting at one time is not fitting at another: and there are certain times assigned to marriage, when it is seemly to give oneself to the begetting of children, while the years are vigorous and there is hope of offspring; but when ripe old age has come, it is a shame to carry the signs of intercourse, even lawful intercourse, and to be burdened with a load belonging to another age, and for the womb to swell with fruit out of its season.

1.title: […] In mense autem sexto, missus est angelus Gabriel
1.title_en: […] “And in the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent”
1.note: The first line of this article's heading is unreadable in the scan's OCR (PDF 403); only its last words, In mense autem sexto, missus est angelus Gabriel, are given.

paras.t: Præcursoris annuntiatione et conceptione descriptis, tanquam quibusdam præambulis, nunc Salvatoris annuntiatio atque conceptio describuntur. Tanta siquidem miraculorum excellentia Præcursorem Deus ornavit in sua annuntiatione, nativitate, ut testimonia ejus de Christo credibiliora consisterent: quæ et ideo describuntur, ut quæ de Christo leguntur, certius firmiusque credantur. In mense autem sexto a conceptione Joannis, qui conceptus dicitur circa finem Septembris. Christus autem circa finem Martii, scilicet vicesima quinta die ejus, nuntiatus, conceptus et passus est, secundum Bedam. Martius vero a Septembri est sextus, non computando minutias ultimæ partis Septembris, scilicet octo ultimos dies ipsius, infra quos Joannes conceptus est: qui et hic non computantur, quia consuetudo Scripturæ est, non facere vim in minutiis numerorum ac temporum. Missus est angelus Gabriel a Deo in civitatem Galilææ, cui nomen Nazareth, ad virginem desponsatam viro, cui nomen erat Joseph, de domo David, et nomen virginis Maria. Summum atque dignissimum descripturus mysterium sacer Evangelista, videlicet unigeniti Filii Dei beatissimam ac benedictissimam incarnationem, omnia ordinatissime ac distincte prosequitur, cunctaque plane elucidat, ut eadem audientes sive legentes, illa quæ gesta sunt quasi præsentia oculis animi proponamus, atque cum summa attentione, devotione, distinctione, singula quæque pensemus; quatenus in recordatione tam ineffabilis beneficii Dei super nos, cordialiter accendamur, intime Deo regratiemur, et nostræ salvationis modum atque historiam mente pura ac jucundissima recolamus. Itaque, circa descriptionem incarnationis Filii Dei, primo commemorat nuntium, quod non homo aut vates, sed angelus fuit: quem etiam nominatim expressit, quod Gabriel exstitit, de quo jam dictum est. Qui in veteri Testamento legitur Danieli apparuisse; cui superior angelus, scilicet Michael princeps tunc Synagogæ, locutus est: Gabriel, fac intelligere istum, scilicet Danielem, visionem. De quo Gabriele Daniel ait: Quumque adhuc orarem, ecce vir Gabriel cito volans tetigit me in hora sacrificii vespertini. Hunc angelum docet Evangelista immediate missum a Deo uno ac trino, non (ut fieri solet) ab angelo superiori, quemadmodum Zacharias propheta accidisse testatur: Ecce angelus qui loquebatur in me, egrediebatur, et alius angelus egrediebatur in occursum ejus, et dixit ad eum: Curre et loquere ad puerum istum. Missum, inquam, in civitatem Galilææ nomine Nazareth. Per quod illud Isaiæ de Christo prædictum monstratur impletum: Nazaræus de radice ejus ascendet. Sic enim Hebraica continet veritas, sicque allegat Matthæus: pro quo Hieronymus transtulit, Flos de radice ejus ascendet. Apte quoque in Galilæa, non in Judæa, nuntiatus est Christus, ad designandum quod Christus relicta Judæa, transmigraturus fuit ad gentes, convertendo illas ad fidem per apostolicam prædicationem. Galilæa etenim, transmigratio interpretatur. Denique, missus est ad virginem desponsatam viro nomine Joseph. Cur autem de virgine desponsata voluerit Christus nasci, multæ rationes traduntur: quæ quia in omnium commentariis leguntur, prætermitto, quasdam brevissime solum tangendo, videlicet: ne pudicissima Virgo de fornicatione diffamaretur, et ne Christus de fornicaria natus diceretur. Itemque, ne Judæi eum juste contempsisse quasi illegitime genitum viderentur; et ut diabolus minorem haberet occasionem æstimandi quod Jesus esset Messias, eo quod de conjuge viri esset exortus, quem noverat de virgine nasciturum. Postremo, ne virgo Maria tanquam adultera lapidaretur, quia et de sacerdotali fuit prosapia. Puella quippe illius prosapiæ fornicans, tanquam adultera lapidabatur, ut patet in Levitico. Nomen quoque virginis fuit Maria: quæ interpretatur maris stella, quoniam ipsa luce a se prodeunte seu nata mundum hunc illustravit. Maria quoque interpretatur amarum mare. Ipsa nempe non solum in Christi passione, sed et ante frequenter, amaritudine maternæ compassionis, angustiæ, et timoris fuit repleta, sicut et infra habetur: Tuam ipsius animam pertransibit gladius. Sicut enim amarissime torquebatur, videns Filium crucifigi, sic frequentissime affligebatur, considerando hunc crucifigendum, atque videndo persecutiones ipsius. Rursus, Maria interpretatur domina: et ipsa utique est cæli regina, domina mundi, quoniam Genitrix Dei. Fuit autem sponsus Virginis castissimus Joseph, de domo, id est semine, tribu, seu familia, David: de qua tribu fuit etiam Virgo beata. Viri enim mulieribus suæ tribus matrimonialiter jungebantur: præsertimque feminæ in parentum hæreditate succedentes, non poterant nubere nisi viris suæ tribus, ne sortium distributio confunderetur. Virgo autem gloriosa unica fuit suo patri: propter quod ei in hæreditate successit.
paras.en: The announcement and conception of the Forerunner having been described as a kind of preamble, now the announcement and conception of the Saviour are described. For God adorned the Forerunner with such excellence of miracles in his announcement and birth that his testimony of Christ might be the more credible: and they are described for this reason, that what we read of Christ may be believed the more surely and firmly. [[1:26|And in the sixth month|In mense autem sexto]] from the conception of John, who is said to have been conceived about the end of September. Christ, however, was announced, conceived and suffered about the end of March, namely on its twenty-fifth day, according to Bede. And March is the sixth month from September, not counting the odd days of the last part of September, namely its last eight days, within which John was conceived: and these are not counted here, because it is the custom of Scripture not to insist on small fractions of numbers and times. [[1:26|the angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee, called Nazareth|Missus est angelus Gabriel a Deo in civitatem Galilææ, cui nomen Nazareth]], [[1:27|To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David: and the virgin's name was Mary.|ad virginem desponsatam viro, cui nomen erat Joseph, de domo David, et nomen virginis Maria.]] Being about to describe the highest and worthiest mystery, namely the most blessed incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, the holy Evangelist goes through everything in the best order and distinctly, and makes all things plain, so that, hearing or reading them, we may set before the eyes of the mind what was done as though it were present, and weigh each thing with the greatest attention, devotion and care; so that in remembering so unspeakable a benefit of God towards us we may be kindled in heart, thank God inwardly, and call to mind the manner and story of our salvation with a pure and most joyful mind. So, in describing the incarnation of the Son of God, he first records the messenger, who was not a man or a prophet but an angel: whom he also names, namely Gabriel, of whom something has already been said. He is read in the Old Testament to have appeared to Daniel; to whom a higher angel, namely Michael, then the prince of the Synagogue, said: [[Dan 8:16|Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision|Gabriel, fac intelligere istum, scilicet Danielem, visionem]], that is, Daniel. Of which Gabriel Daniel says: [[Dan 9:21|As I was yet speaking in prayer, behold the man, Gabriel|Quumque adhuc orarem, ecce vir Gabriel]] [[Dan 9:21|flying swiftly, touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice|cito volans tetigit me in hora sacrificii vespertini]]. The Evangelist teaches that this angel was sent immediately by God, one and three, not (as usually happens) by a higher angel, as the prophet Zacharias testifies to have happened: [[Zach 2:3|And behold the angel that spoke in me went forth, and another angel went out to meet him.|Ecce angelus qui loquebatur in me, egrediebatur, et alius angelus egrediebatur in occursum ejus]] [[Zach 2:4|And he said to him: Run, speak to this young man|et dixit ad eum: Curre et loquere ad puerum istum]]. Sent, I say, into a city of Galilee named Nazareth. By which is shown to be fulfilled that saying of Isaias foretold of Christ: A Nazarene shall rise up out of his root. For so the Hebrew truth has it, and so Matthew cites it[[Matt 2:23||]]: for which Jerome translated, [[Is 11:1|a flower shall rise up out of his root|Flos de radice ejus ascendet]]. Fittingly too was Christ announced in Galilee, not in Judea, to signify that Christ, leaving Judea, would pass over to the gentiles, converting them to the faith by the preaching of the Apostles. For Galilee means “passing over”. Further, He was sent to a virgin espoused to a man named Joseph. Many reasons are given why Christ willed to be born of an espoused virgin: which, since they are read in everyone's commentaries, I pass over, touching only on some very briefly, namely: that the most chaste Virgin should not be defamed as having committed fornication, and that Christ should not be said to be born of a fornicatress. Also, that the Jews should not seem to have despised Him justly as born out of wedlock; and that the devil should have less occasion to think that Jesus was the Messias, since He had sprung from the wife of a man, whereas the devil knew that the Messias would be born of a virgin. Lastly, that the virgin Mary should not be stoned as an adulteress, since she was also of priestly stock. For a girl of that stock who committed fornication was stoned as an adulteress, as is plain in Leviticus[[Lev 21:9||]][[Deut 22:21||]]. The name of the virgin, too, was Mary: which means “star of the sea”, because by the light that went forth or was born from her she lit up this world. Mary also means “bitter sea”. For not only in Christ's passion but often before it she was filled with the bitterness of a mother's compassion, anguish and fear, as is said below: [[Luke 2:35|thy own soul a sword shall pierce|Tuam ipsius animam pertransibit gladius]]. For as she was most bitterly tormented seeing her Son crucified, so she was very often afflicted by considering that He was to be crucified, and by seeing His persecutions. Again, Mary means “lady”: and she indeed is the queen of heaven, the lady of the world, since she is the Mother of God. The spouse of the Virgin was the most chaste Joseph, of the house, that is, the seed, tribe or family, of David: of which tribe was the blessed Virgin too. For men were joined in marriage to women of their own tribe; and especially women who succeeded to their parents' inheritance could marry only men of their own tribe, lest the distribution of the lots should be confused[[Num 36:6||]]. And the glorious Virgin was her father's only child: which is why she succeeded him in the inheritance.

paras.t: Præterea contemplandum quomodo Christus in omnibus quæ abjecta videntur et humiliora elegit. Unde non in Jerusalem civitate metropoli, sed in oppido Nazareth concipi voluit, ut non humana potestate, sed divina virtute, christiana religio agnoscatur firmata ac introducta. Sed et ipsa Galilæa tam despecta fuit Judæis, ut principes dicerent Nicodemo: Scrutare Scripturas, et vide quia a Galilæa non surgit Propheta. Hoc insuper mirabile fuit, quod mundo persuaderi potuit hanc virginem esse, quæ tot annis viro cohabitavit. Denique istud dignationis erat eximiæ, quod Unigenitus Dei eodem angelo annuntiante concipi voluit, quo annuntiante conceptus fuit ejus præcursor, et quod non aliquem aut aliquos de summo ordine angelorum ad tanti mysterii denuntiationem transmisit. Ex quo etiam S. Thomas et alii multi concludunt, quod superiorum ordinum angeli ad exterius ministerium nunquam mittuntur, quum angelus hujus summæ rei nuntiator de choro Archangelorum exstiterit. Quum enim Unigenitus Patris æterni in mundum descenderit, nostramque naturam assumpserit, ut in omnibus verbo et opere humilitatem doceret, ac per eam nos ad veram salutem reverti oportere instrueret, non supremi ordinis agmina ad suam incarnationem misit denuntiandam, sed uno ac consueto nuntio fuit contentus.
paras.en: Moreover we should contemplate how Christ chose in all things what seems lowly and more humble[[1 Cor 1:27||]]. So He willed to be conceived not in the chief city, Jerusalem, but in the town of Nazareth, so that the Christian religion might be known to have been established and brought in not by human power but by divine might. And Galilee itself was so despised by the Jews that the chief men said to Nicodemus: [[John 7:52|Search the scriptures, and see that out of Galilee a prophet riseth not|Scrutare Scripturas, et vide quia a Galilæa non surgit Propheta]]. This, besides, was wonderful: that the world could be persuaded that she was a virgin who had lived so many years with a husband. Further, it was of singular condescension that the Only-begotten of God willed to be conceived at the announcement of the same angel at whose announcement His forerunner had been conceived, and that He did not send one or more of the highest order of angels to announce so great a mystery. From this St Thomas and many others also conclude that the angels of the higher orders are never sent on outward ministry, since the angel who announced this greatest thing was of the choir of the Archangels. For since the Only-begotten of the eternal Father came down into the world and took our nature, so as to teach humility in all things by word and deed, and to instruct us that we must return by it to true salvation, He did not send the hosts of the highest order to announce His incarnation, but was content with one ordinary messenger.

paras.t: Postremo S. Bernardus circa hunc locum sentire videtur, quod angeli sancti mysterium Incarnationis ignoraverunt, ita quod consilium Dei super humani generis salvatione per Verbi incarnationem, nulli patuerit angelorum priusquam Gabrieli hæc legatio dominicæ annuntiationis committeretur. Et id quidem etiam quibusdam Catholicis tempore Bernardi displicuit; et Hugo de S. Victore hinc scripsit Bernardo, ut de hoc intentionem suam plenius aperiret. Cui sanctus Pater rescripsit plenissime ac diserte: Primo, quod verbum illud non asserendo protulerit. Secundo, quod et si asserendo id protulisset, nihilo minus stare posset: quia intelligi posset, non de ipso mysterio seu ejus substantia secundum se, nam hoc Prophetis dudum per angelos fuerat revelatum; sed de mysterio Incarnationis, quantum ad aliquas ejus conditiones, certasque circumstantias, puta quantum ad locum, tempus, modum, personam, ut quod de hac Virgine et hac hora Verbum incarnaretur. Itaque advertendum, quod (ut S. Thomas determinat) mysterium Incarnationis, videlicet quod Unigenitus Dei humanam esset assumpturus naturam, cunctis angelis a principio felicitatis eorum innotuit quoad substantiam mysterii, atque in generali, non autem quantum ad determinatas conditiones, sive in speciali. Omnia namque angelorum ministeria ad incarnationem Verbi potissimum ordinantur: omnes autem sunt administratorii spiritus. Idcirco de isto mysterio omnes a principio communiter sunt edocti; sed postea, quantum ad circumstantias ejus, in ipsius distinctiori notitia profecerunt, imo, ut septimo capitulo Cælestis hierarchiæ divinus et sanctus Dionysius scribit, a Christo tempore ascensionis inde plenius sunt instructi. Sicque potest salvari, quod super Genesim ad litteram loquitur Augustinus: Sic erat absconditum istud mysterium, ut nec angelis innotuerit. Insuper, juxta Gregorium, congrue ad Mariam Gabriel mittitur, qui Dei fortitudo interpretatur, quoniam Christum Dei virtutem et sapientiam, qui potestates superavit aerias, nuntiavit jam incarnandum. Rursus, secundum Bedam, angelum ad Virginem a Deo mitti condecuit, ad denuntiandum Salvatoris adventum, quoniam in principio serpens a diabolo mittebatur ad feminam ad inducendum mundi interitum. Præterea, Christum totius puritatis et integritatis auctorem, corruptorumque et confractorum reformatorem, decuit nasci de virgine integerrima atque purissima, et ut designaret membra sua de virgine Ecclesia spiritualiter nascitura seu regeneranda. Postremo, secundum Hieronymum, bene ad virginem mittitur angelus, quoniam angelis semper cognata est virginitas, et in carne præter carnem vivere, non terrena et humana, sed cælestis atque angelica vita est.
paras.en: Lastly, St Bernard seems to hold on this passage that the holy angels did not know the mystery of the Incarnation, so that God's counsel for the salvation of mankind through the incarnation of the Word was open to none of the angels before this embassy of the Lord's annunciation was entrusted to Gabriel. And this displeased some Catholics even in Bernard's time; and Hugh of St Victor wrote to Bernard about it, asking him to explain his meaning more fully. To whom the holy Father wrote back most fully and clearly: first, that he had not put forward that word as an assertion; secondly, that even if he had put it forward as an assertion, it could still stand: because it could be understood not of the mystery itself or its substance in itself, for this had long since been revealed to the Prophets through angels, but of the mystery of the Incarnation as to some of its conditions and particular circumstances, for example as to place, time, manner and person: as that the Word would be made flesh of this Virgin and at this hour. So it is to be noted that (as St Thomas determines) the mystery of the Incarnation, namely that the Only-begotten of God would take human nature, was known to all the angels from the beginning of their blessedness as to the substance of the mystery and in general, but not as to its particular conditions, that is, in detail. For all the ministries of the angels are ordered above all to the incarnation of the Word: they are all [[Heb 1:14|ministering spirits|administratorii spiritus]]. Therefore all were taught about this mystery in common from the beginning; but afterwards, as to its circumstances, they advanced in a more distinct knowledge of it; indeed, as the divine and holy Dionysius writes in the seventh chapter of the Celestial Hierarchy, they were more fully instructed in it by Christ at the time of the ascension. And so what Augustine says on Genesis to the letter can be upheld: This mystery was so hidden that it was not known even to the angels. Moreover, according to Gregory, Gabriel, whose name means “strength of God”, is fittingly sent to Mary, because he announced that Christ, [[1 Cor 1:24|the power of God and the wisdom of God|Dei virtutem et sapientiam]], who overcame the powers of the air, was now to become incarnate. Again, according to Bede, it was fitting that an angel should be sent by God to the Virgin to announce the Saviour's coming, since in the beginning a serpent was sent by the devil to the woman to bring on the ruin of the world[[Gen 3:1||]]. Further, it was fitting that Christ, the author of all purity and integrity and the restorer of what was corrupt and broken, should be born of a virgin most untouched and most pure, and that He should so signify that His members were to be born, or reborn, spiritually of the virgin Church. Lastly, according to Jerome, an angel is rightly sent to a virgin, because virginity is ever akin to the angels; and to live in the flesh beyond the flesh is a life not earthly and human, but heavenly and angelic.

paras.t: Et ingressus angelus ad eam: non dubium quin in locum secretum, ubi illa sanctissima contemplationi et orationi vacavit, forte in thalamo seu oratorio; estque probabile, quod tunc devotissime pro totius humani generis salvatione et Christi adventu oravit; dixit, cum ingenti reverentia ac humili apparatu sacratissimam Virginem Dei sui mox Genitricem futuram salutans, imo et dignitatem ejus admirans: Ave, gratia plena, id est, gratia habituali gratum faciente, ejusque charismatibus ac donis, virtutibus quoque ei annexis, præeminenter repleta. Fuit ergo jam septem donis Spiritus Sancti excellenter valde ornata, virtutibus theologicis mirabiliter decorata, virtutibus cardinalibus ac moralibus eleganter fulcita, variis quoque donis gratiæ gratis datæ polita, atque in omnibus his protinus multo amplius adimplenda. Dominus, Trinitas superbenedicta, tecum, tanto singularius, quanto gratiosius. Quo enim gratia Virginis exstitit plenior, eo consistentia Dei in ea fuit singularior atque præclarior. Dominus vero Unigenitus Dei mox fuit cum ea, et in ea singularissimo ac eminentissimo modo futurus, utpote corporaliter quieturus in medio virgineorum viscerum ejus, verus et unicus Filius ejus. Benedicta tu in mulieribus, id est, præ omnibus amplius benedicta, quia magis electa, majoribus gratiæ donis referta, et quodammodo quasi infinita dignitate mox sublimanda in Filii Dei conceptione. Etenim esse comparentalem Patri æterno, verum Deum habere Filium, illum concipere, parere et fovere, a quo Spiritus Sanctus verus Deus procedit, omnium creatorem salvatoremque unicum fructum filialem habere, nonne quodammodo infinita est dignitas? Rursus, esse matrem et virginem, nec hoc tantum, sed esse matrem talis tantique filii et virginem, nonne tanto exstat sublimius, quanto et singularius? Si magna perfectio exstat causalitas, quanta perfectio est esse causam seu genitricem causæ causarum? Et mater utique causa est filii. Porro quum benedictio Dei sit collatio munerum ejus, et multiplicatio eorumdem, tanto benedictior est Maria, quanto majora ac singulariora divinitus sortita est dona. Ipsa quoque tam magnifice ab angelo salutatur, non solum ob id quod tunc fuit, sed ob id quod mox erat futura, quodque in prædestinatione fuit æterna.
paras.en: [[1:28|And the angel being come in|Et ingressus angelus]] [[1:28|unto her|ad eam]]: no doubt into a secret place, where that most holy one gave herself to contemplation and prayer, perhaps her chamber or oratory; and it is likely that she was then praying most devoutly for the salvation of the whole human race and the coming of Christ; [[1:28|said|dixit]], greeting with great reverence and lowly bearing the most sacred Virgin who was soon to be the Mother of his God, and indeed wondering at her dignity: [[1:28|Hail, full of grace|Ave, gratia plena]], that is, pre-eminently filled with habitual, sanctifying grace [gratia gratum faciens: the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God], with its gifts and graces, and with the virtues joined to it. So she was already most excellently adorned with the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, wonderfully beautified with the theological virtues, finely upheld by the cardinal and moral virtues, polished with various gifts of grace freely given [gratia gratis data: graces given for the good of others, such as prophecy], and was soon to be filled much more fully with all of these. [[1:28|the Lord|Dominus]], the most blessed Trinity, [[1:28|is with thee|tecum]], the more singularly, the more graciously. For the fuller the Virgin's grace, the more singular and glorious was God's dwelling in her. And the Lord, the Only-begotten of God, was soon with her, and was to be in her in a most singular and eminent way, namely resting bodily in the midst of her virgin womb, her true and only Son. [[1:28|blessed art thou among women|Benedicta tu in mulieribus]], that is, blessed more than all, because more chosen, filled with greater gifts of grace, and soon to be raised in some way to an almost infinite dignity in the conception of the Son of God. For to share parenthood with the eternal Father, to have true God for one's Son, to conceive, bear and cherish Him from whom the Holy Ghost, true God, proceeds, and to have the Creator and only Saviour of all as the fruit of one's womb: is this not in some way an infinite dignity? Again, to be mother and virgin, and not only this, but to be mother of such and so great a son and a virgin: is this not the more sublime, the more singular it is? If causality is a great perfection, how great a perfection is it to be the cause, or mother, of the cause of causes? And a mother is surely a cause of her son. Further, since God's blessing is the bestowing of His gifts and their multiplying, Mary is the more blessed, the greater and more singular the gifts she has received from God. She is also greeted so magnificently by the angel not only for what she then was, but for what she was soon to be, and what she was in eternal predestination.

paras.t: Quæ quum audisset, turbata est in sermone ejus, hoc est in tam excellenti, inopinata, et antea nusquam audita salutatione angelica. Turbatio ista nec imperfectionis fuit, nec culpæ, sed admirationis ac verecundiæ virginalis. Fuitque vehemens quædam immutatio, concussio sive commotio potentiæ affectivæ. Nempe quum Virgo sacratissima in oculis suis minima esset, ac laudabiliter pudorata, vehementissime de tanto suo mirabatur præconio, seque laudari, et cunctis præferri mulieribus erubuit atque obstupuit, eo utique amplius, quo minus de se tale aliquid suspicabatur aut sentiebat. Quo enim fuerit homo humilior, eo sua laudatio et exaltatio sibi ipsi mirabilior, et sæpe gravior quoque videtur. Hujuscemodi sancta turbatio, excellentiori etiam modo fuit in Christo, juxta illud Joannis: Jesus ut vidit Mariam, scilicet Magdalenam, plorantem, infremuit spiritu, et turbavit se ipsum. Et alio loco ipsemet protestatur: Nunc, inquiens, anima mea turbata est. Est autem et alia turbatio immoderata et vitiosa, quieti pacique mentis contraria, rationis impeditiva, quæ longe fuit a Christo et Virgine prælecta: imo de hac turbatione loquendo, laborare debemus habere animum imperturbatum. Præterea considerandum, quod sancta Maria in sermone angeli fertur turbata, non in visione ipsius, quia (ut dicitur) solita erat conspicere angelos. Verumtamen aliqui probabiliter adstruunt, quod angelus vice hac apparuit ei cum lumine multo præclariore, apparatu ac habitu venustiore, secundum quod magnitudo causæ suæ legationis exegit, ideoque aliqualiter turbata in ejus apparitione exstiterat. Et cogitabat qualis esset ista salutatio. Non dubitavit quin esset vera, et vere angelico ore prolata. Non enim caruit gratiosa Puella gratia discretionis spirituum. Cogitabat tamen qualis esset, quid prætenderet, quo tenderet, cur exhibita esset: et id fuit prudentiæ, quod sic cogitavit. Nec statim respondit, tam magnifica salutatione reputans se indignam, quia consideravit se secundum id quod fuit in se, et quod habuit ex se. Juxta quem modum ait Apostolus, Non sum dignus vocari Apostolus: et, Venit Jesus Christus peccatores salvos facere, quorum ego primus sum: nihilo minus ait, Nihil mihi conscius sum; et, Nihil minus feci ab his qui sunt supra modum Apostoli: illud sibi et propriæ voluntati, istud Deo et gratiæ ejus attribuens. De eadem enim re secundum diversas ejus considerationes, diversa feruntur judicia.
paras.en: [[1:29|Who having heard, was troubled at his saying|Quæ quum audisset, turbata est in sermone ejus]], that is, at so excellent, unlooked-for and never before heard angelic greeting. This trouble was neither of imperfection nor of fault, but of wonder and virginal modesty. It was a certain strong change, shaking or stirring of the affective power. For since the most sacred Virgin was least in her own eyes, and praiseworthily modest, she wondered most vehemently at so great a praise of herself, and blushed and was amazed at being praised and set above all women; the more so, the less she suspected or felt any such thing of herself. For the humbler a man is, the more wonderful, and often the heavier, his own praise and exaltation seem to him. A holy trouble of this kind was in Christ too, in a more excellent way, according to that saying of John: Jesus, when He saw Mary (namely Magdalen) weeping, [[John 11:33|groaned in the spirit and troubled himself|infremuit spiritu, et turbavit se ipsum]]. And in another place He Himself declares: [[John 12:27|Now is my soul troubled.|Nunc, inquiens, anima mea turbata est]] But there is another trouble, immoderate and sinful, contrary to the quiet and peace of the mind and hindering reason, which was far from Christ and from the chosen Virgin: indeed, speaking of this trouble, we must strive to have an untroubled mind. Moreover, it should be considered that holy Mary is said to have been troubled at the angel's saying, not at the sight of him, because (as is said) she was used to seeing angels. Yet some probably maintain that the angel appeared to her this time with a far brighter light and a fairer bearing and dress, as the greatness of the cause of his embassy required, and that she was therefore somewhat troubled at his appearing. [[1:29|and thought with herself what manner of salutation this should be|Et cogitabat qualis esset ista salutatio]]. She did not doubt that it was true and truly spoken by an angel's mouth. For the gracious Maiden did not lack the grace of the discerning of spirits. Yet she thought what kind of greeting it was, what it meant, where it tended, why it had been given: and it was the part of prudence to think thus. Nor did she answer at once, deeming herself unworthy of so magnificent a greeting, because she considered herself according to what she was in herself and what she had from herself. In which manner the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 15:9|not worthy to be called an apostle|Non sum dignus vocari Apostolus]]; and, [[1 Tim 1:15|Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the chief|Venit Jesus Christus peccatores salvos facere, quorum ego primus sum]]; and yet he says, [[1 Cor 4:4|I am not conscious to myself of anything|Nihil mihi conscius sum]]; and, [[2 Cor 12:11|I have no way come short of them that are above measure apostles|Nihil minus feci ab his qui sunt supra modum Apostoli]]: attributing the former to himself and his own will, the latter to God and His grace. For different judgements are made about the same thing according to different ways of considering it.

paras.t: Et ait angelus ei: Ne timeas, Maria. Nominatim pudicissimam Virginem exprimit, ejus teneritudini, turbationi, virgineoque pudori quasi compatiens, et blande ac familiariter alloquendo eamdem consolans. Quamvis ergo timor et pudor Mariæ non fuerunt culpabiles, imo laudabiles: tamen abjiciendi monentur, ut meliores divinioresque actus succedant, videlicet contemplatio cælestium secretorum, gratiarum actio pro eisdem, tranquillissima quoque serenitas mentis in Deo. Cur autem timere non habeat, subditur: Invenisti enim gratiam apud Deum, hoc est, Deo accepta et placita ei es inventa, pietatem quoque et gratiam quam ab eo quærebas, adepta es, imo et amplius multum. Ecce rem novam et magnam, concipies in utero, hoc est, fecundaberis sine virginalis reseratione signaculi, operante in te virtute Spiritus Sancti, et paries filium tui ipsius Creatorem, omniumque filiorum hominum Salvatorem; et vocabis nomen ejus Jesum. Cujus appellationis Christi rationem angelus Joseph exposuit, dicens: Ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum a peccatis eorum. Jesus enim, salvator, salus, aut salutaris interpretatur. Hinc de sua nuncupatione ait Filius de Patre per Isaiam: Dominus ab utero vocavit me, de ventre matris meæ recordatus est nominis mei. Denique, hujus Jesu Domini nostri re et nomine figura fuerunt, Jesus filius Nave, alias Josue et Osee dictus; itemque Jesus filius Josedec pontifex. Nam ille filios Israel in terram promissionis induxit, iste in spiritualibus præfuit: ita et Jesus nunc spiritualiter præsidens cordibus electorum, eos in terram Ecclesiæ militantis ac triumphantis perducit.
paras.en: [[1:30|And the angel said to her: Fear not, Mary|Et ait angelus ei: Ne timeas, Maria]]. He names the most modest Virgin, as though feeling for her tenderness, her trouble and her virgin shame, and comforting her by speaking to her gently and familiarly. So although Mary's fear and shame were not blameworthy, indeed were praiseworthy, yet she is told to put them away, so that better and more godly acts may follow, namely the contemplation of heavenly secrets, thanksgiving for them, and a most tranquil serenity of mind in God. Why she has no cause to fear is added: [[1:30|for thou hast found grace with God|Invenisti enim gratiam apud Deum]], that is, thou hast been found acceptable and pleasing to God, and thou hast obtained the mercy and grace thou didst seek from Him, and indeed much more. Behold a new and great thing: [[1:31|Behold thou shalt conceive in thy womb|Ecce concipies in utero]], that is, thou shalt be made fruitful without the breaking of the virginal seal, the power of the Holy Ghost working in thee, [[1:31|and shalt bring forth a son|et paries filium]], thy own Creator and the Saviour of all the sons of men; [[1:31|and thou shalt call his name Jesus|et vocabis nomen ejus Jesum]]. The reason for this name of Christ the angel explained to Joseph, saying: [[Matt 1:21|For he shall save his people from their sins.|Ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum a peccatis eorum.]] For Jesus means saviour, salvation, or saving. Hence of His naming the Son says of the Father through Isaias: [[Is 49:1|The Lord hath called me from the womb, from the bowels of my mother he hath been mindful of my name.|Dominus ab utero vocavit me, de ventre matris meæ recordatus est nominis mei.]] Further, figures of this Jesus our Lord, in deed and name, were Jesus the son of Nave, also called Josue and Osee[[Ecclus 46:1||]][[Num 13:17||]], and also Jesus the son of Josedec, the high priest[[Agg 1:1||]]. For the one led the children of Israel into the land of promise, the other presided in spiritual things: so too Jesus, now presiding spiritually over the hearts of the elect, leads them into the land of the Church militant and triumphant.

paras.t: Hic erit magnus. Nam secundum divinitatem, ab æterno fuit, incommutabiliter est, indeficienterque erit magnus, non mole, sed perfectione, potestate, et dignitate; atque tam magnus, ut dicat Psalmista: Magnus Dominus et laudabilis nimis, et magnitudinis ejus non est finis. Porro secundum naturam humanam, non differt ab aliis hominibus quantum ad essentialia speciei; sed per dona gratiæ hypostaticamque unionem suæ humanitatis cum Verbo, tantæ est magnitudinis, dignitatis, et perfectionis, ut major sit toto universo seu omni creatura intellectuali ac inferiori. Unde ob hanc magnitudinem etiam in utero matris, vir fuit, juxta illud Jeremiæ: Novum creavit Dominus super terram: Femina circumdabit virum. Et Filius Altissimi vocabitur, non adoptivus ut ceteri, sed naturalis, coæternus, unicus, coæqualis, juxta illud: Dominus dixit ad me, Filius meus es tu; et rursus, Ex utero ante luciferum genui te. Unde tam Patrem quam Filium ineffabilem esse Salomon docens ait: Quod nomen ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti? Nec obstat, quod nunc vocari jubetur Dei Filius Jesus. Non enim Salomon ideo illa ait, quod Pater et Filius omni careant nomine, sed quia deficit omne nomen, prout nos illud comprehendere possumus, a superbenedicta et superviventi et superessentiali dignitate Patris ac Filii, defectu immenso. Nec aliud de majestate Spiritus Sancti quis sentiat. Et dabit illi, secundum humanam naturam, Dominus Deus, Pater æternus, seu tota Trinitas adoranda, cujus indivisa sunt dona ac opera, sedem, hoc est regiam dignitatem ac potestatem, David patris ejus, hoc est, quam David in typo habebat. Quidquid enim potestatis et eminentiæ fuit in David, multo sublimius datum est Christo homini, secundum quod ait: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo et in terra. Hinc Christus vere rex Israel fuit, plenariamque potestatem super Judæos accepit in spiritualibus ac corporalibus, quamvis ea quantum ad temporalem ac corporalem præsidentiam usus non fuerit. Propter quod dixit Pilato: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Et quum vellent eum Judæi facere regem, fugit. Et regnabit in domo Jacob, hoc est in cordibus verorum ac electorum Israelitarum, non solum corporaliter a Jacob patriarcha descendentium, sed omnium quoque ejus virtutes sequentium, in æternum: puta, in via per dona gratiæ et per suos vicarios præsidet Christus fidelibus, et regnat in eis qui suæ obediunt legi, in patria autem per dona gloriæ et per se ipsum. Et regni ejus non erit finis. Sive regnum dicatur plebs fidelis, puta Ecclesia, quæ frequenter regnum cælorum vocatur, sive dominium Christi in ea, sive triumphans Ecclesia, vel præsidentia Christi in ipsa: constat quod regni ejus non erit finis. Nam status Ecclesiæ militantis usque in finem mundi durabit: quo hic finem sumente, transferentur electi ad patriam, in qua finis divinæ gubernationis non erit. Hæc eadem per Isaiam prædicta noscuntur: Super solium (inquit) David, et super regnum ejus sedebit, ut confirmet illud in judicio et justitia, amodo et usque in sempiternum. Etenim de Christi principatu super Judæos, Ezechiel, Jeremias, Zacharias, ceterique Prophetæ concorditer sunt locuti.
paras.en: [[1:32|He shall be great|Hic erit magnus]]. For according to the Godhead He was great from eternity, is great unchangeably, and will be great unfailingly, not in bulk but in perfection, power and dignity; and so great that the Psalmist says: [[Ps 144:3|Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised: and of his greatness there is no end.|Magnus Dominus et laudabilis nimis, et magnitudinis ejus non est finis.]] And according to human nature He does not differ from other men as to what is essential to the species; but through the gifts of grace and the hypostatic union of His humanity with the Word He is of such greatness, dignity and perfection that He is greater than the whole universe, that is, than every intellectual and lower creature. Hence, because of this greatness, even in His mother's womb He was a man, according to that saying of Jeremias: [[Jer 31:22|the Lord hath created a new thing upon the earth: A WOMAN SHALL COMPASS A MAN.|Novum creavit Dominus super terram: Femina circumdabit virum.]] [[1:32|and shall be called the Son of the Most High|Et Filius Altissimi vocabitur]], not adopted like the rest, but natural, co-eternal, only and co-equal, according to that saying: [[Ps 2:7|The Lord hath said to me: Thou art my son|Dominus dixit ad me, Filius meus es tu]]; and again, [[Ps 109:3|from the womb before the day star I begot thee|Ex utero ante luciferum genui te]]. Hence Solomon, teaching that both the Father and the Son are unspeakable, says: [[Prov 30:4|what is his name, and what is the name of his son, if thou knowest?|Quod nomen ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti?]] Nor is it against this that the Son of God is now commanded to be called Jesus. For Solomon does not say this because the Father and the Son lack every name, but because every name, as we can grasp it, falls immeasurably short of the more than blessed, more than living and more than essential dignity of the Father and the Son. Nor should anyone think otherwise of the majesty of the Holy Ghost. [[1:32|And the Lord God shall give unto him|et dabit illi Dominus Deus]], according to His human nature, the Lord God, the eternal Father, or the whole adorable Trinity, whose gifts and works are undivided, [[1:32|the throne of David his father|sedem David patris ejus]], that is, the royal dignity and power which David had in figure. For whatever power and eminence there was in David was given far more sublimely to Christ as man, as He says: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth.|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo et in terra.]] So Christ was truly king of Israel, and received full power over the Jews in spiritual and bodily things, although He did not use it as to temporal and bodily rule. Which is why He said to Pilate: [[John 18:36|My kingdom is not of this world.|Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo.]] And when the Jews wished to make Him king, He fled[[John 6:15||]]. [[1:32|and he shall reign in the house of Jacob|Et regnabit in domo Jacob]], that is, in the hearts of the true and elect Israelites, not only those descended bodily from the patriarch Jacob but all who follow his virtues, [[1:32|for ever|in æternum]]: that is, on the way Christ presides over the faithful by the gifts of grace and by His vicars, and reigns in those who obey His law; and in the fatherland, by the gifts of glory and by Himself. [[1:33|And of his kingdom there shall be no end.|Et regni ejus non erit finis.]] Whether the kingdom be called the faithful people, that is, the Church, which is often called the kingdom of heaven, or Christ's lordship in it, or the Church triumphant, or Christ's rule in it, it is certain that of His kingdom there shall be no end. For the state of the Church militant will last until the end of the world; and when it ends here, the elect will be carried over to the fatherland, in which there will be no end of the divine government. These same things are known to have been foretold by Isaias: [[Is 9:7|he shall sit upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom; to establish it and strengthen it with judgment and with justice, from henceforth and for ever|Super solium (inquit) David, et super regnum ejus sedebit, ut confirmet illud in judicio et justitia, amodo et usque in sempiternum]]. Indeed, of Christ's rule over the Jews Ezechiel[[Ezech 34:1||]], Jeremias, Zacharias and the other Prophets spoke with one voice [the margin gives further references here, of which only Ezech. xxxiv is legible in the OCR].

paras.t: Dixit autem Maria ad angelum: Quomodo fiet istud, quod scilicet Filium Dei concipiam, quoniam virum non cognosco, hoc est, nequaquam cognoscere decrevi, et vovi quantum in me est? Jam enim, ut dicunt doctores, virginitatem promisit, tamen sub honestissima conditione, utpote nisi Deus aliter de ea disponeret. Aliqui vero affirmant, quod antequam desponsaretur, habuit virginitatis custodiam in proposito et affectu, non tamen promisit; postea autem desponsata Joseph simile habenti propositum, simul cum ipso votum emisit. Quærit autem de modo, non de facto secundum se, quia non dubitavit, sed de virginitatis observatione sollicita, sciscitata est operis modum. Verumtamen, teste Ambrosio, legit Maria illud Isaiæ, Ecce virgo concipiet; modum vero non legit. Ex quo concluditur, quod litterata fuit, et in lege atque Prophetis humano quoque studio erudita. Nam et Origenes testatur, quod legis habebat scientiam.
paras.en: [[1:34|And Mary said to the angel: How shall this be done|Dixit autem Maria ad angelum: Quomodo fiet istud]], namely that I should conceive the Son of God, [[1:34|because I know not man?|quoniam virum non cognosco]] That is, I have resolved never to know one, and have vowed it as far as lies in me. For, as the doctors say, she had already promised virginity, yet under a most honourable condition, namely unless God should dispose otherwise of her. But some affirm that before she was espoused she held the keeping of virginity in purpose and desire, but did not promise it; and that afterwards, espoused to Joseph, who had a like purpose, she made the vow together with him. She asks about the manner, not about the deed in itself, because she did not doubt; but, anxious for the keeping of her virginity, she asked the manner of the work. Yet, on Ambrose's testimony, Mary had read that saying of Isaias, [[Is 7:14|Behold a virgin shall conceive|Ecce virgo concipiet]]; but she had not read the manner. From which it is concluded that she was lettered, and learned in the law and the Prophets by human study too. For Origen also testifies that she had knowledge of the law.

paras.t: Et respondens angelus, dixit ei: Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in te: hoc est, non naturali via, non virili concursu, non potestate angelica, sed superveniente, id est desuperveniente et supra id quod nunc contulit tibi, tunc abundantius influente Spiritu Sancto, concipies, quia ipse te fecundabit, ex tuis purissimis sanguinibus corpus Verbo Dei aptando, formando, et subito organizando: quemadmodum per Zachariam ait, Ego exculpam sculpturam ejus. Unde ad innuendum quod Christus de matre sit editus, viro eam non fecundante, sed virtute cælesti in ea agente, scriptum est in Isaia: Ascendet coram eo sicut virgultum, et sicut radix de terra sitienti. Quod autem ibidem loquatur ad litteram Isaias de Christo, certum est omni capitulum illud rite pensanti. Et virtus Altissimi, hoc est omnipotens Deus Pater obumbrabit tibi, id est, suam potestatem immensam tuæ capacitati contemperabit, ut ejus influentiam ferre queas. Itaque non secundum plenitudinem suæ claritatis immensam tibi irradiabit, sed velut umbram suæ resplendentiæ causans in te, effectum suæ potestatis exercebit in te proportionabiliter ad tuam declivitatem, faciendo in te immediate per se, quod in aliis efficit per viri causalitatem seu formativam virtutem. Verba hæc ab aliis multipliciter exponuntur, sed quæ in omnium commentis satis leguntur, præterire decrevi. Quod autem Spiritus Sanctus superveniat non locum mutando, sed influendo, ac operando, certissimum reor. Insuper, innotescit ex his, quod multi sint plenitudinis gratiæ gradus. Nam et Virgo beata ante hæc verba, dicta est gratia plena: nihilo minus in conceptione Filii Dei maxime aucta est gratia Dei in ea, in tantum ut tunc fomes dicatur omnino exstinctus in ea, qui et ante ita fuerat debilitatus, quod nunquam in culpabilem surrexerit motionem. Attamen nunc præcipue sermo est de collatione gratiæ gratis datæ, videlicet maternitatis Dei seu maternæ fecunditatis in Virgine, quantum ad Christum. Quemadmodum autem prophetia et apostolatus, ita et ista materna fecunditas, donum est gratiæ gratis datæ. Propter quod, juxta Augustinum, beatior fuit Maria Christum concipiendo mente quam corpore, et ista corporalis conceptio sine illa spirituali ei non profuisset. Postremo, plenitudo, perfectio, atque immensitas, soli Deo competunt absolute et proprie, creaturis vero comparative, improprie, particulariter, in certoque genere. Ideoque et quod nascetur ex te sanctum, id est Christus ex te nasciturus: qui secundum divinitatem substantialiter sanctus est, et sanctitas ipsa, atque immensa sanctitatis superessentialis essentia; secundum naturam quoque assumptam majoris est sanctitatis, quam omnes pariter prædestinati; vocabitur Filius Dei: sicut nunc dictum est, Hic erit magnus, et Filius Altissimi vocabitur. Itaque ex tam divina et supernaturali conceptione Christi, innotescit fidelibus quod ipse sit Filius Dei, cui soli talis servabatur conceptio. Fonti etenim puritatis, et confractorum reparatori, corruptorumque integratori, purissima debebatur conceptio, nativitasque mundissima, ut Matris integritatem et puritatem non minueret, sed sacraret et confirmaret, quatenus ante partum, in partu, et post partum intacta consisteret, clausa atque mundissima. Præterea, quum in verbis inductis superbenedicta Trinitas distincte exprimatur ab angelo, clarum est Virginem sapientem, etiam ante hanc angelicam allocutionem, habuisse summæ Trinitatis fidem expressam, ac distinctam notitiam. Alioqui, quid angelus verbis istis insinuaret, non intellexisset; sed dicere potuisset, quod in Actibus quidam responderunt Apostolo sciscitanti, Si Spiritum Sanctum accepistis, credentes? Sed neque si Spiritus Sanctus est, audivimus.
paras.en: [[1:35|And the angel answering, said to her: The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee|Et respondens angelus, dixit ei: Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in te]]: that is, thou shalt conceive not by the way of nature, not by the coming together of a man, not by an angel's power, but by the Holy Ghost coming upon thee, that is, coming down from above, and flowing in more abundantly than in what He has now bestowed on thee; for He will make thee fruitful, fitting, forming and at once organizing a body for the Word of God from thy most pure blood: as He says through Zacharias, [[Zach 3:9|I will grave the graving thereof|Ego exculpam sculpturam ejus]]. Hence, to hint that Christ was born of a mother with no man making her fruitful, but with heavenly power working in her, it is written in Isaias: [[Is 53:2|he shall grow up as a tender plant before him, and as a root out of a thirsty ground|Ascendet coram eo sicut virgultum, et sicut radix de terra sitienti]]. And that Isaias there speaks literally of Christ is certain to anyone who rightly weighs that whole chapter. [[1:35|and the power of the Most High|Et virtus Altissimi]], that is, almighty God the Father, [[1:35|shall overshadow thee|obumbrabit tibi]], that is, will temper His immeasurable power to thy capacity, so that thou canst bear its inflowing. So He will not shine on thee with the immeasurable fulness of His brightness, but, causing as it were a shadow of His splendour in thee, will work the effect of His power in thee in proportion to thy lowliness, doing in thee immediately by Himself what in others He does through the causality, or forming power, of a man. These words are expounded by others in many ways, but since these are read sufficiently in everyone's commentaries, I have decided to pass them over. That the Holy Ghost comes upon her not by changing place but by flowing in and working I hold most certain. Moreover, it is known from this that there are many degrees of fulness of grace. For the blessed Virgin was called full of grace before these words: and yet in the conception of the Son of God the grace of God in her was increased to the utmost, so much so that the fomes [the tinder of sin, the inclination to evil left by original sin] is said to have been then wholly extinguished in her, which before had been so weakened that it never rose to a blameworthy movement. However, the talk here is chiefly of the bestowing of a grace freely given, namely the divine motherhood, or motherly fruitfulness, in the Virgin with respect to Christ. For like prophecy and apostleship, this motherly fruitfulness is a gift of grace freely given. That is why, according to Augustine, Mary was more blessed in conceiving Christ in mind than in body, and that bodily conception would not have profited her without the spiritual one. Lastly, fulness, perfection and immensity belong absolutely and properly to God alone, but to creatures comparatively, improperly, partially and in a certain kind. [[1:35|And therefore also the Holy which shall be born of thee|Ideoque et quod nascetur ex te sanctum]], that is, Christ who is to be born of thee: who according to the Godhead is substantially holy, and holiness itself, and the immeasurable more than essential being of holiness; and according to the nature He took is of greater holiness than all the predestined together; [[1:35|shall be called the Son of God|vocabitur Filius Dei]]: as was just said, [[1:32|He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High|Hic erit magnus, et Filius Altissimi vocabitur]]. So from so divine and supernatural a conception of Christ it is made known to the faithful that He is the Son of God, for whom alone such a conception was reserved. For to the fountain of purity, the restorer of the broken and the healer of the corrupt, a most pure conception and a most clean birth were due, such as would not lessen His Mother's integrity and purity but hallow and confirm it, so that before the birth, in the birth and after the birth she remained untouched, closed and most pure. Moreover, since in the words given the most blessed Trinity is distinctly expressed by the angel, it is clear that the wise Virgin, even before this address of the angel, had explicit faith and distinct knowledge of the most high Trinity. Otherwise she would not have understood what the angel meant by these words, but could have said what some in the Acts answered the Apostle when he asked, [[Acts 19:2|Have you received the Holy Ghost since ye believed? But they said to him: We have not so much as heard whether there be a Holy Ghost.|Si Spiritum Sanctum accepistis, credentes? Sed neque si Spiritus Sanctus est, audivimus.]]

paras.t: Consequenter, ut Mariæ credulitas augeatur, anima exhilaretur, devotio inflammetur, sicque ardentissima, jucundissima ac devotissima mente consentiat, atque concipiat Unigenitum Dei, proponit ei angelus sanctus exemplum, ut mirabilis conceptio futura, per conceptionem mirabilem factam approbetur, et caritativa Puella suæ cognatæ beneficiis congratuletur. Ecce Elisabeth cognata tua, et ipsa concepit filium in senectute sua, quamvis duplex habuerit impedimentum, scilicet senectutis, naturalisque sterilitatis; et hic mensis, scilicet Martius, in quo tibi appareo, est sextus illi, ex quo concepit, quæ vocatur sterilis: quia jamdudum sic vocabatur, nec usus sic eam vocandi fuit abolitus; quia non erit impossibile apud Deum omne verbum: hoc est, quidquid sermone significatur, Deus potest implere, si contradictionem non implicet, illudque facere, potestatis sit magis quam infirmitatis. Unde, quod Deus in sua natura non potest peccare, infirmari, comedere, currere, moveri, dormire, potestatis est, non infirmitatis. Huic verbo consonat illud Jeremiæ: Domine Deus, non erit tibi difficile omne verbum. Quum enim potestas Dei sit infinita, omnipotens utique est, et quidquid voluerit, potest in instanti peragere, nec potest in tot aut tanta, quin possit infinite in plura atque majora.
paras.en: Next, so that Mary's belief might be increased, her soul gladdened and her devotion kindled, and so that she might consent with a most ardent, joyful and devout mind and conceive the Only-begotten of God, the holy angel sets an example before her, so that the wonderful conception to come might be confirmed by a wonderful conception already accomplished, and the loving Maiden might rejoice in the blessings given to her kinswoman. [[1:36|And behold thy cousin Elizabeth, she also hath conceived a son in her old age|Ecce Elisabeth cognata tua, et ipsa concepit filium in senectute sua]], although she had a twofold hindrance, namely of old age and of natural barrenness; [[1:36|and this is the sixth month|et hic mensis, scilicet Martius, in quo tibi appareo, est sextus]], namely March, in which I appear to thee, [[1:36|with her|illi]], from when she conceived, [[1:36|that is called barren|quæ vocatur sterilis]]: because she had long been so called, and the habit of calling her so had not been given up; [[1:37|Because no word shall be impossible with God|quia non erit impossibile apud Deum omne verbum]]: that is, whatever is signified by speech God can fulfil, if it does not imply a contradiction and if to do it is a matter of power rather than of weakness. So that God in His nature cannot sin, fall sick, eat, run, be moved or sleep is a matter of power, not of weakness. With this word agrees that saying of Jeremias: [[Jer 32:17|O Lord God, behold thou hast made heaven and earth by thy great power, and thy stretched out arm: no word shall be hard to thee|Domine Deus, non erit tibi difficile omne verbum]]. For since God's power is infinite, He is indeed almighty, and can accomplish in an instant whatever He wills; nor can He do so many or so great things that He could not do infinitely more and greater.

paras.t: His auditis, pia et docilis Virgo cito præbet consensum. Tamque incomparabiliter commendata nescit extolli, sed eo profundius humiliavit se ipsam, quo ampliorem circa se Dei advertit clementiam, suis nil viribus tribuens. Quemadmodum enim vitiosi suis laudibus stulte atque inaniter intumescunt, sic virtuosi inde plus se ipsos dejiciunt. Quo equidem quis majora a Deo sortitus est bona, eo debet illi gratior esse, itemque subjectior. Dixit autem Maria, de beneficio suæ cognatæ collato exhilarata: Ecce ancilla Domini ego sum, idcirco ad omnia ei placita offero me paratam. Audiens quoque se in Domini Dei sui matrem electam, non aliud quam ejus se appellat ancillam. Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum, hoc est, Spiritu Sancto superveniente, Filium Dei concipiam, ut dixisti. His verbis consensit: quibus prolatis immediate Unigenitum Patris æterni concepit. Itaque in instanti Spiritus Sanctus ex ejus purissimo sanguine corpus formavit, et perfecte quantum ad membrorum distinctionem organizavit; in quo item instanti anima Christi est creata, carni unita, atque utrumque Verbo hypostatica seu personali unione est conjunctum. Itaque in eodem instanti fuit sanguinis separatio, consolidatio, figuratio, animatio, et deificatio. Verumtamen distinctio membrorum oculis perceptibilis vix fuisset ob corporis parvitatem. Præterea, mox ut Virgo assensit, celebratæ sunt in utero ejus nuptiæ hypostaticæ unionis, videlicet conjunctio humanæ naturæ cum Verbo: de quibus Gregorius ait, quod tunc Deus Pater Filio nuptias fecit, quum ei in utero Virginis naturam sociavit humanam. Tunc quoque celebratæ sunt nuptiæ Sponsi cælestis cum sua Sponsa singulari, quæ est Mater virginea, Virgo Christifera, quæ Filium Dei concipiendo, facta est Sponsa ipsius singularis. Porro tota Trinitas superbenedicta (cujus quum una consistat essentia, indivisa sunt opera) naturam humanam Filio suppositaliter copulavit. Solus vero Filius naturam istam assumpsit, eamque in se ipso suppositavit: ita quod ipsummet Verbum æternum, est assumptæ humanitatis hypostasis, quæ in Verbo subsistit personalitate increata Verbi. Estque in Christo una personalitas tantum, et filiatio una dumtaxat, quum sit una persona: filiatio autem concernit personam. Duæ vero generationes ponuntur in eo, sicut et duæ naturæ: generatio enim concernit naturam. Et discessit angelus ab ea. Et arbitror quod non velut improvise et ex abrupto ab ipsa abierit, sicut a ceteris Sanctis legitur sæpius recessisse seu disparuisse; sed cum grandi reverentia, maxima congratulatione, jucundissimo apparatu, quasi licentiam postulans recedendi a Domina sua, quam ut sui ac omnium Creatoris Matrem, jam orsus est honorare, provise abscessit atque disparuit.
paras.en: Having heard this, the loving and docile Virgin quickly gives her consent. And though praised beyond compare, she knows not how to be lifted up, but humbled herself the more deeply, the greater the mercy of God towards her that she perceived, attributing nothing to her own strength. For as the vicious swell foolishly and vainly at their praises, so the virtuous are cast down the more by them. Indeed, the greater the goods a man has received from God, the more grateful and also the more subject he ought to be to Him. [[1:38|And Mary said|Dixit autem Maria]], gladdened by the blessing given to her kinswoman: [[1:38|Behold the handmaid of the Lord|Ecce ancilla Domini]], I am; therefore I offer myself ready for all that pleases Him. Hearing that she has been chosen to be the mother of the Lord her God, she calls herself nothing other than His handmaid. [[1:38|be it done to me according to thy word|Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum]], that is, by the coming of the Holy Ghost upon me let me conceive the Son of God, as thou hast said. With these words she consented: and as soon as they were spoken she conceived the Only-begotten of the eternal Father. So in an instant the Holy Ghost formed a body from her most pure blood and organized it perfectly as to the distinction of its members; and in the same instant the soul of Christ was created and united to the flesh, and both were joined to the Word in a hypostatic or personal union. So in the same instant there was the separating of the blood, its making firm, shaping, ensouling and deifying. Yet the distinction of the members would scarcely have been visible to the eye because of the smallness of the body. Moreover, as soon as the Virgin assented, the marriage of the hypostatic union was celebrated in her womb, namely the joining of human nature to the Word: of which Gregory says that God the Father then made a marriage for His Son, when He joined human nature to Him in the Virgin's womb. Then too was celebrated the marriage of the heavenly Bridegroom with His singular Bride, who is the virgin Mother, the Christ-bearing Virgin, who by conceiving the Son of God became His singular Bride. Further, the whole most blessed Trinity (whose works are undivided, since its essence is one) joined human nature to the Son in His person. But the Son alone took this nature and made it subsist in Himself: so that the eternal Word Himself is the hypostasis of the humanity He took, which subsists in the Word by the uncreated personality of the Word. And in Christ there is only one personality and only one sonship, since He is one person: for sonship concerns the person. But two generations are placed in Him, as also two natures: for generation concerns the nature. [[1:38|And the angel departed from her.|Et discessit angelus ab ea.]] And I think that he did not go away from her suddenly and abruptly, as he is often read to have withdrawn or vanished from other Saints; but with great reverence, the greatest rejoicing and a most joyful bearing, as though asking leave of his Lady to withdraw, whom he had now begun to honour as the Mother of his and everyone's Creator, he went away deliberately and vanished.

paras.t: Exsurgens autem Maria a loco orationis, a quiete contemplationis, ab habitaculo mansionis, in diebus illis, statim quum Dei Unigenitum concepisset, abiit in montana, id est per loca alta, montuosa, et aspera, quibus plena est Judæa, cum festinatione, in civitatem Juda; et intravit in domum Zachariæ, et salutavit Elisabeth. Celeriter ivit, dans exemplum virginibus cunctisque feminis, ne libenter tardent in publico, neque in communibus sine rationabili causa itineribus inveniantur. Et quia jam plena fuit Spiritu Sancto, spiritualique gaudio, caritatis fervore, et sanctæ devotionis dulcedine, festinanter processit, præsertim quia et cognatæ suæ congaudere optavit et obsequi, ejusque fetum ex sui præsentia Filii desideravit donis amplioribus perornari. Porro, per civitatem Juda, quidam intelligunt ipsam Jerusalem per quam asserunt transisse Mariam, urbem versus in qua habitaverunt parentes Joannis, quam dicunt fere per quatuor aut quinque milliaria fuisse ultra Jerusalem. Nihilo minus per civitatem Juda, urbs habitationis parentum Joannis intelligi potest. Et salutavit Elisabeth: ut habetur in Ecclesiastico, Amicum salutare non confundar. Et quia humillima fuit, et forte prior suam salutavit cognatam. Forma autem salutationis digesta seu scripta non est. Secundum Ambrosium autem, condecens est, ut quanto castior virgo, tanto humilior sit.
paras.en: [[1:39|And Mary rising up|Exsurgens autem Maria]] from the place of prayer, from the quiet of contemplation, from the room where she dwelt, [[1:39|in those days|in diebus illis]], as soon as she had conceived the Only-begotten of God, [[1:39|went into the hill country|abiit in montana]], that is, through the high, mountainous and rough places of which Judea is full, [[1:39|with haste into a city of Juda|cum festinatione, in civitatem Juda]]; [[1:40|And she entered into the house of Zachary and saluted Elizabeth.|et intravit in domum Zachariæ, et salutavit Elisabeth.]] She went quickly, giving an example to virgins and all women not to linger willingly in public, nor to be found on the common roads without reasonable cause. And because she was already full of the Holy Ghost, of spiritual joy, of the fervour of charity and of the sweetness of holy devotion, she went in haste, especially because she wished to rejoice with her kinswoman and serve her, and desired that her child should be adorned with fuller gifts by the presence of her own Son. Now by the city of Juda some understand Jerusalem itself, through which they say Mary passed towards the town in which John's parents lived, which they say was some four or five miles beyond Jerusalem. Nevertheless, by the city of Juda the town where John's parents lived can be understood. [[1:40|and saluted Elizabeth|et salutavit Elisabeth]]: as we have in Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 22:31|I will not be ashamed to salute a friend|Amicum salutare non confundar]]. And because she was most humble, perhaps she greeted her kinswoman first. But the form of the greeting is not set down or written. According to Ambrose, it is most fitting that the more chaste a virgin is, the more humble she should be.

paras.t: Et factum est, ut audivit salutationem Mariæ Elisabeth, exsultavit infans in utero ejus. Exsultatio ex aliqua prævia cognitiva apprehensione solet oriri. Communiter itaque tenent doctores, quod per omnipotentiam Dei acceleratus est usus rationis in Joanne nondum progenito: ita quod revelante Spiritu Sancto, noverit Unigenitum Dei jam incarnatum, atque in utero Virginis tunc præsentem; tuncque præsertim in eo impletum sit quod angelus nuntiavit, quia Spiritu Sancto replebitur adhuc ex utero matris suæ. Hinc secundum Ambrosium et Glossam, sicut Elisabeth Mariæ, ita Joannes Christi sensit adventum. Aliqui vero dixerunt, quod Joannes Christi præsentiam non cognovit, nec tunc usus sit ratione, sed miraculose movebatur, et instar exsultantis se habuit in utero matris, ad declarationem dignitatis Christi Genitricisque ejus. Augustinus vero tangit utrumque hunc modum, neutrum autem assertive determinat; sed primus verior reputatur. Et repleta est Spiritu Sancto Elisabeth. Dicunt quidam, quod Maria ante conceptum, Elisabeth vero post conceptum repleta sit Spiritu Sancto. Verumtamen, quum de Elisabeth nondum fecundata jam dixerit Evangelista quod erant ambo, videlicet maritus ejus et ipsa, justi ante Deum, etc., certum quod etiam ante prolis suæ conceptionem fuit quodammodo, imo et eminenter, plena Spiritu Sancto, utpote in numero perfectorum annumerari condigna; sed consuetudo Scripturæ est, ut dicat tunc hominem Spiritu Sancto repleri, quum gratia notabiliter exuberantiori perfunditur, quemadmodum de primitiva Ecclesia, quæ in die Pentecostes repleta fuit Spiritu Sancto, scriptum est in Actibus: Quum orassent, motus est locus in quo erant, et repleti sunt Spiritu Sancto. Itaque, sancta Elisabeth tam grande miraculum in prolis suæ nondum natæ exsultatione perpendens, Christi quoque et beatissimæ Virginis præsentiam venerandam advertens, totis in Deo gloriabatur præcordiis, et gratia ampliori mirabiliter implebatur, spiritumque prophetiæ suscepit.
paras.en: [[1:41|And it came to pass that when Elizabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the infant leaped in her womb.|Et factum est, ut audivit salutationem Mariæ Elisabeth, exsultavit infans in utero ejus.]] Leaping for joy usually arises from some knowing apprehension that goes before it. So the doctors commonly hold that by the almighty power of God the use of reason was hastened in John while he was not yet born: so that, by the revelation of the Holy Ghost, he knew that the Only-begotten of God was now incarnate and then present in the Virgin's womb; and that then especially was fulfilled in him what the angel announced, that [[1:15|he shall be filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother's womb|Spiritu Sancto replebitur adhuc ex utero matris suæ]]. Hence, according to Ambrose and the Gloss, as Elizabeth perceived the coming of Mary, so John perceived the coming of Christ. But some have said that John did not know Christ's presence nor then use reason, but was moved miraculously and behaved like one leaping for joy in his mother's womb, to declare the dignity of Christ and of His Mother. Augustine touches on both ways but determines neither by assertion; but the first is held to be truer. [[1:41|And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost.|Et repleta est Spiritu Sancto Elisabeth.]] Some say that Mary was filled with the Holy Ghost before the conception, but Elizabeth after the conception. However, since the Evangelist has already said of Elizabeth, before she was made fruitful, that [[1:6|they were both just before God|erant ambo, videlicet maritus ejus et ipsa, justi ante Deum]], namely her husband and she, etc., it is certain that even before the conception of her child she was in some way, indeed eminently, full of the Holy Ghost, as worthy to be counted among the perfect; but it is the custom of Scripture to say that a man is filled with the Holy Ghost when he is flooded with grace in a notably more abundant way, as is written in the Acts of the primitive Church, which was filled with the Holy Ghost on the day of Pentecost: [[Acts 4:31|when they had prayed, the place was moved wherein they were assembled: and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost|Quum orassent, motus est locus in quo erant, et repleti sunt Spiritu Sancto]]. So holy Elizabeth, weighing so great a miracle in the leaping of her unborn child, and perceiving the venerable presence of Christ and of the most blessed Virgin, gloried in God with her whole heart, was wonderfully filled with fuller grace, and received the spirit of prophecy.

paras.t: Et exclamavit voce magna: ex plenitudine devotionis et interioris lætitiæ in vocem prorupit sublimem. Ex abundantia namque cordis os loquitur. Et dixit: Benedicta tu inter mulieres, hoc est præ feminis universis, sicut expositum est. Siquidem verba ista eumdem habent sensum cum verbis illis angelicis, Benedicta tu in mulieribus. Et benedictus fructus ventris tui, id est Christus jam filius tuus effectus: de quo ait Psalmista, Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini; et, Terra nostra dabit fructum suum. De quo scriptum est in Isaia: In die illo erit germen Domini in magnificentia et gloria, et fructus terræ sublimis. Porro Christus secundum utramque naturam benedictus est, sed diversimode. Nam ut Deus, per naturam seu substantialiter benedictus et sanctus est, juxta illud Danielis: Benedictus es, Domine, Deus patrum nostrorum. Dicitur enim Deus in se ipso benedictus, quia essentialiter sanctus, omnique benedictione ac laude dignissimus, totius quoque benedictionis et gratiæ collativus. Secundum naturam vero humanam, dicitur benedictus per gratiam, quoniam plenitudinem gratiæ sumpsit, non ad mensuram, puta in copia tanta, quod tota creatæ mentis capacitas fuit in eo completa. Et unde hoc mihi, ut veniat Mater Domini mei ad me, scilicet Mater Christi? quasi dicat, Digna non sum, nec meis hoc meritis tribuo. In quo humilitas Elisabeth innotescit, quæ quum esset grandæva, et tanto sacerdoti in conjugem sociata, ac supernaturaliter fecundata, indignam tamen se a juvencula fabro lignario desponsata visitari professa est. Quod et verum fuit, habendo respectum ad excellentiam dignitatis gratiæque Mariæ, et ad id quod Elisabeth fuerat per naturam: vel etiam ad opera ejus bona, secundum quod a libero procedebant arbitrio; sed in quantum ex supernaturalibus habitibus gratiæ gratum facientis, et virtutum infusarum, itemque actuali motione Spiritus Sancti procedebant, non tantum digna fuit a Matre Domini visitari, sed et Divinitate beatifice in patria frui, communi obstaculo per Christi passionem ablato: juxta modum quo opera virtuosa dicuntur æternæ meritoria vitæ, et de condigno, secundum opinionem probabilem, quamvis aliqui dicant oppositum.
paras.en: [[1:42|And she cried out with a loud voice|Et exclamavit voce magna]]: out of the fulness of devotion and inward joy she broke out into a lofty voice. For [[Matt 12:34|out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh|Ex abundantia namque cordis os loquitur]]. [[1:42|and said: Blessed art thou among women|Et dixit: Benedicta tu inter mulieres]], that is, above all women, as has been explained. For these words have the same sense as those words of the angel, [[1:28|blessed art thou among women|Benedicta tu in mulieribus]]. [[1:42|and blessed is the fruit of thy womb|Et benedictus fructus ventris tui]], that is, Christ, now made thy son: of whom the Psalmist says, [[Ps 117:26|Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord|Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini]]; and, [[Ps 84:13|our earth shall yield her fruit|Terra nostra dabit fructum suum]]. Of whom it is written in Isaias: [[Is 4:2|In that day the bud of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth shall be high|In die illo erit germen Domini in magnificentia et gloria, et fructus terræ sublimis]]. Now Christ is blessed according to both natures, but in different ways. For as God He is blessed and holy by nature, or substantially, according to that saying of Daniel: [[Dan 3:52|Blessed art thou, O Lord, the God of our fathers|Benedictus es, Domine, Deus patrum nostrorum]]. For God is called blessed in Himself because He is essentially holy, most worthy of all blessing and praise[[Ecclus 43:33||]], and the giver of all blessing and grace. But according to human nature He is called blessed by grace, because He received the fulness of grace, not by measure[[John 3:34||]], that is, in such abundance that the whole capacity of a created mind was filled in Him. [[1:43|And whence is this to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?|Et unde hoc mihi, ut veniat Mater Domini mei ad me]] That is, the Mother of Christ; as if she said: I am not worthy, nor do I attribute this to my merits. In which the humility of Elizabeth is made known, who, though advanced in years, joined in marriage to so great a priest, and made fruitful beyond nature, yet professed herself unworthy to be visited by a young girl espoused to a carpenter. And this was true, having regard to the excellence of Mary's dignity and grace, and to what Elizabeth had been by nature: or also to her good works, so far as they proceeded from free will; but in so far as they proceeded from the supernatural habits of sanctifying grace and the infused virtues, and from the actual moving of the Holy Ghost, she was worthy not only to be visited by the Mother of the Lord but to enjoy the Godhead blessedly in the fatherland, the common obstacle having been removed by Christ's passion: in the way in which virtuous works are said to merit eternal life, and that de condigno [by a merit of strict worth, not merely of fittingness], according to a probable opinion, although some say the opposite.

paras.t: Præterea, nunc occurrit memoriæ quod circa verba præscripta, Repleta est Spiritu Sancto Elisabeth, scribit Ambrosius: Non prius repleta mater (puta Elisabeth) quam filius ejus. Quod intelligendum est de illa repletione abundanti prætacta. Additque: Sed quum filius (scilicet Joannes) repletus est Spiritu Sancto, replevit et matrem. Quæritur, quomodo Joannes nondum natus, matrem suam Spiritu Sancto impleverit. Et certum quod non auctoritative, quum hoc Deo sit proprium; nec ministerialiter, sicut in dispensationibus seu administrationibus sacramentorum, ministri Ecclesiæ dicuntur suscipientes replere. Aliqui dicunt, quod per modum causæ meritoriæ instrumentalis hoc fecit, ita quod in ipso acceleratus fuit per gratiam usus rationis, liberi quoque arbitrii. Quidam vero affirmant, quod nullo prædictorum modorum id accidit, sed ideo matrem suam fertur implesse, quoniam privilegio ejus datum est matri suæ hujuscemodi divinorum charismatum incrementum. Potest etiam probabiliter dici, quod occasionaliter matrem suam Spiritu Sancto implevit, quoniam illa filii sui miraculosam exsultationem experiens, ex hoc in Deum mente effusa est, ejusque cor caritate apertum ac dilatatum patulumque effectum, factum est gratiæ capax majoris, quemadmodum aliquis videns alium in magna devotione consistentem, devotione accenditur.
paras.en: Moreover, it now comes to mind that on the words written above, [[1:41|And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost|Repleta est Spiritu Sancto Elisabeth]], Ambrose writes: The mother (namely Elizabeth) was not filled before her son. Which is to be understood of that abundant filling mentioned above. And he adds: But when the son (namely John) was filled with the Holy Ghost, he filled his mother too. It is asked how John, not yet born, filled his mother with the Holy Ghost. And it is certain that it was not by authority, since this belongs to God; nor by ministry, as in the dispensing or administering of the sacraments the ministers of the Church are said to fill those who receive them. Some say that he did this as a meritorious instrumental cause, the use of reason and of free will having been hastened in him by grace. But others affirm that it happened in none of these ways, but that he is said to have filled his mother because by his privilege such an increase of divine gifts was given to his mother. It can also probably be said that he filled his mother with the Holy Ghost as the occasion of it, because she, experiencing the miraculous leaping of her son, was poured out in mind towards God because of it, and her heart, opened, enlarged and made wide by charity, was made capable of greater grace: as someone who sees another in great devotion is kindled to devotion.
