paras.t: Ecce enim, o Maria, ut facta est, hoc est audita, vox salutationis tuæ, qua me tam caritative atque humiliter salutasti, in auribus meis, statim exsultavit in gaudio, formaliter sive causaliter, infans in utero meo: ita quod illa exsultatio fuit gaudium, vel exsultatio ad corpus per redundantiam pertinens, quæ ex mentis gaudio nascebatur. Itaque Joannes Sponsi amicus, de Sponsi gaudebat præsentia, secundum quod ipse postea ore tenus fatebitur: Amicus sponsi, qui stat et audit vocem ejus, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Propter quod ait Ambrosius: Joannes exsultavit ratione mysterii, utpote quoniam Unigenitum Dei jam novit incarnatum, veraciterque præsentem. Ex quo evidens reor, quod et Joannes interiori auditu internam Christi allocutionem seu illustrationem advertit. Dicit autem Gorra hoc loco: Ecce quantæ virtutis est beatæ Virginis salutatio, quæ confert gaudium, confert et Spiritum Sanctum, confert revelationem divinorum secretorum, confert et prophetiæ actum. Verum intelligendum est hoc de collatione per modum causæ meritoriæ. Maria enim tam ardenter et humiliter salutando cognatam, præfata bona meruit ei quodammodo. Insuper, sicut et Beda fatetur, certum est quod non nisi revelante Spiritu Sancto, Elisabeth novit quod Maria esset jam Mater Christi effecta, ab angelo salutata, ejusque verbis crediderit, quod item exsultatio Joannis esset ob Christi corporalem præsentiam. Hinc et Elisabeth addidit: Et beata quæ credidisti. Concordat quod ait Salvator: Beati qui non viderunt, et crediderunt. Porro Gregorius super Ezechielem: Simul, inquit, de præterito et præsenti ac futuro per prophetiæ spiritum tacta est Elisabeth, quæ beatam Mariam promissionibus angeli credidisse cognovit, et matrem nominans, quia Redemptorem in utero portaret, intellexit; et quum omnia perficienda prædiceret, quid et in futuro sequeretur, adspexit. Itaque cognitio fidei, est inchoatio quædam cognitionis beatæ in patria; ipsum quoque credere ex caritate, meritorium est beatitudinis consummatæ, ad illam se habens sicut meritum ad præmium. Denique, sicut aperta visio est felicitas patriæ, sic cognitio fidei beatitudo est viæ. Beatitudo etiam viæ est imperfecta, et dispositio ad perfectam patriæ felicitatem. Cur autem beata fuit credendo, subjungitur: quoniam perficientur in te ea quæ dicta sunt tibi a Domino, hoc est, completum sortientur effectum seu plenarium complementum, et quod credidisti per fidem, videbis per speciem. Christum quoque quem concepisti, paries, et usque ad virilia incrementa perduces. Dicit autem Augustinus, quod Virgo beata felicior fuit Dei Filium mente per fidem spiritualiter concipiendo, sive credendo, quam eumdem ventre corporaliter concipiendo. Ambrosius quoque: Quicumque, inquit, crediderit anima, scilicet fide caritati unita, concipit et generat Dei Verbum; et si secundum carnem una est Mater Christi, secundum fidem tamen omnium fructus est Christus. Et ait Maria. Hic describitur canticum, hymnus, laus, seu gratiarum actio Virginis gloriosæ.
paras.en: [[1:44|For behold as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in my ears|Ecce enim … ut facta est … vox salutationis tuæ … in auribus meis]], O Mary (sounded, that is, was heard), the greeting with which thou didst greet me so lovingly and humbly, at once [[1:44|the infant in my womb leaped for joy|exsultavit in gaudio infans in utero meo]], formally or causally: so that that leaping was joy, or a leaping belonging to the body by overflow, born of the joy of the mind. So John, the friend of the Bridegroom, rejoiced at the presence of the Bridegroom, as he himself will later declare with his own lips: [[John 3:29|the friend of the bridegroom, who standeth and heareth Him, rejoiceth with joy because of the bridegroom's voice|Amicus sponsi, qui stat et audit vocem ejus, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi]]. That is why Ambrose says: John leaped by reason of the mystery, namely because he now knew the Only-begotten of God to be incarnate and truly present. From which I think it evident that John too, by an inward hearing, perceived an inward speaking or enlightening of Christ. And Gorra [Nicholas of Gorran] says on this passage: See of what great power is the greeting of the blessed Virgin, which bestows joy, bestows the Holy Ghost, bestows the revelation of divine secrets, and bestows the act of prophecy. But this is to be understood of bestowing by way of meritorious cause. For Mary, by greeting her kinswoman so ardently and humbly, in some way merited these goods for her. Moreover, as Bede also says, it is certain that only by the revelation of the Holy Ghost did Elizabeth know that Mary had now been made the Mother of Christ, had been greeted by the angel and had believed his words, and also that John's leaping was because of Christ's bodily presence. Hence Elizabeth added: [[1:45|And blessed art thou that hast believed|Et beata quæ credidisti]]. With this agrees what the Saviour says: [[John 20:29|blessed are they that have not seen and have believed|Beati qui non viderunt, et crediderunt]]. And Gregory on Ezechiel says: Elizabeth was touched by the spirit of prophecy at once about the past, the present and the future: she knew that blessed Mary had believed the angel's promises; in calling her mother she understood that she bore the Redeemer in her womb; and in foretelling that all would be accomplished she saw what would also follow in the future. So the knowledge of faith is a certain beginning of the blessed knowledge in the fatherland; and believing out of charity merits consummated blessedness, standing to it as merit to reward. Further, as open vision is the happiness of the fatherland, so the knowledge of faith is the blessedness of the way. And the blessedness of the way is imperfect, and a disposition to the perfect happiness of the fatherland. Why she was blessed in believing is added: [[1:45|because those things shall be accomplished that were spoken to thee by the Lord|quoniam perficientur in te ea quæ dicta sunt tibi a Domino]], that is, they will obtain their complete effect, or full accomplishment, and what thou hast believed by faith thou shalt see by sight. Christ too, whom thou hast conceived, thou shalt bring forth and bring up to the growth of manhood. And Augustine says that the blessed Virgin was happier in conceiving the Son of God spiritually in mind by faith, that is, by believing, than in conceiving Him bodily in her womb. And Ambrose too: Every soul, he says, that has believed (namely with faith joined to charity) conceives and begets the Word of God; and if according to the flesh Christ has one Mother, yet according to faith Christ is the fruit of all. [[1:46|And Mary said|Et ait Maria]]. Here is described the canticle, hymn, praise or thanksgiving of the glorious Virgin.

1.title: Expositio evangelici cantici Christiferæ Virginis Mariæ, videlicet: Magnificat anima mea Dominum; et exsultavit spiritus meus, etc.
1.title_en: Exposition of the gospel canticle of Mary, the Virgin who bore Christ, namely: “My soul doth magnify the Lord; and my spirit hath rejoiced,” etc.

paras.t: Quibusdam veteris Testamenti Sanctis concessum est, ut perceptis beneficiis Dei præcipuis, canticum Deo componerent et offerrent. Sic nunc agit S. Maria. Considerans enim ineffabilia Dei beneficia super se, et in se, laudes gratiasque referre non distulit, præsertim quia ex ea incarnari dignatus fuit Unigenitus Dei. Cujus rei typus in Anna præcessit, quæ supernaturali Dei munere Samuelem enixa, cecinit carmen, primo Regum contentum, Exsultavit cor meum in Domino: quod in aliquibus cum carmine Virginis divinæ coincidit.
paras.en: To certain Saints of the Old Testament it was granted that, having received special benefits from God, they should compose a canticle and offer it to God. So now does holy Mary. For, considering the unspeakable benefits of God upon her and within her, she did not delay to return praise and thanks, above all because the Only-begotten of God had deigned to become incarnate of her. A type of this went before in Anna, who, having brought forth Samuel by a supernatural gift of God, sang the song contained in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 2:1|My heart hath rejoiced in the Lord|Exsultavit cor meum in Domino]]; which in some things agrees with the canticle of the divine Virgin [the margin gives I Reg. vi, 1; Anna's song is at 1 Kings 2:1].

paras.t: Itaque, devotissima atque gratissima mente fatetur Domina mundi, Regina cœli, Genitrix Dei: Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Magnificentia et excellentia cantici hujus, primo ex parte actricis perpenditur, quæ quanto gratiosior, illuminatior, atque divinior erat, eo præclarius canticum edidit; secundo, ex sententiæ ubertate ac majestate; tertio, ex igne devotionis in ipso exuberantis. Sic ergo: Magnificat, inquit, anima mea Dominum. Tanquam dicat: Tu me, o Elisabeth, laudas, extollis, magnificas; verum ego, sciens quod a me ipsa nil habeo, universa bona Deo adscribo, ipsum laudo, me deprimo, illum magnifico, id est, magnum, summum, immensum fateor, contestor, demonstro, illum totis viribus magnificenter honoro, omni zelo venerari desidero, me parvi pendo. Dicimur itaque Deum sanctificare, magnificare, glorificare, dum verbis et actibus ejus sanctitatem, majestatem, beatitudinem, protestamur, extollimus, demonstramus. Impii vero dicuntur nomen Dei polluere, parvi facere, inhonorare, quoniam quantum in ipsis est, verbis et factis ostendunt, seu ita se habent, quasi Deus non esset honore et gloria omnique reverentia dignus, sed parvi pendendus, neque curandus; alios quoque ad Dei offensam, irreverentiam, injuriamque inducunt. Hinc per Ezechielem Deus frequenter improperat filiis Israel, quod polluerint nomen suum sanctum in gentibus.
paras.en: So, with a most devout and most grateful mind, the Lady of the world, the Queen of heaven, the Mother of God, declares: [[1:46|My soul doth magnify the Lord|Magnificat anima mea Dominum]]. The magnificence and excellence of this canticle is weighed, first, on the part of her who made it, who, the more full of grace, the more enlightened and the more divine she was, so much the more glorious a canticle she brought forth; secondly, from the richness and majesty of its meaning; thirdly, from the fire of devotion overflowing in it. Thus, then, she says: *My soul doth magnify the Lord*. As if she said: Thou, O Elisabeth, praisest me, extollest me, magnifiest me; but I, knowing that of myself I have nothing, ascribe all good things to God: Him I praise, myself I abase; Him I magnify, that is, I confess, testify and show Him to be great, supreme, immense; Him I honour magnificently with all my strength, Him I desire to worship with all zeal, myself I hold of little account. So we are said to sanctify, magnify and glorify God when by words and deeds we profess, extol and show forth His holiness, majesty and blessedness. The wicked, on the other hand, are said to defile the name of God, to make little of it and dishonour it, because, as far as in them lies, they show by words and deeds, or behave as if, God were not worthy of honour and glory and all reverence, but to be held of little account and not cared for; and they lead others too to offend God, to irreverence and to injury against Him. Hence through Ezechiel God often reproaches the children of Israel that they have profaned His holy name among the nations[[Ezech 36:20||]] [the margin's numerals are unclear (read as xxxvi, 20 with further references); the reproach is made at Ezech 36:20–23].

paras.t: Fecit ergo Maria quod sanctus pater ejus, propheta David, admonuit: Magnificate Dominum mecum. Porro, secundum Ambrosium, magnificamus Dominum seu Dominus magnificatur, non quod ei quidquam accrescat, sed quia magnificatur in nobis, hoc est, per suos in nobis effectus, seu actus nostros ejus auxilio exhibitos, magnus ostenditur. Propterea addit Ambrosius: Imago enim Dei Christus est, et ideo, si quid justum religiosumque fecerit anima, imaginem Dei, ad cujus similitudinem est creata, magnificat. Quod sumptum videtur ex verbis Origenis dicentis: Salvator noster est imago Dei invisibilis, et anima nostra est imago illius imaginis: quum ergo illam, cogitatione, sermone, et operatione magnifico, tunc imago Dei in me grandis efficitur, et ipse Dominus cujus imago est anima mea, amplius in me magnificatur.
paras.en: Mary, then, did what her holy father, the prophet David, urged: [[Ps 33:4|O magnify the Lord with me|Magnificate Dominum mecum]] [the margin reads Ps. xxvi; the words are those of Ps 33:4]. Further, according to Ambrose, we magnify the Lord, or the Lord is magnified, not because anything is added to Him, but because He is magnified in us; that is, He is shown to be great through His effects in us, or through our acts performed with His help. Therefore Ambrose adds: For Christ is the image of God; and so, if the soul has done anything just and devout, it magnifies the image of God, to whose likeness it was created[[Gen 1:27||]]. This seems taken from the words of Origen, who says: Our Saviour is [[Col 1:15|the image of the invisible God|imago Dei invisibilis]], and our soul is the image of that image: when, therefore, I magnify it in thought, word and deed, then the image of God is made great in me, and the Lord Himself, whose image my soul is, is magnified the more in me.

paras.t: Præterea, advertendum quod in cantico isto, nomine Dei et Domini intelligi potest absolute ipse Deus unus ac trinus, seu quælibet divina Persona: quamvis nonnulli per Deum ac Dominum specialiter Filii personam intelligant, asserentes quod Virgo dignissima in cantico isto Filium suum commendat. Et non ait, Magnifico, sed, Magnificat anima mea Dominum, ad innuendum quod ex præcordiali id agat devotione. Quo arguuntur qui sine reverentia Deum orant et laudant, nec eum sicut verum Deum tota cordis honorant custodia: de quibus per Isaiam Dominus loquitur, Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me.
paras.en: Moreover, it should be noted that in this canticle by the name of *God* and *Lord* may be understood absolutely God Himself, one and three, or any divine Person: although some understand by *God* and *Lord* specially the Person of the Son, asserting that in this canticle the most worthy Virgin praises her Son. And she does not say, *I magnify*, but *My soul doth magnify the Lord*, to hint that she does it from devotion of the inmost heart. By this are reproved those who pray to God and praise Him without reverence, and do not honour Him as the true God with all the watchfulness of the heart: of whom the Lord speaks through Isaias: [[Matt 15:8|This people honoureth me with their lips: but their heart is far from me|Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me]] [Denis names Isaias (Is 29:13), but gives the words in the form Christ quotes them at Matt 15:8; the margin gives both].

paras.t: Et exsultavit spiritus meus, scilicet anima mea rationalis, in Deo salutari meo, in contemplatione ac dilectione sui ipsius in se, et beneficiorum ejus circa me. Exsultatio autem seu gaudium, ex contemplatione et caritatis actu, seu actuali dilectione procedit. Quo igitur in divinorum contemplatione illuminatior, eorumdemque amore ferventior fuit Maria, eo plenius exsultavit, non in se, sed in Domino tanquam in causa, objecto et fine, sicut Apostolus scribit: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Porro Dominus dicitur ratione gubernationis; Deus, ratione causalitatis et creationis; Salutare vel Salutaris, ratione justificationis seu recreationis, et glorificationis: qui singulariter fuit et est Deus, ac Dominus, et Salutare Mariæ, propter præcipua beneficia ejus ad eam, et maximam devotionem, dilectionem et cultum illius ad illum. Quamvis autem anima et spiritus hominis realiter idem sint, tamen ratione sunt differentes: nam anima dicitur quoniam informat et animat corpus, illudque bene regendo, Deum magnificat: spiritus vero vocatur ob subtilitatem naturæ, et quoniam contemplatur cœlestia, sicque competit sibi exsultare, et præ ingenti lætitia, quasi extra se saltare in Deum. Hinc Virgo Deipara distincte locuta est: Magnificat anima mea Dominum; et exsultavit spiritus meus in Deo.
paras.en: [[1:47|And my spirit hath rejoiced|Et exsultavit spiritus meus]], that is, my rational soul, [[1:47|in God my Saviour|in Deo salutari meo]], in contemplating and loving Him in Himself, and His benefits towards me. Now exultation, or joy, proceeds from contemplation and from the act of charity, that is, from actual love. The more enlightened, then, Mary was in the contemplation of divine things, and the more fervent in loving them, so much the more fully did she rejoice: not in herself, but in the Lord as in her cause, object and end, as the Apostle writes: [[1 Cor 1:31|He that glorieth may glory in the Lord|Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur]]. Further, He is called *Lord* by reason of governing; *God*, by reason of causing and creating; *Saviour* [*Salutare* or *Salutaris*], by reason of justifying, or re-creating, and glorifying: and He was and is in a singular way the God, the Lord and the Saviour of Mary, because of His special benefits towards her, and her very great devotion, love and worship towards Him. And although the soul and the spirit of man are really the same, yet they differ in concept: for it is called *soul* [*anima*] because it informs and animates the body, and by ruling it well magnifies God; but it is called *spirit* because of the subtlety of its nature, and because it contemplates heavenly things, and so it belongs to it to *exult* [*exsultare*], and for very great joy to leap, as it were, out of itself into God [Denis plays on *exsultare*, from *saltare*, “to leap”]. Hence the Virgin Mother of God spoke distinctly: *My soul doth magnify the Lord; and my spirit hath rejoiced in God*.

paras.t: Postremo, ut totis viribus Deum magnificemus, magnificent eum nostra memoria, ejus beneficia jugiter recolendo, nostra intelligentia, ejus veritatem et excellentiam contemplando, nostra voluntas, ejus bonitatem amando ac appetendo, nostra interpretativa seu expressiva, eum ore laudando.
paras.en: Lastly, that we may magnify God with all our powers, let our memory magnify Him by ever recalling His benefits; our understanding, by contemplating His truth and excellence; our will, by loving and desiring His goodness; our power of utterance, or expression, by praising Him with the mouth.

paras.t: Et quia pro suis beneficiis gratiarum actio et vox laudis Deo debentur, consequenter Virgo præclara cantici sui rationem subjungit: Quia respexit per approbationem, oculo suæ pietatis immensæ, humilitatem ancillæ suæ, hoc est me humilem ejus ancillam, meamque humilitatem ac parvitatem. Et merito specialiter suæ meminit humilitatis magis quam virginitatis, caritatis, aut reliquarum virtutum, quibus præeminenter fulgebat: quia per humilitatem præcipue meruit taliter exaltari, eratque per eam præsertim disposita ad concipiendum Unigenitum Dei, secundum quod in Incarnationis mysterio consideratur incarnati majestas: quæ tanta est, ut non nisi ab humillima et pene incomparabiliter humili puella, decuit eum incarnari et concipi. Virginitas autem fuit dispositio magis remota, nec ipsa sine humilitate Domino placuisset. Verumtamen in Incarnationis mysterio, utriusque naturæ immediatam et hypostaticam unionem pensando, Virgo sacra per caritatem, ejusque ardentissimum actum, fuit summe et immediate disposita ad unigeniti Filii Dei conceptionem. Nam caritas præstantissima ac divinissima Deoque placentissima virtus est, conjunctionem, transformationem et insolubilem colligationem efficiens. Quamvis itaque tota Trinitas superbenedicta Mariæ humilitatem superclementer adspexit, præcipue tamen Filius, ex ea humanam induendo naturam, faciens se ejus prolem, atque subjiciens ei se ipsum. Sed et Deus Pater eam adspexit in tantum, ut eumdem cum ea habere Filium dignaretur: similiter Spiritus Sanctus, illo eam germine fecundans adorando, a quo ipse vere æternaliterque procedit. Secundum Origenem, humilitas in Scripturis una de virtutibus dicitur quæ a philosophis modestia nominatur; sed et nos eam possumus appellare quodam circuitu, quum aliquis non est inflatus, sed ipse se dejicit.
paras.en: And since for His benefits [[Is 51:3|thanksgiving, and the voice of praise|gratiarum actio et vox laudis]] are owed to God, the glorious Virgin next adds the reason for her canticle: [[1:48|Because he hath regarded|Quia respexit]], with approval, with the eye of His immense loving-kindness, [[1:48|the humility of his handmaid|humilitatem ancillæ suæ]], that is, me, His lowly handmaid, and my lowliness and littleness. And rightly she makes special mention of her humility rather than of her virginity, her charity or the other virtues in which she shone pre-eminently: because it was above all through humility that she merited to be so exalted, and it was chiefly by humility that she was disposed to conceive the Only-begotten of God, inasmuch as in the mystery of the Incarnation the majesty of Him who became incarnate is considered: which is so great that it was fitting for Him to be made flesh and conceived only by a most humble maiden, humble almost beyond compare. Virginity, however, was a more remote disposition, and it would not itself have pleased the Lord without humility. Yet, weighing in the mystery of the Incarnation the immediate and hypostatic union of the two natures [that is, their union in the one Person of the Word], the holy Virgin was supremely and immediately disposed for the conception of the only-begotten Son of God by charity and its most ardent act. For charity is the most excellent, most divine and most pleasing to God of the virtues, bringing about union, transformation and an indissoluble bond. So although the whole most blessed Trinity looked most mercifully upon Mary's humility, yet the Son did so chiefly, by putting on human nature from her, making Himself her child and subjecting Himself to her. But God the Father too looked upon her so far as to deign to have the same Son with her; and likewise the Holy Ghost, making her fruitful with that Offspring, adorable, from whom He Himself truly and eternally proceeds. According to Origen, humility in the Scriptures is said to be one of the virtues, which the philosophers call modesty; but we too can name it by a kind of circumlocution: when someone is not puffed up, but casts himself down.

paras.t: Ecce enim ex hoc tempore, et ratione tanti beneficii mihi collati, ex hac quoque mea humilitate, beatam me dicent omnes generationes, hoc est quidam ex omnibus, ut sit distributio pro generibus singulorum. Omnes quippe ex Judæis et gentilitate conversi, beatam, imo et beatissimam profitentur Virginem tam incomparandam: sed et Sarraceni, qui legem Mahometi suscipiunt, dicunt eam præ universis mulieribus omnium sæculorum electam, sicut et Christum Filium ejus fatentur suo legislatore Mahometo majorem. Sic et Lia, de qua orta est virgo Maria, cernens se tam fecundam: Hoc, inquit, pro beatitudine mea; beatam quippe me dicent mulieres: sicut in Genesi legitur.
paras.en: [[1:48|for behold from henceforth|ecce enim ex hoc]] time, and by reason of so great a benefit conferred on me, and also because of this my humility, [[1:48|all generations shall call me blessed|beatam me dicent omnes generationes]], that is, some from all of them, so that the distribution is “for the kinds of individual things” [that is, *all* here means people of every kind, not every single person]. For all who have been converted from the Jews and from the Gentiles profess the Virgin, so beyond compare, to be blessed, nay most blessed: and even the Saracens, who receive the law of Mahomet, say that she was chosen above all the women of all ages, as they also confess Christ her Son to be greater than their lawgiver Mahomet. So too Lia, from whom the Virgin Mary sprang, seeing herself so fruitful, said: [[Gen 30:13|This is for my happiness: for women will call me blessed|Hoc, inquit, pro beatitudine mea; beatam quippe me dicent mulieres]], as we read in Genesis.

paras.t: Quia fecit mihi magna qui potens est, hoc est, præclarissima mihi beneficia est largitus, in sanctificatione, in gratiarum augmentatione, in totius perfectionis collatione, et nunc potissimum in Incarnatione, in qua veri Dei vera Mater effecta, quodammodo infinitæ dignitatis prærogativam sum consecuta ab eo qui potens est, imo omnipotens est, et adeo potens, ut ejus respectu, omnis creatura sit impotens, nec sine illius manutenentia per momentum subsistere valens (illi equidem idem est esse et potentem esse: cujus essentia est sua potentia independens, illimitata, et penitus infinita; cui sunt omnia æque facilia: qui dominatur in virtute sua in æternum; a quo omnis potestas, dicente Apostolo, Non est potestas nisi a Deo: unde scriptum est, Sapiens corde est, et fortis robore, qui facit magna et inscrutabilia et mirabilia, quorum non est numerus) qui per me mundum liberare dignatus est, et præ omni creatura me honoravit, ita quod Deum omnium Creatorem ac Dominum concepi et porto.
paras.en: [[1:49|Because he that is mighty hath done great things to me|Quia fecit mihi magna qui potens est]], that is, He has bestowed on me most glorious benefits: in my sanctification, in the increase of graces, in the bestowal of all perfection, and now above all in the Incarnation, in which, made the true Mother of the true God, I have obtained a prerogative of in some way infinite dignity from Him *that is mighty*, nay almighty, and so mighty that in respect of Him every creature is powerless and could not subsist for a moment without His upholding (for to Him being and being mighty are the same: His essence is His own power, independent, unlimited and wholly infinite; to Him all things are equally easy; [[Ps 65:7|Who by his power ruleth for ever|qui dominatur in virtute sua in æternum]]; from Him is all power, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:1|there is no power but from God|Non est potestas nisi a Deo]]; whence it is written: [[Job 9:4|He is wise in heart, and mighty in strength|Sapiens corde est, et fortis robore]], [[Job 9:10|Who doth things great and incomprehensible, and wonderful, of which there is no number|qui facit magna et inscrutabilia et mirabilia, quorum non est numerus]]); who has deigned to set the world free through me, and has honoured me above every creature, so that I have conceived and bear God, the Creator and Lord of all.

paras.t: Et sanctum nomen ejus nominatum: id est, ipsemet nomine nominante designatus, in se ipso essentialiter purus, virtuosus et sanctus est, imo sanctitas prima, fontana, exemplaris, immensa: in quo quidquid perfectionis, sanctitatis atque virtutis est cogitarive potest, cum immensa plenitudine supersimplicissime continetur. De quo ait Psalmista: Adorate in monte sancto ejus, quoniam sanctus Dominus Deus noster; et iterum, Confiteantur nomini tuo magno, quoniam terribile et sanctum est. Unde scriptum est: Deus sanctus et fortis æmulator est, nec ignoscet sceleribus vestris. In Job quoque dicitur: Absit a Deo impietas, et ab Omnipotente iniquitas. Denique tam sanctus est Deus noster omnipotens, ut ejus comparatione, omnis sanctitas et æquitas nostra sit quasi pannus menstruatæ. Ecce enim luna non splendet, et stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus: qui et in angelis suis reperit pravitatem. Siquidem, quid est ipsa divina essentia, nisi sapientia superessentialis, veritas exemplaris, virtus prima, æquitas summa, caritas infinita, lux incircumscripta, puritas impermixta? Nemo ergo se jactet, aut aliquid putet, aut alium spernat, nec ad publicos transgressores se comparet; sed in divinæ sanctitatis conspectu atque præsentia se semper constituens, quidquid in se virtutis est aut esse posse adverterit, illius intuitu pro nihilo habeat, seque in profundo humilitatis incessanter conservare conetur.
paras.en: [[1:49|and holy is his name|Et sanctum nomen ejus]], the one named: that is, He who is signified by the naming name is Himself, in Himself, essentially pure, virtuous and holy; nay, He is holiness first, the fountain, the exemplar, immense: in whom whatever of perfection, holiness and virtue there is or can be thought is contained, with immense fullness, in the most perfect simplicity. Of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 98:9|adore at his holy mountain: for the Lord our God is holy|Adorate in monte sancto ejus, quoniam sanctus Dominus Deus noster]]; and again: [[Ps 98:3|Let them give praise to thy great name: for it is terrible and holy|Confiteantur nomini tuo magno, quoniam terribile et sanctum est]]. Whence it is written: [[Jos 24:19|he is a holy God, and mighty and jealous, and will not forgive your wickedness|Deus sanctus et fortis æmulator est, nec ignoscet sceleribus vestris]]. In Job too it is said: [[Job 34:10|far from God be wickedness, and iniquity from the Almighty|Absit a Deo impietas, et ab Omnipotente iniquitas]]. Lastly, our almighty God is so holy that in comparison with Him all our holiness and justice is [[Is 64:6|as the rag of a menstruous woman|quasi pannus menstruatæ]]. For [[Job 25:5|Behold even the moon doth not shine, and the stars are not pure in his sight|Ecce enim luna non splendet, et stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus]]: [[Job 4:18|in his angels he found wickedness|in angelis suis reperit pravitatem]]. For what is the divine essence itself but wisdom above being, exemplary truth, first virtue, supreme justice, infinite charity, uncircumscribed light, unmixed purity? Let no one, then, boast, or think himself anything, or despise another, or compare himself with open transgressors; but always placing himself in the sight and presence of the divine holiness, let him, in the light of it, hold as nothing whatever virtue he finds is or can be in himself, and strive ceaselessly to keep himself in the depth of humility.

paras.t: Hucusque sancta Maria recoluit beneficia sibi singulariter data; nunc generaliter sibi ac aliis præstita exprimit. Et misericordia ejus, id est suæ æternæ pietatis effectus et gratia, extenditur et fuit a progenie, quæ ab initio mundi ante diluvium fuit, in progenies posteriores. Misericordia enim Domini plena est terra. Vel, A progenie Judæorum, in progenies gentium. Salus namque gentibus communicata, ex Judæis fluxit et cœpta est, quemadmodum Christus testatur: Salus ex Judæis est. Nam et Christus ex eis incarnari elegit, et per Apostolorum (natione Judæorum) doctrinam conversus est mundus. Timentibus eum timore filiali ac casto. Nam talibus tantum finaliter prodest gratia Dei, et ipsi dumtaxat participes sunt fructus ac meriti dominicæ passionis, quæ licet se ad universos extendat per suam sufficientiam, non tamen per efficientiam, sed ad solos electos. Hinc ait Psalmista: Misericordia autem Domini ab æterno et usque in æternum super timentes eum. In Ecclesiastico quoque habetur: Qui sine timore est, justificari non potest. Verumtamen nullus tam reprobus est, ut divinæ clementiæ penitus expers consistat; sed misericordia ad salutem veram perducens, solis timentibus Deum filiali et reverentiali timore, qui est fuga mali culpæ, impenditur.
paras.en: Up to this point holy Mary has recalled the benefits given to her alone; now she expresses those bestowed in general on herself and on others. [[1:50|And his mercy|Et misericordia ejus]], that is, the working and grace of His eternal loving-kindness, reaches and has been [[1:50|from generation|a progenie]], the generation that was from the beginning of the world before the flood, [[1:50|unto generations|in progenies]] that came after. For [[Ps 32:5|the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord|Misericordia enim Domini plena est terra]]. Or: from the generation of the Jews unto the generations of the Gentiles. For the salvation imparted to the Gentiles flowed and began from the Jews, as Christ testifies: [[John 4:22|For salvation is of the Jews|Salus ex Judæis est]]. For Christ too chose to become incarnate of them, and the world was converted by the teaching of the Apostles, who were Jews by nation. [[1:50|to them that fear him|Timentibus eum]] with a filial and chaste fear. For the grace of God profits in the end only such as these, and they alone share in the fruit and merit of the Lord's passion, which, though it extends to all by its sufficiency, yet by its efficacy reaches the elect alone [the scholastic distinction: Christ's passion is *sufficient* for all men, *efficacious* only in those who are saved]. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 102:17|But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon them that fear him|Misericordia autem Domini ab æterno et usque in æternum super timentes eum]]. In Ecclesiasticus too we have: [[Ecclus 1:28|he that is without fear, cannot be justified|Qui sine timore est, justificari non potest]]. Yet no one is so reprobate as to be wholly without a share in the divine clemency; but the mercy that leads to true salvation is bestowed only on those who fear God with a filial and reverent fear, which is the flight from the evil of sin.

paras.t: Fecit potentiam, id est, potenter operatus est et potentes egit effectus, in brachio suo, id est sua sublimi virtute, juxta illud in Exodo: Eduxit filios Israel in brachio excelso. Vel, In brachio suo, id est per Unigenitum suum incarnatum: et tunc refertur ad Patrem, de cujus Filio loquitur Isaias: Brachium Domini cui revelatum est? Quem Apostolus nominat Dei virtutem. Porro per Filium Pater universa creavit, per ipsum redemit mundum, prostravit diabolum, fregit infernum, aperuit cœlum, infinita quoque per ipsum fecit miracula. Unde et Filius protestatur: A me ipso facio nihil; Pater vero in me manens, ipse facit opera. Nihilo minus Christus ut Deus, propria operabatur virtute, quæ in tribus supersanctis Personis una est in se, indivisa quoque in opere. Denique magnificentissimum opus Dei in Incarnatione seu Verbo incarnato apparuit, dum naturæ duæ in infinitum distantes, in unam convenerunt personam, dum Christus de clauso Virginis utero prodiit, dum Sacramentum altaris instituit. Magnam demum Deus potestatem exercuit, tam humilem juvenculam faciendo suam Matrem, angelorumque Dominam, et omni pura creatura, prout in esse creato subsistente, præstantiorem.
paras.en: [[1:51|He hath shewed might|Fecit potentiam]], that is, He has worked mightily and brought about mighty effects, [[1:51|in his arm|in brachio suo]], that is, by His sublime power, according to that in Exodus: He brought the children of Israel out [[Acts 13:17|with an high arm|in brachio excelso]][[Ex 6:6||]] [Denis says “in Exodus”; the words are nearest Acts 13:17, and the margin gives both Exod. vi, 6 and Act. xiii, 17]. Or: *in his arm*, that is, through His only-begotten Son made flesh: and then it refers to the Father, of whose Son Isaias speaks: [[Is 53:1|to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?|Brachium Domini cui revelatum est?]] [the margin reads Is. iii, 4; the words are those of Is 53:1]. Him the Apostle calls [[1 Cor 1:24|the power of God|Dei virtutem]]. Now through the Son the Father created all things, through Him He redeemed the world, laid low the devil, broke hell, opened heaven, and through Him worked miracles without number. Hence the Son too declares: [[John 8:28|I do nothing of myself|A me ipso facio nihil]]; [[John 14:10|But the Father who abideth in me, he doth the works|Pater vero in me manens, ipse facit opera]]. Nonetheless Christ as God worked by His own power, which in the three most holy Persons is one in itself, and undivided in its working too. Lastly, the most magnificent work of God appeared in the Incarnation, or in the Word made flesh: when two natures infinitely distant came together in one person; when Christ came forth from the closed womb of the Virgin; when He instituted the Sacrament of the altar. And God exercised great power in making so lowly a young maiden His Mother, Lady of the angels, and more excellent than every mere creature, as subsisting in created being.

paras.t: Quoniam universæ viæ Domini misericordia et veritas seu æquitas, commendato Deo ratione suæ clementiæ, commendat eum nunc Virgo sapientissima ab effectibus suæ justitiæ. Dispersit superbos, id est, per varios errores ac vitia dispergi permisit, et per diversa supplicia perdidit ac damnavit effective elatos, quorum spiritus tumet inique, qui Deo subjici et parere omittunt, nec curant sub ejus omnipotenti manu se humiliare; mente, id est intentione et libito, cordis, id est intellectus sui, quo cuncta discernit, judicat et disponit. Hinc in Ecclesiastico scribitur: Radices gentium superbarum arefecit Deus. Qui per Sophoniam quoque minatur: Visitabo super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur; et apud Isaiam, Incurvabitur sublimitas hominum, et humiliabitur altitudo virorum. Dæmones quoque superbientes Christus in mundum veniens dispersit, vicit, et de hominum cordibus expulit. Sed et superbos Judæos videmus ab eo in omnem regionem dispersos.
paras.en: Since [[Ps 24:10|All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth|universæ viæ Domini misericordia et veritas]], or equity, the most wise Virgin, having praised God for His clemency, now praises Him from the effects of His justice. [[1:51|he hath scattered the proud|Dispersit superbos]], that is, He has let them be scattered through various errors and vices, and by various punishments has in effect destroyed and condemned the lifted up, whose spirit swells wickedly, who fail to submit to God and obey Him, and care not to humble themselves under His almighty hand[[1 Pet 5:6||]]; [[1:51|in the conceit of their heart|mente]] [*mente cordis sui*, literally “in the mind of their heart”], that is, in the intention and pleasure of their heart, that is, of their understanding, by which a man discerns, judges and disposes all things. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:18|God hath made the roots of proud nations to wither|Radices gentium superbarum arefecit Deus]]. He threatens too through Sophonias: [[Soph 1:9|I will visit in that day upon every one that entereth arrogantly|Visitabo super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur]]; and in Isaias: [[Is 2:17|the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be humbled|Incurvabitur sublimitas hominum, et humiliabitur altitudo virorum]] [the margin reads Is. iii, 17; the words are those of Is 2:17]. The proud demons, too, Christ scattered at His coming into the world, conquered them and drove them out of the hearts of men. And we see the proud Jews also scattered by Him into every land.

paras.t: Deposuit potentes de sede. Non de quibuscumque potentibus dicitur hoc, quum in libro Job dicatur, Deus potentes non abjicit, quum ipse sit potens; sed de potentibus sua potestate vitiose utentibus, de quibus scriptum est in Ecclesiastico: Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis. Verum, quum hujusmodi potentes videamus usque ad senectutem regnare, quomodo Deus deponit eos de sede dignitatis ac præsidentiæ? Et respondendum, quod saltem in morte: et frequenter propter eorum peccata occiduntur, plagantur, seu ante tempus naturalis periodi auferuntur: Omnis enim potentatus brevis vita; sicut et rex hodie est, et cras morietur. De quibus loquitur Isaias: Et quidem neque satus, neque radicatus in terra truncus eorum; repente flavit in eos et aruerunt. Hinc scriptum est: Vidi impios Domino flante periisse; et rursus in libro eodem, Iniqui ante tempus suum sublati sunt. Insuper, potentes Judæorum magistros Deus de sede doctrinæ amovit. Judiciariam quoque potestatem pauperibus tribuit in die Judicii exercendam: Sedebitis, inquiens, super sedes duodecim.
paras.en: [[1:52|He hath put down the mighty from their seat|Deposuit potentes de sede]]. This is not said of any and every mighty man, since it is said in the book of Job: [[Job 36:5|God doth not cast away the mighty, whereas he himself also is mighty|Deus potentes non abjicit, quum ipse sit potens]]; but of the mighty who use their power viciously, of whom it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:17|God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes, and hath set up the meek in their stead.|Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis.]] But since we see such mighty men reigning even into old age, how does God put them down from the seat of dignity and rule? The answer is: at least in death; and often for their sins they are slain, stricken, or taken away before the time of their natural span: for [[Ecclus 10:11|All power is of short life|Omnis enim potentatus brevis vita]]; [[Ecclus 10:12|so also a king is to day, and to morrow he shall die|sicut et rex hodie est, et cras morietur]]. Of them Isaias says: [[Is 40:24|And surely their stock was neither planted, nor sown, nor rooted in the earth: suddenly he hath blown upon them, and they are withered|Et quidem neque satus, neque radicatus in terra truncus eorum; repente flavit in eos et aruerunt]]. Hence it is written: I have seen the wicked [[Job 4:9|Perishing by the blast of God|Domino flante periisse]] [Denis gives the sense of Job 4:8–9 in brief]; and again in the same book: [[Job 22:16|Who were taken away before their time|ante tempus suum sublati sunt]]. Moreover, God removed the mighty masters of the Jews from the seat of teaching. And He gave the poor the power of judging, to be exercised on the day of Judgement: [[Matt 19:28|you also shall sit on twelve seats|Sedebitis, inquiens, super sedes duodecim]], He says.

paras.t: Et exaltavit humiles, nunc per dona gratiæ gratum facientis et gratis datæ, quia et tales frequenter ad prælationem erexit; in futuro autem per dona gloriæ et sublimationem usque ad cœlum empyreum. Propter quod ait Scriptura: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam; et denuo, Beati pauperes spiritu, scilicet humiles, quoniam vestrum est regnum cœlorum (quo nihil est altius). Potissimum autem Christus exaltavit suos Apostolos vere humillimos: quos constituit principes super omnem terram; de quibus scriptum est, Quoniam dii fortes terræ vehementer elevati sunt. Ceteros quoque primitivæ Ecclesiæ filios, suos discipulos, non mediocriter exaltavit, non in futuro dumtaxat, sed etiam in præsenti, dans eis virtutem calcandi super serpentes et scorpiones, omnemque inimici virtutem.
paras.en: [[1:52|and hath exalted the humble|Et exaltavit humiles]]: now, by the gifts of sanctifying grace and of grace freely given [*gratia gratum faciens*, which makes the soul pleasing to God, and *gratia gratis data*, given for the good of others], since He has also often raised such men to high office; and in the life to come by the gifts of glory and by lifting them up even to the empyrean heaven. Wherefore Scripture says: [[Jas 4:6|God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble|Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam]]; and again: [[Luke 6:20|Blessed are ye poor|Beati pauperes]] in spirit, that is, the humble, for yours is the kingdom of heaven (than which nothing is higher) [Denis joins Luke 6:20, which the margin gives, with the words of Matt 5:3]. Above all Christ exalted His Apostles, who were truly most humble: whom He [[Ps 44:17|shalt make them princes over all the earth|constituit principes super omnem terram]]; of whom it is written: [[Ps 46:10|for the strong gods of the earth are exceedingly exalted|Quoniam dii fortes terræ vehementer elevati sunt]]. The other sons of the primitive Church as well, His disciples, He exalted in no small measure, not only in the life to come but also in the present, giving them [[Luke 10:19|power to tread upon serpents and scorpions|virtutem calcandi super serpentes et scorpiones]], and upon all the power of the enemy.

paras.t: Esurientes, id est spiritualia bona avide cupientes, implevit bonis, id est gratiæ donis, internis divitiis, refectionibus mentis. Pauperes quoque corporaliter famescentes Deus alit et implet, quemadmodum scriptum est: Oculi omnium in te sperant, Domine, et tu das escam illorum in tempore opportuno; itemque: Omnia a te exspectant ut des illis escam in tempore; dante te illis colligent. De esurientibus autem primo modo ait Salvator: Beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur; et in Apocalypsi, Ego sitienti dabo de fonte aquæ vitæ gratis.
paras.en: [[1:53|He hath filled the hungry|Esurientes]], that is, those who eagerly desire spiritual goods, [[1:53|with good things|bonis]], that is, with the gifts of grace, with inward riches, with refreshments of the mind. The poor too who hunger in body God feeds and fills, as it is written: [[Ps 144:15|The eyes of all hope in thee, O Lord: and thou givest them meat in due season.|Oculi omnium in te sperant, Domine, et tu das escam illorum in tempore opportuno.]] and again: [[Ps 103:27|All expect of thee that thou give them food in season.|Omnia a te exspectant ut des illis escam in tempore]] [[Ps 103:28|What thou givest to them they shall gather up|dante te illis colligent]]. Of those who hunger in the first way the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:6|Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice: for they shall have their fill.|Beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam: quoniam ipsi saturabuntur.]] and in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:6|To him that thirsteth, I will give of the fountain of the water of life, freely|Ego sitienti dabo de fonte aquæ vitæ gratis]].

paras.t: Et divites, id est divitiarum corporalium inordinatos amatores, terrena cœlestibus præferentes, dimisit inanes, id est a spiritualibus bonis vacuos, suisque vanitatibus inhærentes. De quibus loquitur Christus: Possibilius est camelum transire per foramen acus, quam divitem intrare in regnum cœlorum. Jacobus quoque in sua Canonica: Agite nunc, divites, plorate, ululantes in miseriis, quæ advenient vobis. De quo infra habetur: Væ vobis divitibus, qui nunc habetis consolationem vestram. Divitiæ enim pene ad omnia vitia præbent fomentum, ad superbiam, gulam, luxuriam, otiositatem scelerum matrem. Propter quod beatus scribit Apostolus: Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem et laqueum diaboli, et desideria multa, inutilia et nociva, quæ mergunt hominem in interitum et perditionem. Ideo ait Scriptura: Nihil est iniquius quam amare pecuniam; hic enim animam suam habet venalem. Verumtamen sunt aliqui divites virtuosi, sua opulentia bene liberaliterque utentes, misericorditer distribuentes, non delicate viventes, nec ad terrena inordinate affecti, sicut hortatur Psalmista: Divitiæ si affluant, nolite cor apponere. Sed quam pauci sint tales, liquet ex eo quod scriptum est in Ecclesiastico: Beatus dives qui inventus est sine macula, qui post aurum non abiit, nec speravit in pecunia et thesauris: quis est hic? et laudabimus eum. Fecit enim mirabilia in vita sua. Nemo ergo se committat periculo, sed acquiescat Apostolo: Habentes, inquit, victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus. Hinc in Proverbiis Salomon deprecatur: Mendicitatem et divitias, Domine, ne dederis mihi; tribue tantum victui meo necessaria.
paras.en: [[1:53|and the rich|Et divites]], that is, the inordinate lovers of bodily riches, who prefer earthly things to heavenly, [[1:53|he hath sent empty away|dimisit inanes]], that is, empty of spiritual goods and clinging to their own vanities. Of whom Christ says: [[Matt 19:24|It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven|Possibilius est camelum transire per foramen acus, quam divitem intrare in regnum cœlorum]]. James too in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jas 5:1|Go to now, ye rich men: weep and howl in your miseries, which shall come upon you|Agite nunc, divites, plorate, ululantes in miseriis, quæ advenient vobis]]. Of this we have below: [[Luke 6:24|woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation|Væ vobis divitibus, qui nunc habetis consolationem vestram]]. For riches feed nearly all the vices: pride, gluttony, lust, and idleness, the mother of crimes. Wherefore the blessed Apostle writes: [[1 Tim 6:9|they that will become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil and into many unprofitable and hurtful desires, which drown men into destruction and perdition|Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem et laqueum diaboli, et desideria multa, inutilia et nociva, quæ mergunt hominem in interitum et perditionem]]. Therefore Scripture says: [[Ecclus 10:10|There is not a more wicked thing than to love money|Nihil est iniquius quam amare pecuniam]]; for such a one [[Ecclus 10:10|setteth even his own soul to sale|animam suam habet venalem]]. Yet there are some rich men who are virtuous, using their wealth well and liberally, distributing it mercifully, not living delicately, nor inordinately attached to earthly things, as the Psalmist exhorts: [[Ps 61:11|if riches abound, set not your heart upon them|Divitiæ si affluant, nolite cor apponere]] [the margin reads Ps. xxi, 11; the words are those of Ps 61:11]. But how few such men are is plain from what is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 31:8|Blessed is the rich man that is found without blemish: and that hath not gone after gold, nor put his trust in money nor in treasures|Beatus dives qui inventus est sine macula, qui post aurum non abiit, nec speravit in pecunia et thesauris]]: [[Ecclus 31:9|Who is he, and we will praise him? for he hath done wonderful things in his life.|Quis est hic? et laudabimus eum: fecit enim mirabilia in vita sua.]] Let no one, then, put himself in danger, but let him rest content with the Apostle: [[1 Tim 6:8|having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content|Habentes, inquit, victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus]]. Hence Solomon prays in Proverbs: [[Prov 30:8|Give me neither beggary, nor riches: give me only the necessaries of life|Mendicitatem et divitias, Domine, ne dederis mihi; tribue tantum victui meo necessaria]].

paras.t: Quidam per esurientes bonis impletos, intelligunt gentiles conversos, quibus verbum Dei cum magno desiderio audientibus, maxima gratiarum charismata contulit Deus; per divites vero inanes relictos, intelligunt magistros Judæorum, in Scripturis abundantes, qui in sua cæcitate dimissi sunt.
paras.en: Some understand by *the hungry filled with good things* the converted Gentiles, on whom, as they heard the word of God with great desire, God bestowed the greatest gifts of grace; and by *the rich sent empty away* the masters of the Jews, rich in the Scriptures, who were left in their blindness.

paras.t: Consequenter tangit beata Virgo beneficia Judæis exhibita. Suscepit ipse Dominus, Israel puerum suum, id est, Israeliticum populum sibi nunc gratiose ac pie applicuit et conjunxit, de ipso naturam assumendo humanam: per quod totum populum illum quantum in se fuit, salvare proposuit. Propter quod ad Hebræos scribit Apostolus: Nusquam angelos, sed semen Abrahæ apprehendit. Recordatus misericordiæ suæ, id est, memorem se ostendens pietatis et gratiæ, quam populo huic promisit, quod scilicet de eo formam servi acciperet. In incommutabili autem Deo nec recordatio, nec oblivio proprie locum habent; sed per modum recordantis se habet, dum misereri non differt, per modum obliviscentis, dum differt.
paras.en: Next the blessed Virgin touches on the benefits shown to the Jews. [[1:54|He hath received|Suscepit]] (the Lord Himself) [[1:54|Israel his servant|Israel puerum suum]], that is, He has now graciously and lovingly drawn to Himself and joined to Himself the people of Israel, by taking human nature from it: whereby He purposed, as far as lay in Him, to save that whole people. Wherefore the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: [[Heb 2:16|For nowhere doth he take hold of the angels: but of the seed of Abraham he taketh hold|Nusquam angelos, sed semen Abrahæ apprehendit]]. [[1:54|being mindful of his mercy|Recordatus misericordiæ suæ]], that is, showing Himself mindful of the loving-kindness and grace that He promised to this people: namely, that He would take from it [[Phil 2:7|the form of a servant|formam servi]]. In the unchangeable God, however, neither remembering nor forgetting properly has place; but He behaves in the manner of one who remembers when He does not put off showing mercy, and in the manner of one who forgets when He puts it off.

paras.t: Sicut locutus est ad patres nostros Abraham et semini ejus in sæcula. Primo enim Abrahæ, deinde Isaac, postea ipsi Jacob, facta legitur in Genesi divina illa promissio: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Deinceps dictum est David: De fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem tuam. Generaliter quoque sancti Patriarchæ ac vates de Christi adventu locuti sunt, quemadmodum in Actibus Petrus affirmat: Omnes Prophetæ a Samuele et deinceps annuntiaverunt dies istos. Porro clausula illa, In sæcula, referri potest ad verbum illud, Suscepit, item ad, Recordatus, necnon et ad complexum istud, Semini ejus: nam illa gratiosa susceptio electorum, et recordatio Dei circa eos semenque Abrahæ, in prædestinatis manet perpetuo, et nunquam periturum habet effectum.
paras.en: [[1:55|As he spoke to our fathers: to Abraham and to his seed for ever|Sicut locutus est ad patres nostros Abraham et semini ejus in sæcula]]. For we read in Genesis that this divine promise was made first to Abraham, then to Isaac, afterwards to Jacob himself: [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes]][[Gen 26:4||]][[Gen 28:14||]]. Afterwards it was said to David: [[Ps 131:11|of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne|De fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem tuam]]. In general, too, the holy Patriarchs and prophets spoke of Christ's coming, as Peter affirms in the Acts: [[Acts 3:24|all the prophets, from Samuel and afterwards, who have spoken, have told of these days|Omnes Prophetæ a Samuele et deinceps annuntiaverunt dies istos]]. Further, the closing words *for ever* can be referred to the word *He hath received*, also to *being mindful*, and to the phrase *to his seed*: for that gracious receiving of the elect, and God's remembrance of them and of the seed of Abraham, remains for ever in the predestined, and has an effect that will never perish.

paras.t: Ecce canticum istud dulcissimum, quam sententiosum est sub brevitate verborum. Quod Spiritus Sancti consilio statuit Ecclesia in Vesperis decantandum, ut hora illa dum advesperascit et inclinata est dies, incipiat se mens nostra ab exterioribus ad interiora colligere, ad Deum erigere, ejusque bonitatem beneficiaque pensare, ei ex toto affectu gratias agere, ipsum cum jucunditate laudare, atque pro viribus verbo et opere in omnibus honorare. Itaque ad summi Dei honorem et tantæ Virginis reverentiam, non sine mentali attentione et actuali sanctæ devotionis fervore, canticum istud promamus: imo et tunc recordemur, cum quanta devotione et alacritate beatissima Virgo carmen istud cecinerit, et quam ineffabilem ei gratiam præstiterit Deus; sicque eidem Virgini congratulemur in Domino.
paras.en: See how full of meaning this sweetest canticle is, under its brevity of words. By the counsel of the Holy Ghost the Church has appointed it to be sung at Vespers, so that at that hour, when [[Luke 24:29|it is towards evening and the day is now far spent|advesperascit et inclinata est dies]], our mind may begin to gather itself from outward things to inward, to lift itself up to God, to weigh His goodness and benefits, to give Him thanks with all its affection, to praise Him with gladness, and to honour Him in all things, as far as it can, in word and deed. Let us, then, bring forth this canticle to the honour of the most high God and in reverence for so great a Virgin, not without attention of mind and the actual fervour of holy devotion: nay, let us then recall with what great devotion and eagerness the most blessed Virgin sang this song, and what unspeakable grace God gave her; and so let us rejoice with that same Virgin in the Lord.

paras.t: Postremo, quilibet nostrum canticum hoc in propria potest decantare persona, dicendo intimis ex medullis: Magnificat anima mea Dominum, et exsultavit spiritus meus in Deo, etc., juxta expositionem præhabitam. Sic autem Deum laudare, est actus omnino angelicus et præclarus. Quia respexit humilitatem ancillæ suæ, id est animæ meæ, quæ in oculis suis vilis et modica est; vel, Ancillæ suæ, id est creaturæ, quæ ego sum: creatura enim Creatoris sui ministra est. Ecce enim ex hoc beatam me creaturam dicent, ut pie confido, omnes generationes electæ. Nil enim, ut ait Hieronymus, felicius Christiano, cui regna promittuntur cœlorum. In patria quoque unusquisque electorum ab aliis beatus dicetur. Sed et Christiani veraciter sibi invicem dicere possunt grata et humili mente illud Baruch: Beati sumus nos, quoniam quæ Deo placita sunt, manifesta sunt nobis; denique: Beata gens cujus Dominus Deus ejus, populus quem elegit in hereditatem sibi. Quia fecit mihi magna. Hoc dicendo, cogitet unusquisque beneficia Dei circa se generalia et specialia, bona naturæ, dona gratiæ, promissaque gloriæ, quanta pro se Filius Dei fecit, assumpsit ac pertulit, quoties sibi in peccatis pepercit, quod ad istam pœnitentiæ gratiam se adduxit. Cetera specialem expositionem non exigunt, sed juxta interpretationem præscriptam a quolibet queunt proferri.
paras.en: Lastly, any one of us can sing this canticle in his own person, saying from his inmost heart: [[1:46|My soul doth magnify the Lord|Magnificat anima mea Dominum]], [[1:47|And my spirit hath rejoiced in God|et exsultavit spiritus meus in Deo]], etc., according to the exposition already given. To praise God so is an act wholly angelic and glorious. [[1:48|Because he hath regarded the humility of his handmaid|Quia respexit humilitatem ancillæ suæ]], that is, of my soul, which is base and small in its own eyes; or, *of his handmaid*, that is, of the creature that I am: for the creature is the handmaid of its Creator. [[1:48|For behold from henceforth|Ecce enim ex hoc]] all the elect generations shall call me a blessed creature, as I loyally trust. For nothing, as Jerome says, is happier than a Christian, to whom the kingdom of heaven is promised. In the fatherland, too, each of the elect will be called blessed by the others. And Christians can truly say to one another, with grateful and humble mind, that word of Baruch: [[Bar 4:4|We are happy, O Israel: because the things that are pleasing to God, are made known to us|Beati sumus nos, quoniam quæ Deo placita sunt, manifesta sunt nobis]]; and again: [[Ps 32:12|Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord: the people whom he hath chosen for his inheritance|Beata gens cujus Dominus Deus ejus, populus quem elegit in hereditatem sibi]]. [[1:49|hath done great things to me|Quia fecit mihi magna]]. In saying this, let each one think of the benefits of God towards him, general and particular: the goods of nature, the gifts of grace, and the promises of glory; how much the Son of God did, took upon Himself and suffered for him; how often He spared him in his sins; that He has brought him to this grace of penance. The rest needs no special exposition, but can be said by anyone according to the interpretation given above.

paras.t: Mansit autem Maria cum illa (Elisabeth) quasi mensibus tribus, et reversa est in domum suam, in Nazareth. Communiter dicunt doctores, quod non recesserit Maria quousque nasceretur Joannes. Unde in Scholastica fertur historia, quod ipsa infantem levavit de terra, ut scribitur in Libro justorum, id est Nazaræorum, ut quidam explanant. Verumtamen aliqui, ut Theophilus et Græcus, affirmant quod imminente partu Elisabeth, Maria abierit, eo quod jam aliæ feminæ ad Elisabeth confluxissent, et quoniam in partu mulierum virgines adesse non solent. Evangelista quoque primo scribit recessisse Mariam, quam de partu Elisabeth.
paras.en: [[1:56|And Mary abode with her|Mansit autem Maria cum illa]] (Elizabeth) [[1:56|about three months. And she returned to her own house|quasi mensibus tribus, et reversa est in domum suam]], in Nazareth. The doctors commonly say that Mary did not leave until John was born. Hence it is related in the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor] that she lifted the infant from the ground, as is written in the Book of the Just, that is, of the Nazarenes, as some explain. Yet some, such as Theophilus [Theophylact] and the Greek [commentator], affirm that Mary went away when Elizabeth's delivery was at hand, because other women had already gathered to Elizabeth, and because virgins are not wont to be present when women give birth. The Evangelist, too, writes of Mary's going away before he writes of Elizabeth's delivery.

1.title: Explanatio residuæ partis hujus primi capituli, in qua et canticum Zachariæ elucidatur
1.title_en: Explanation of the rest of this first chapter, in which the canticle of Zachary is also explained
1.note: Some lines at the foot of PDF 428 (p. 408) are unreadable in the scan's OCR; the gaps are marked […].

paras.t: Subinde nativitas Præcursoris describitur. Elisabeth autem impletum est tempus pariendi, id est, ipsi Elisabeth mensis nonus advenit, et peperit filium. Et audierunt vicini et cognati ejus, quia magnificavit Dominus misericordiam suam cum illa, id est, valde clementer egit cum ipsa, pietatis suæ effectus circa eam exercens tam gratiose, quod scilicet non obstante naturali sterilitate ac senio, prolem concepisset ac peperisset, essetque a sterilitatis opprobrio liberata; et congratulabantur ei, ex dilectione qua eam ejusque maritum amabant: quia sine querela inter alios conversabantur Zacharias et Elisabeth. Unde sua conversatione pacifica, benigna et justa, utpote ex justitia et pietate convenienter temperata, universis se exhibuerunt amabiles: propter quod eorum prosperitati congratulati sunt alii.
paras.en: Next the birth of the Forerunner is described. [[1:57|Now Elizabeth's full time of being delivered was come|Elisabeth autem impletum est tempus pariendi]], that is, the ninth month came for Elizabeth, [[1:57|and she brought forth a son|et peperit filium]]. [[1:58|And her neighbors and kinsfolks heard that the Lord had shewed his great mercy towards her|Et audierunt vicini et cognati ejus, quia magnificavit Dominus misericordiam suam cum illa]] [literally “had magnified His mercy with her”], that is, had dealt very mercifully with her, showing the effects of His loving-kindness towards her so graciously that, in spite of her natural barrenness and old age, she had conceived and brought forth a child and was freed from the reproach of barrenness; [[1:58|and they congratulated with her|et congratulabantur ei]], out of the love with which they loved her and her husband: for Zachary and Elizabeth lived among others without blame. So by their peaceable, kindly and just manner of life, tempered fittingly by justice and loving-kindness, they made themselves lovable to all: and for this reason others rejoiced with them in their good fortune.

paras.t: Et factum est in die octavo a nativitate infantis, venerunt circumcidere puerum. Illo etenim die secundum legis præceptum circumcisio fieri consuevit, juxta illud in Genesi: Infans octo dierum circumcidetur. Et vocabant eum nomine patris sui Zachariam. Primogenitis namque, et præsertim unigenitis, solet frequenter nomen patris imponi. Istis autem spes non erat quod Zacharias et Elisabeth amplius prolificarent. Porro, sicut in novo Testamento nomen imponitur in Baptismo, ita tunc in circumcisione. Sed quum Joannes sanctificatus esset in utero, et ab originali purgatus, cur circumcisus fuit, quum circumcisio esset remedium contra originale peccatum? Respondent quidam, quod circumcisus sit non ob indigentiam remedii, sed propter observationem præcepti; item ne alii scandalizarentur, et causa singularitatis vitandæ, et quia fortasse per circumcisionem illam ita pœnalem ad gratiam disponebatur majorem.
paras.en: [[1:59|And it came to pass that on the eighth day|Et factum est in die octavo]] from the birth of the infant, [[1:59|they came to circumcise the child|venerunt circumcidere puerum]]. For on that day, according to the precept of the law, circumcision was wont to be done, according to the word in Genesis: [[Gen 17:12|An infant of eight days old shall be circumcised|Infans octo dierum circumcidetur]]. [[1:59|and they called him by his father's name Zachary|Et vocabant eum nomine patris sui Zachariam]]. For the father's name is often given to first-born sons, and especially to only sons; and these people had no hope that Zachary and Elizabeth would have any more children. Further, as in the New Testament the name is given in Baptism, so then it was given in circumcision. But since John had been sanctified in the womb and cleansed from original sin, why was he circumcised, seeing that circumcision was a remedy against original sin? Some answer that he was circumcised not because he needed the remedy, but in order to keep the precept; also so that others should not be scandalised, and to avoid singularity, and because perhaps by that circumcision, painful as it was, he was disposed to greater grace.

paras.t: Et respondens mater ejus, dixit: Nequaquam nomine patris appellabitur, sed vocabitur Joannes. Quod enim sic esset vocandus, imo et ab angelo jam vocatus, vocarique jussus, cognovit per spiritum prophetiæ sancta Elisabeth, quia id nulli homini, nisi viro ejus in templo fuerat intimatum, qui ex tunc mutus permansit: nisi forte quis opinetur quod Zacharias scripto id suæ insinuaverit conjugi, sicut in sequentibus enarratur hoc ceteris indicasse. Forte enim quæ sibi in templo fuerant revelata atque illata, taliter indicavit uxori. Et dixerunt ad illam: Quia nemo est in cognatione tua, id est inter consanguineos tuos, qui vocetur hoc nomine: idcirco miramur quod ita vis eum vocari.
paras.en: [[1:60|And his mother answering, said: Not so|Et respondens mater ejus, dixit: Nequaquam]]: he shall not be named by his father's name, [[1:60|But he shall be called John|sed vocabitur Joannes]]. For holy Elizabeth knew by the spirit of prophecy that he was to be so called, nay, that he had already been so called by the angel and ordered to be so called, since this had been made known to no man except her husband in the temple, who from then on remained dumb: unless perhaps someone thinks that Zachary made it known to his wife in writing, as in what follows he is told to have made it known to the others. For perhaps he made known to his wife in this way what had been revealed and laid upon him in the temple. [[1:61|And they said to her: There is none of thy kindred|Et dixerunt ad illam: Quia nemo est in cognatione tua]], that is, among thy blood relations, [[1:61|that is called by this name|qui vocetur hoc nomine]]: and so we wonder that thou wilt have him so called.

paras.t: Innuebant autem, hoc est, signis seu nutibus sensibilibus per modum quæstionis significabant, patri ejus, quem, id est quo nomine, vellet vocari eum. Quia nunc dicitur quod innuebant patri ejus, doctores eliciunt quod Zacharias ob suam incredulitatem præfatam non mutus tantum, sed et surdus fuerat factus: si enim audisset, non nutu, sed verbo ejus voluntatem interrogassent. Et postulans, nutu quodam, non verbo, pugillarem, id est calamum scriptoris, seu tabulam quæ pugillo potest includi, scripsit, dicens verbo scripto, non vocali: Joannes est nomen ejus. Quasi dicat: Non ego, aut mater, infanti nomen impono, sed divinitus per angelum impositum pando. Et mirati sunt universi, videntes in processu negotii miracula miraculis jungi, totque insolita fieri, iterum quod Zacharias et conjux ejus sic concordabant, qui simul a conceptione Joannis conferre non poterant.
paras.en: [[1:62|And they made signs|Innuebant autem]], that is, by signs or nods that could be seen they asked, by way of question, [[1:62|to his father, how he would have him called|patri ejus, quem vellet vocari eum]], that is, by what name. Because it is said here that they made signs to his father, the doctors conclude that Zachary, on account of the unbelief spoken of above, had been made not only dumb but also deaf: for if he had heard, they would have asked his wish not by a sign but by word. [[1:63|And demanding|Et postulans]], by a sign, not by word, [[1:63|a writing table|pugillarem]] [*pugillaris*, from *pugillus*, “a small fist”], that is, a scribe's pen, or a tablet that can be held in the hand, [[1:63|he wrote, saying|scripsit, dicens]], with a written, not a spoken word: [[1:63|John is his name|Joannes est nomen ejus]]. As if he said: It is not I, or his mother, who give the infant his name; I am making known the name given him by God through the angel. [[1:63|And they all wondered|Et mirati sunt universi]], seeing that as the affair went on miracles were joined to miracles, and so many unwonted things happened; and again, that Zachary and his wife so agreed, though they had not been able to confer together since John's conception.

paras.t: Apertum est autem illico os ejus et lingua ejus: id est, mox quum fidem suam scripto indicasset, restitutus est ori et linguæ Zachariæ pristinus usus loquendi; nec dubium quin interim os ejus aperiebatur ad cibum sumendum, sed non ad loquendum. Quemadmodum autem suæ incredulitatis demerito fuit loquela privatus, ita suæ fidelis confessionis merito, loquelæ est restitutus. Propter quod dicit Ambrosius: Linguam quam incredulitas vinxerat, fides solvit. Et loquebatur, benedicens Deum benedictione laudis et gratiarum actionis, qui eum ob suum excessum paternaliter castigavit, et clementer sanavit, juxta illud Tobiæ: Benedico te, Domine Deus Israel, quia tu castigasti me, et tu sanasti me. Sed et ob alias causas benedixit Deum, sicut mox in suo cantico elucescit.
paras.en: [[1:64|And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed|Apertum est autem illico os ejus et lingua ejus]]: that is, as soon as he had shown his faith in writing, the former use of speech was restored to Zachary's mouth and tongue; and no doubt in the meantime his mouth was opened to take food, but not to speak. And as he was deprived of speech through the demerit of his unbelief, so through the merit of his faithful confession he was given back his speech. Wherefore Ambrose says: The tongue which unbelief had bound, faith has loosed. [[1:64|and he spoke, blessing God|Et loquebatur, benedicens Deum]], with a blessing of praise and thanksgiving, who had chastised him like a father for his fault and mercifully healed him, according to the word of Tobias: [[Tob 11:17|I bless thee, O Lord God of Israel, because thou hast chastised me, and thou hast saved me|Benedico te, Domine Deus Israel, quia tu castigasti me, et tu sanasti me]] [Denis has *sanasti*, “healed”, where the Vulgate has *salvasti*]. But he blessed God for other reasons too, as soon becomes clear in his canticle.

paras.t: Et factus est timor super omnes vicinos eorum: id est, vicini Zachariæ et Elisabeth, visis tot mirabilibus, ex consideratione divinæ potentiæ conceperunt timorem, admirationem, stuporem. Causam enim, scilicet omnipotentiam Dei, in suis supernaturalibus perpenderunt effectibus, et tanquam vere præsentem, ac vitia punientem attenderunt. Sic et in Evangelio scriptum est, quod turba visis Christi miraculis, timuerunt. Denique, homo propriæ fragilitatis et culpæ sibimet conscius, considerata Altissimi potestate, non immerito expavescit. Propter quod apud Jeremiam scriptum est: Non est similis tui, Domine; magnus es tu, et magnum nomen tuum in fortitudine: quis non timebit te, o Rex gentium? Et super omnia montana Judææ divulgabantur omnia verba hæc: id est, fama horum mirabilium de punitione et curatione Zachariæ, de Joannis mirabili conceptione, nativitate, appellatione, Judæis in omnibus locis suæ regionis montuosis mirantibus insinuabatur. Magna namque et rara solent undique divulgari, quia libenter audiuntur: siquidem nova placent, et insolita admirationem inducunt. Homo autem naturaliter est animal admirativum, varietatisque cupidum, præsertim quum omnes homines naturaliter scire desiderant.
paras.en: [[1:65|And fear came upon all their neighbours|Et factus est timor super omnes vicinos eorum]]: that is, the neighbours of Zachary and Elizabeth, having seen so many wonders, conceived fear, wonder and amazement from considering the divine power. For they weighed the cause, namely the almighty power of God, in its supernatural effects, and took heed of Him as truly present and as punishing faults. So too it is written in the Gospel that the multitude, seeing Christ's miracles, feared[[Matt 9:8||]]. Lastly, a man conscious of his own frailty and guilt is not without reason struck with dread when he considers the power of the Most High. Wherefore it is written in Jeremias: [[Jer 10:6|There is none like to thee, O Lord: thou art great, and great is thy name in might.|Non est similis tui, Domine; magnus es tu, et magnum nomen tuum in fortitudine]] [[Jer 10:7|Who shall not fear thee, O king of nations?|quis non timebit te, o Rex gentium?]] [[1:65|and all these things were noised abroad over all the hill country of Judea|Et super omnia montana Judææ divulgabantur omnia verba hæc]]: that is, the report of these wonders, of the punishment and healing of Zachary, of the wonderful conception, birth and naming of John, was spread among the Jews, who marvelled at it in all the hilly places of their country. For great and rare things are wont to be spread abroad everywhere, because they are gladly heard: new things please, and unwonted things cause wonder. And man is by nature an animal given to wonder and eager for variety, especially since all men by nature desire to know [as Aristotle says at the opening of the *Metaphysics*].

paras.t: Et posuerunt omnes qui audierant in corde suo, id est, mentibus suis ista tenaciter impresserunt, atque memoriæ diligenter commendaverunt, dicentes, vel quilibet intra se, seu unus ad alium, imo modo utroque: Quis, putas, puer iste erit? quasi dicerent: Notabilis valde consistet, et crescet in virum eximium. Talia enim mirabilia non consueverunt contingere, nisi circa valde electas personas. Ideo subditur: Etenim manus Domini erat cum illo: id est, virtus, gratia, auxilium, operatio supernaturalis ipsius Dei, fuit cum Joanne in ejus sanctificatione, exsultatione in utero matris, ceterisque præfatis: ex quibus probabiliter arguebant, quod tempore procedente futura esset manus Dei cum ipso.
paras.en: [[1:66|And all they that had heard them laid them up in their heart|Et posuerunt omnes qui audierant in corde suo]], that is, they firmly impressed these things on their minds and carefully committed them to memory, [[1:66|saying|dicentes]], either each within himself or one to another, or indeed in both ways: [[1:66|What an one, think ye, shall this child be?|Quis, putas, puer iste erit?]] As if they said: He will be very remarkable, and will grow into an outstanding man. For such wonders are not wont to happen except about persons greatly chosen. Therefore it is added: [[1:66|For the hand of the Lord was with him|Etenim manus Domini erat cum illo]]: that is, the power, grace, help and supernatural working of God Himself was with John in his sanctification, in his leaping in his mother's womb, and in the other things spoken of: from which they argued with likelihood that as time went on the hand of God would be with him.

paras.t: Et Zacharias pater ejus impletus est Spiritu Sancto, et prophetavit, dicens. Quocirca scribit Ambrosius: Vide quam bonus Deus, et facilis indulgere peccatis. Non solum ablata restituit, sed etiam insperata concedit: ille dudum mutus prophetat. Denique, etiam ante hanc horam impletus fuit Zacharias Spiritu Sancto: sed nunc impletus asseritur, quia in donis gratiæ gratificantis ac gratis datæ, jam eminenter profecit, et gratiam prophetalem recenter sortitus est. Recteque prius fertur Spiritu Sancto repletus, quam vaticinatus, eo quod prophetare opus sit Dei, juxta illud Petri: Non voluntate humana allata est aliquando prophetia; sed Spiritu Sancto inspirati, locuti sunt sancti Dei homines.
paras.en: [[1:67|And Zachary his father was filled with the Holy Ghost. And he prophesied, saying|Et Zacharias pater ejus impletus est Spiritu Sancto, et prophetavit, dicens]]. On which Ambrose writes: See how good God is, and how ready to forgive sins. He not only restores what He had taken away, but also grants what was not hoped for: he who was lately dumb prophesies. Moreover, Zachary had been filled with the Holy Ghost even before this hour: but he is now said to be filled, because he had now advanced eminently in the gifts of sanctifying grace and of grace freely given [*gratia gratificans*, the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God; *gratia gratis data*, gifts given for the good of others], and had newly received the grace of prophecy. And rightly is he said first to have been filled with the Holy Ghost and then to have prophesied, because to prophesy is the work of God, according to the word of Peter: [[2 Pet 1:21|For prophecy came not by the will of man at any time: but the holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Ghost.|Non voluntate humana allata est aliquando prophetia; sed Spiritu Sancto inspirati, locuti sunt sancti Dei homines]]

paras.t: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel. In cantico isto Zacharias gratias refert Deo super variis beneficiis ejus, potissimum de Verbi incarnatione ac passione, generisque humani, potissimum Israelitici, salvatione. Quamvis autem in cantico isto, per Dominum Deum Israel intelligi possit Deus absolute, seu Trinitas tota superbenedicta, quælibetque divina Persona; appropriatius tamen de Filio totum exponitur.
paras.en: [[1:68|Blessed be the Lord God of Israel|Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel]]. In this canticle Zachary gives thanks to God for His various benefits, above all for the incarnation and passion of the Word, and for the salvation of mankind, and especially of Israel. And although in this canticle *the Lord God of Israel* can be understood of God absolutely, that is, of the whole most blessed Trinity, or of any divine Person, yet the whole is expounded more fittingly of the Son.

paras.t: Itaque, Benedictus est, et æternaliter benedictus sit, atque ab omnibus jugiter benedicatur, Dominus universorum, ratione possessionis, gubernationis ac præsidentiæ omnium. De quo in Genesi Abraham ait: Levo manum meam ad Dominum Deum possessorem cœli et terræ. De quo etiam scriptum est in libro Job: Quem constituit alium super terram? aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est? Præterea, nomen et ratio Domini, soli omnipotenti Deo plene, summe, pure ac proprie competit: quippe qui solus universale, primordiale, independens, ac nulli subjectum habet dominium; omnium vero sequentium angelorum hominumque dominia sunt particularia, secundaria, indigentia, ac servituti permixta, quia Deo supposita. Hinc apud Isaiam, Jeremiam quoque et Amos, ait Scriptura: Dominus exercituum nomen ejus; et in Psalmo: Dominus nomen illi. Qui iterum ait per Isaiam: Ego Dominus: hoc est nomen meum; gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Deus Israel: qui omnium Deus generaliter fuit jure creationis; specialiter autem Deus tunc dicebatur Israel, id est Israelitici populi, de Jacob (qui alio nomine dictus est Israel) nati: quoniam præcipua ac specialia beneficia populo illi donavit, quemadmodum scriptum est, Qui annuntiat verbum suum Jacob, justitias et judicia sua Israel; et quia a populo illo specialiter colebatur, ceteris ad idololatriam lapsis. Unde in Deuteronomio Moyses huic populo ait: Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram, quia dilexit vos Dominus.
paras.en: So: *Blessed* is, and be eternally blessed, and be blessed unceasingly by all, *the Lord* of all things, by reason of His possessing, governing and presiding over all. Of whom Abraham says in Genesis: [[Gen 14:22|I lift up my hand to the Lord God|Levo manum meam ad Dominum Deum]] [[Gen 14:22|the possessor of heaven and earth|possessorem cœli et terræ]].
