Of whom it is also written in the book of Job: [[Job 34:13|What other hath he appointed over the earth? or whom hath he set over the world which he made?|Quem constituit alium super terram? aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est?]] Moreover, the name and the notion of *Lord* belong fully, supremely, purely and properly to the almighty God alone: for He alone has a lordship that is universal, primordial, independent and subject to none; while the lordships of all the angels and men who come after Him are particular, secondary, needy, and mixed with servitude, because they are subject to God. Hence in Isaias, and in Jeremias and Amos too, Scripture says: [[Is 47:4|the Lord of hosts is his name|Dominus exercituum nomen ejus]][[Jer 10:16||]][[Amos 4:13||]] [the margin's numerals for Isaias are unclear: Is 47:4 or 48:2, which have the same words; the margin also gives Jer. x, 16 and Amos iv, 13]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 67:5|the Lord is his name|Dominus nomen illi]]. And again He says through Isaias: [[Is 42:8|I the Lord, this is my name: I will not give my glory to another|Ego Dominus: hoc est nomen meum; gloriam meam alteri non dabo]]. [[1:68|God of Israel|Deus Israel]]: who was God of all in general by right of creation; but He was then called in a special way the God of Israel, that is, of the people of Israel, born of Jacob (who by another name was called Israel[[Gen 35:10||]]): because He gave chief and special benefits to that people, as it is written: [[Ps 147:8|Who declareth his word to Jacob: his justices and his judgments to Israel|Qui annuntiat verbum suum Jacob, justitias et judicia sua Israel]] [the margin reads Ps. cxlvii, 19, the numbering of the Hebrew]; and because He was worshipped in a special way by that people, when the others had fallen into idolatry. Hence in Deuteronomy Moses says to this people: [[Deut 7:6|The Lord thy God hath chosen thee, to be his peculiar people of all peoples that are upon the earth|Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram]], [[Deut 7:8|because the Lord hath loved you|quia dilexit vos Dominus]].

paras.t: Quia visitavit, id est, per incarnationem accessit, et sicut piissimus ac peritissimus medicus operari aggressus est, et fecit redemptionem plebis suæ, id est liberationem Israeliticæ plebis ab invisibilibus hostibus, a damnatione æterna, a reatu originalis peccati, imo ab omni peccato, quantum in ipso est: quemadmodum per Osee loquitur, De manu mortis liberabo eos, de morte redimam eos. De quo etiam per Isaiam dictum est: Dominus rex noster, ipse veniet et salvabit nos. Qui et apud Zachariam hortatur: Lauda et lætare, filia Sion, quia ecce venio, et habitabo in medio tui. Christi equidem incarnatio, nostra est deificatio, ut asserit Leo Papa. Itaque ejus incarnatio, inchoatio fuit nostræ redemptionis atque salutis, quæ per Christi passionem completæ sunt. Non enim per solam suam incarnationem nos salvare decrevit, sed salvationem nostram per suam passionem consummare instituit. Unde quod Zacharias locutus est, Fecit, more prophetico accipi potest per modum futuri, id est, facturus est, quoniam sua passione fuit redemptionem istam plene facturus, utpote nostra crimina deleturus, nosque Deo reconciliaturus, secundum illud Isaiæ: Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra: et rursus, Posuit Dominus in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Etenim Christus sua passione ac obedientia pro omnibus satisfecit; sed si fructum suæ passionis consequi debemus, oportet ut meritum ejus nobis per sacramenta, seu modo alio, applicetur et communicetur. Hinc Christus de se ipso testatur: Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat.
paras.en: [[1:68|because he hath visited|Quia visitavit]], that is, He drew near by the incarnation, and like a most loving and most skilful physician set about His work, [[1:68|and wrought the redemption of his people|et fecit redemptionem plebis suæ]], that is, the deliverance of the people of Israel from its invisible enemies, from eternal damnation, from the guilt of original sin, nay from all sin, as far as lies in Him: as He says through Osee: [[Osee 13:14|I will deliver them out of the hand of death. I will redeem them from death|De manu mortis liberabo eos, de morte redimam eos]]. Of whom it was also said through Isaias: [[Is 33:22|the Lord is our king: he will save us|Dominus rex noster, ipse veniet et salvabit nos]] [Denis adds *veniet*, “will come”]. And He exhorts through Zacharias: [[Zach 2:10|Sing praise, and rejoice, O daughter of Sion: for behold I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee|Lauda et lætare, filia Sion, quia ecce venio, et habitabo in medio tui]]. Christ's incarnation, indeed, is our deification, as Pope Leo asserts. And so His incarnation was the beginning of our redemption and salvation, which were completed by Christ's passion. For He did not decree to save us by His incarnation alone, but ordained to consummate our salvation by His passion. Hence Zachary's word *wrought* can be taken in the prophetic manner as a future, that is, *will work*: since by His passion He was to work this redemption fully, blotting out our crimes and reconciling us to God, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 53:5|But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins|Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra]]; and again: [[Is 53:6|the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all|Posuit Dominus in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum]]. For Christ made satisfaction for all by His passion and obedience; but if we are to obtain the fruit of His passion, His merit must be applied and communicated to us through the sacraments, or in some other way. Hence Christ testifies of Himself: [[Luke 19:10|the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost|Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat]].

paras.t: Denique, per plebem suam seu populum Dei, intelligi potest non solum plebs Judæorum, sed tota gens electorum: qui sunt populus Dei per prædestinationem æternam, et spiritualiter Israel, id est Deum videns, seu fide contemplans. De quo populo dicit Apostolus: Pax super Israel Dei. Verumtamen, per plebem suam, hoc loco litteralius intelligitur populus Judæorum, ad quorum redemptionem Christus primo, directe, ac principaliter venit, secundum quod asserit: Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel. Quibus verbum Dei spernentibus, justa facta est Apostolorum transmigratio ad instruendos gentiles, pro quorum salvatione Christus quasi secundario venit. Propter quod Paulus et Barnabas dixerunt Judæis: Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei; sed quoniam repulistis illud, convertimur ad gentes.
paras.en: Further, by *His people*, the people of God, can be understood not only the people of the Jews but the whole nation of the elect: who are the people of God by eternal predestination, and spiritually Israel, that is, “seeing God”, or contemplating Him by faith. Of which people the Apostle says: [[Gal 6:16|peace on them and mercy: and upon the Israel of God|Pax super Israel Dei]]. Yet by *His people* is here understood more literally the people of the Jews, for whose redemption Christ came first, directly and principally, as He asserts: [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel]]. When they spurned the word of God, the Apostles justly passed over to instruct the Gentiles, for whose salvation Christ came, as it were, secondarily. Wherefore Paul and Barnabas said to the Jews: [[Acts 13:46|To you it behoved us first to speak the word of God|Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei]]; but since you have rejected it, [[Acts 13:46|we turn to the Gentiles|convertimur ad gentes]].

paras.t: Et erexit, id est, suscitavit, levavit et declaravit, cornu salutis, hoc est annuntiationem beatitudinis veræ atque cœlestis, nobis, id est ad nostram salvationem, ut ei credendo salvemur, in domo David pueri sui, hoc est in tribu seu familia David prophetæ, de cujus semine ortus est Christus, juxta illud Apostoli ad Romanos, Qui factus est ex semine David secundum carnem.
paras.en: [[1:69|And hath raised up|Et erexit]], that is, has stirred up, lifted up and made known, [[1:69|an horn of salvation|cornu salutis]], that is, the announcement of true and heavenly beatitude, [[1:69|to us|nobis]], that is, for our salvation, so that by believing in Him we may be saved, [[1:69|in the house of David his servant|in domo David pueri sui]], that is, in the tribe or family of David the prophet, of whose seed Christ was born, according to that of the Apostle to the Romans: [[Rom 1:3|who was made to him of the seed of David, according to the flesh|Qui factus est ex semine David secundum carnem]].

paras.t: Sed quomodo Deus Israel, scilicet Christus, erexit hoc cornu salutis? Et respondendum, quod per hoc, quod jam ore angelico revelavit Zachariæ statim se incarnandum, venturum et salvaturum genus humanum: cujus utique Christi incarnationem novit Zacharias in Virgine Davidicæ stirpis peractam. Itaque per cornu, publica denuntiatio magnæ rei significatur, quia per cornua solent magnalia notificari: et jam non solum per angelum, sed et per Mariam Deus de hac re prophetavit. Hinc dicit Theophilus: Videbatur Deus dormire, peccata multa respiciens, neque hæc curans; sed in novissimis temporibus incarnatus, excitatus est, contrivitque dæmones nos odientes. — Insuper, per cornu, potestas seu altitudo exprimitur, eo quod cornua sint in animali partes eminentes ac solidæ: eritque sensus, quod Deus robur apicemque salutis, hoc est inviolabilem et cœlestem felicitatem, nobis denuntiavit, in domo David, id est in Christo de progenie David exorto, per quem et in quo beatitudo hæc datur, quia non nisi in Christum credenti præstatur, quemadmodum in Actibus princeps Apostolorum disseruit: Non est aliud nomen sub cœlo datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri.
paras.en: But how did the God of Israel, that is, Christ, raise up this horn of salvation? The answer is: by having already revealed to Zachary, by the mouth of the angel[[1:17||]], that He would forthwith become incarnate, come, and save mankind: and Zachary knew that this incarnation of Christ had been accomplished in the Virgin of David's stock. So by the *horn* is signified the public proclamation of a great thing, since great things are wont to be made known by horns [that is, by the blowing of trumpets]: and now God had prophesied of this not only by the angel but also by Mary[[1:54||]]. Hence Theophilus [Theophylact] says: God seemed to sleep, looking upon many sins and not heeding them; but in the last times, made flesh, He was roused, and crushed the demons that hate us. — Moreover, by *horn* power or loftiness is expressed, because the horns are the prominent and solid parts of an animal: and the sense will be that God has proclaimed to us the strength and summit of salvation, that is, inviolable and heavenly happiness, *in the house of David*, that is, in Christ, sprung from the line of David, through whom and in whom this beatitude is given, since it is granted only to one who believes in Christ, as the prince of the Apostles declared in the Acts: [[Acts 4:12|there is no other name under heaven given to men, whereby we must be saved|Non est aliud nomen sub cœlo datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri]].

paras.t: Postremo, per cornu designatur rex, regia potestas, seu regnum, præsertim in Apocalypsi et Daniele. Unde in Apocalypsi legitur: Vidi de mari ascendentem bestiam habentem capita septem, et cornua decem; et in Daniele: Bestia quarta habebat cornua decem; et ecce cornu aliud parvulum ortum est de medio eorum, et tria de cornibus primis evulsa sunt a facie ejus. Itaque, hic per cornu intelligi potest Christus Rex regum, seu regnum ipsius. Hoc enim cornu erexit, id est, per incarnationem apparere fecit, et declaravit primo in domo David, id est in progenie Davidica, de qua natus est Christus, qui primo in terris visus et conversatus est inter quosdam de sua hac genealogia progenitos. Sic ergo, erexit Deus Pater seu Trinitas, vel Christus secundum quod Deus, cornu salutis, id est Christum regem nostræ salutis: erexit, inquam, eum nobis, secundum quod homo est. Christus nempe secundum divinitatem, erexit se ipsum secundum humanitatem. Quidam istam erectionem referunt ad Christi resurrectionem vel ascensionem, quia tunc Christus cornu salutis, id est potestatem et gloriam beatitudinis, erexit seu publice demonstravit, resurgendo ad vitam immortalem, patres quoque educendo de limbo, et regna ascendendo cœlestia. Sic Zacharias loquitur de futuro per modum præteriti, ut mos est Prophetarum.
paras.en: Lastly, by *horn* is meant a king, royal power, or a kingdom, especially in the Apocalypse and Daniel. Hence we read in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 13:1|I saw a beast coming up out the sea, having seven heads and ten horns|Vidi de mari ascendentem bestiam habentem capita septem, et cornua decem]]; and in Daniel: [[Dan 7:7|a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful, and exceeding strong, it had great iron teeth, eating and breaking in pieces, and treading down the rest with his feet: and it was unlike to the other beasts which I had seen before it, and had ten horns|bestia quarta terribilis atque mirabilis, et fortis nimis: dentes ferreos habebat magnos, comedens atque comminuens, et reliqua pedibus suis conculcans: dissimilis autem erat ceteris bestiis quas videram ante eam, et habebat cornua decem]]; [[Dan 7:8|and behold another little horn sprung out of the midst of them: and three of the first horns were plucked up at the presence thereof|et ecce cornu aliud parvulum ortum est de medio eorum, et tria de cornibus primis evulsa sunt a facie ejus]]. So here by the *horn* can be understood Christ the King of kings, or His kingdom. For this horn He raised up, that is, made it appear through the incarnation, and made it known first *in the house of David*, that is, in the line of David, of which Christ was born, who was first seen on earth and conversed[[Bar 3:38||]] among some who had sprung from this His own lineage. Thus, then, God the Father, or the Trinity, or Christ as God, *raised up an horn of salvation*, that is, Christ the King of our salvation: raised Him up, I say, *for us*, as He is man. For Christ according to His divinity raised up Himself according to His humanity. Some refer this raising up to Christ's resurrection or ascension, since then Christ raised up, or publicly showed, the horn of salvation, that is, the power and glory of beatitude, by rising to immortal life, by leading the fathers out of limbo, and by ascending to the heavenly kingdom. So Zachary speaks of the future in the manner of the past, as is the custom of the Prophets.

paras.t: Hoc itaque Deus fideliter egit, non improvise; sed sicut prædixit, vere implevit. Hinc subditur: Sicut locutus est per os sanctorum, qui a sæculo sunt, Prophetarum ejus, hoc est, sicut prænuntiavit per sanctos Prophetas qui a principio mundi fuerunt, qui verbis, signis, figuris seu factis, de Christo locuti sunt, et ejus mysteria prædixerunt: quia in nulla mundi ætate defuit prophetia de Christo, ut Augustinus declarat. Nam et Adam de Christo verbis et rebus locutus est; similiter ceteri Patriarchæ ac vates. Propter quod in Actibus Petrus testatur: Deus qui prænuntiavit per os omnium Prophetarum pati Christum suum, implevit sic. Et alibi ait: Huic omnes Prophetæ testimonium perhibent. Tantum quippe mysterium, decuit diu ante ac multipliciter prænuntiari, ut ejus dignitas agnoscatur, et factum credibilius ostendatur, firmiusque credatur. Unde in hoc fides nostra certissime confirmatur, quod omnia quæ de Christo credimus et tenemus, taliter prophetata probamus. Sed et ipsi Hebræorum doctores fatentur, quod omnes Prophetæ non sunt locuti, nisi super dies Messiæ, id est pro tempore Christi: quia videlicet quidquid locuti sunt ad Christum finaliter retulerunt, et de ipso principaliter sunt effati. Unde nunc singulariter dicitur, Per os sanctorum, eo quod omnes uno spiritu concorditer sint locuti.
paras.en: This, then, God did faithfully, not unforeseen; but as He foretold, so He truly fulfilled it. Hence there follows: [[1:70|As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who are from the beginning|Sicut locutus est per os sanctorum, qui a sæculo sunt, Prophetarum ejus]], that is, as He foretold through the holy Prophets who have been from the beginning of the world, who spoke of Christ by words, signs, figures or deeds, and foretold His mysteries: for in no age of the world was prophecy of Christ lacking, as Augustine declares. For Adam too spoke of Christ in words and in things; and likewise the other Patriarchs and seers. Wherefore Peter testifies in the Acts: [[Acts 3:18|those things which God before had shewed by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled|Deus qui prænuntiavit per os omnium Prophetarum pati Christum suum, implevit sic]]. And elsewhere he says: [[Acts 10:43|To him all the prophets give testimony|Huic omnes Prophetæ testimonium perhibent]]. For it was fitting that so great a mystery should be foretold long beforehand and in many ways, so that its dignity might be recognised, and the deed shown to be the more credible, and be the more firmly believed. Hence our faith is most surely confirmed in this, that we find all that we believe and hold of Christ to have been so prophesied. Nay, the doctors of the Hebrews themselves confess that all the Prophets spoke only of the days of the Messias, that is, of the time of Christ: since whatever they said they referred in the end to Christ, and spoke principally of Him. Hence it is here said in the singular, *by the mouth of his holy prophets*, because they all spoke in harmony with one spirit.

paras.t: Salutem ex inimicis nostris, et de manu omnium qui oderunt nos. His verbis exponit, quid sit quod dixit, Erexit cornu salutis nobis. Ut sit sensus: Erexit, etc., sicut locutus est, id est, sicut per Prophetas promisit erigere seu procurare nobis, salutem, id est salvationem, ex inimicis nostris, præsertim invisibilibus, hoc est liberationem a dæmonibus, imo etiam a carne et mundo, omnique veræ beatitudinis impedimento. Unde in epistola Joannis scriptum est: In hoc apparuit Filius Dei ut dissolvat opera diaboli. Porro, quod ait, De manu omnium qui oderunt nos, quidam exponunt de gentilibus, quos Christus convertit: et sic inter illos et Judæos conversos pax fuit, inter quos ante inimicitia erat. Potest quoque de cunctis perversis hominibus accipi, a quibus liberantur electi: non quod ab illis in vita hac non tribulentur aut trucidentur; sed quia per timorem inordinatum eis non subjiciuntur, nec ad vitia inducuntur, et per temporalem quam ab illis patiuntur persecutionem, ad gloriam perducuntur æternam, sicque æternaliter liberantur ab omni infestatione illorum, quemadmodum plenius Augustinus declarat super illud Psalmi, A timore inimici eripe animam meam. Hoc est quod apud Michæam promissum est primitivæ Ecclesiæ: Exaltabitur manus tua super hostes tuos, et omnes inimici tui interibunt. Et ibidem de Christo prædictum est: Et erit iste pax, quum venerit, et quando calcaverit in domibus nostris.
paras.en: [[1:71|Salvation from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us|Salutem ex inimicis nostris, et de manu omnium qui oderunt nos]]. With these words he explains what he meant by *hath raised up an horn of salvation to us*. So that the sense is: He hath raised up, etc., *as he spoke*, that is, as He promised through the Prophets to raise up or procure for us *salvation*, that is, saving, *from our enemies*, above all the invisible ones, that is, deliverance from the demons, nay also from the flesh and the world, and from every hindrance to true beatitude. Hence it is written in the epistle of John: [[1 John 3:8|For this purpose the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil|In hoc apparuit Filius Dei ut dissolvat opera diaboli]]. Further, the words *from the hand of all that hate us* some expound of the Gentiles, whom Christ converted: and so there was peace between them and the converted Jews, between whom there had been enmity before[[Eph 2:14||]]. It can also be taken of all perverse men, from whom the elect are delivered: not that they are not afflicted or slain by them in this life, but because they are not made subject to them through inordinate fear, nor led into vice, and through the temporal persecution they suffer from them they are brought to eternal glory, and so are eternally delivered from all their assaults; as Augustine declares more fully on that verse of the Psalm: [[Ps 63:2|deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy|timore inimici eripe animam meam]]. This is what was promised to the primitive Church in Micheas: [[Mich 5:9|Thy hand shall be lifted up over thy enemies, and all thy enemies shall be cut off.|Exaltabitur manus tua super hostes tuos, et omnes inimici tui interibunt.]] And in the same place it was foretold of Christ: [[Mich 5:5|And this man shall be our peace, when|Et erit iste pax, quum]] … [[Mich 5:5|and when he shall set his foot in our houses|quando calcaverit in domibus nostris]] [in Micheas it is the Assyrian who *shall come* and *set his foot in our houses*; Denis runs the words together].

paras.t: Sic ergo erexit nobis salutem, Ad faciendam misericordiam cum patribus nostris, id est ad hoc, ut Patriarchis et justis olim defunctis consummatam misericordiam, utpote plenam felicitatem, impenderet, educendo eos de limbo, et constituendo in cœlesti palatio, quemadmodum apud Zachariam Christo dicitur: Tu quoque, in sanguine testamenti tui, emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu in quo non est aqua. Vel, Ad faciendam misericordiam cum patribus nostris, id est ad hoc, ut misericorditer impleat quod ipsis se præstiturum prædixit. Ideo quoque hæc verba dicuntur, quia non ob nostram justitiam, sed propter suam pietatem immensam Christus hæc nobis largitus est, nostramque assumpsit naturam, sicut ad Titum scribit Apostolus: Apparuit benignitas et humanitas Salvatoris nostri Dei, non ex operibus justitiæ quæ fecimus nos, sed secundum suam misericordiam salvos nos fecit. Et memorari testamenti sui sancti, id est ad hoc, ut per operis exhibitionem ostendat se memorem sancti testamenti, hoc est pacti seu fœderis sui firmissimi quod fecit et iniit cum Patriarchis et vatibus veteris Testamenti, quibus promisit Christus se incarnandum atque in mundum venturum, secundum illud Isaiæ: Propter hoc sciet populus meus nomen meum in die illa, quia ego ipse qui loquebar, ecce adsum. Cujus testamenti ostendit se memorem, naturam assumendo humanam ex Virgine.
paras.en: So, then, He raised up salvation for us, [[1:72|To perform mercy to our fathers|Ad faciendam misericordiam cum patribus nostris]]: that is, to this end, that He might bestow on the Patriarchs and the just long since dead a mercy brought to completion, namely full happiness, by leading them out of limbo and setting them in the heavenly palace; as is said to Christ in Zacharias: [[Zach 9:11|Thou also by the blood of thy testament hast sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit, wherein is no water.|Tu quoque, in sanguine testamenti tui, emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu in quo non est aqua]]. Or, *to perform mercy to our fathers*, that is, to this end, that He might mercifully fulfil what He had foretold to them that He would do. These words are said also because Christ bestowed these things on us, and took our nature, not on account of our justice but because of His own immense loving-kindness; as the Apostle writes to Titus: [[Tit 3:4|the goodness and kindness of God our Saviour appeared|benignitas et humanitas Salvatoris nostri Dei]]: [[Tit 3:5|Not by the works of justice which we have done, but according to his mercy, he saved us|non ex operibus justitiæ quæ fecimus nos, sed secundum suam misericordiam salvos nos fecit]]. [[1:72|and to remember his holy testament|Et memorari testamenti sui sancti]]: that is, to this end, that by showing it in deed He might prove Himself mindful of His holy testament, that is, of His most firm pact or covenant, which He made and entered into with the Patriarchs and prophets of the Old Testament, to whom Christ promised that He would become incarnate and come into the world; according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 52:6|Therefore my people shall know my name in that day: for I myself that spoke, behold I am here.|Propter hoc sciet populus meus nomen meum in die illa, quia ego ipse qui loquebar, ecce adsum]] And He showed Himself mindful of this testament by taking human nature from the Virgin.

paras.t: Sic ergo memoratus est testamenti sui, quod est, Jusjurandum, quia juramento firmatum, quod juravit, jurando per se ipsum, ad Abraham patrem nostrum: quemadmodum in Genesi habetur: Per memetipsum juravi, dicit Dominus: quia fecisti hanc rem, et non pepercisti unigenito tuo propter me, multiplicabo te, et benedicam tibi; et benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes. Ubi per semen Abrahæ intelligitur Christus, secundum Apostolum. Sicque verbis illis promisit Deus Pater Unigenitum suum ex semine Abrahæ incarnandum; vel ipsemet unicus Dei Patris Filius verbis illis promisit se taliter incarnandum. Pater autem dando nobis Filium suum per Incarnationis mysterium, etiam et se ipsum præstitit nobis per gratiam ampliorem.
paras.en: So, then, He remembered His testament, which is [[1:73|The oath|Jusjurandum]], because it was confirmed by an oath, [[1:73|which he swore|quod juravit]], swearing by Himself, [[1:73|to Abraham our father|ad Abraham patrem nostrum]]: as we have it in Genesis: [[Gen 22:16|By my own self have I sworn, saith the Lord: because thou hast done this thing, and hast not spared thy only begotten son for my sake|Per memetipsum juravi, dicit Dominus: quia fecisti hanc rem, et non pepercisti unigenito tuo propter me]], [[Gen 22:17|I will bless thee, and I will multiply thy seed|multiplicabo te, et benedicam tibi]]; [[Gen 22:18|And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|et benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes]]. Where by the seed of Abraham Christ is understood, according to the Apostle[[Gal 3:16||]] [Denis gives the oath in brief: *I will multiply thee, and bless thee*]. And so by those words God the Father promised that His Only-begotten would become incarnate of the seed of Abraham; or the only Son of God the Father Himself promised by those words that He would so become incarnate. And the Father, in giving us His Son through the mystery of the Incarnation, also gave Himself to us by a more abundant grace.

paras.t: Hinc subditur: daturum se nobis. Filius quippe dedit se nobis, exhibendo se fratrem, salvatorem, advocatumque nostrum; imo et aliis modis communicavit se nobis, quia nascendo et conversando in mundo fecit se socium hominum, in Cœna dedit se nobis in cibum, moriendo in pretium liberativum, in patria demum dat se ipsum in objectale ac beatificum præmium. Quod S. Thomas in hymno de Sacramento compendiose tetigit, dicens: Se nascens dedit socium, / Convescens, in edulium, / Se moriens, in pretium, / Se regnans dat in præmium. Hinc etiam Abrahæ in Genesi ait: Ego protector tuus et merces tua magna nimis. Denique illis dicitur Deus se dare, quibus caritatem et gratiam suam infundit: illi etenim habent et possident Deum tanquam suæ dilectionis et occupationis objectum. In quo plena liberalitas, summa dignatio, purissimaque Dei ad nos dilectio demonstratur, quoniam dando nobis dona sua, pariter præstat se ipsum, videlicet ad habendum, ad possidendum, ad intuendum, ad diligendum, ad perfruendum, ad conservandum, ad auxiliandum, ad defendendum, ad commanendum in sempiternum. Illa namque est liberalissima dilectio, qua quis alteri præstat se ipsum. Ideo ait Psalmista: Dominus pars hæreditatis meæ, et calicis mei. Et in libro Threnorum legitur: Pars mea Dominus, dixit anima mea; propterea exspectabo eum. Nunc autem ad litteram sermo est de datione qua Unigenitus datus est nobis, per hoc quod nostram assumpsit naturam, ad peragendam nostram salutem. Unde in Isaia habetur: Parvulus natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis.
paras.en: Hence there follows: [[1:73|that he would grant to us|daturum se nobis]] [literally, “that He would give Himself to us”]. For the Son gave Himself to us, showing Himself our brother[[Matt 28:10||]] [the margin reads Matth. xxvi, 10; Christ calls the disciples His brethren at Matt 28:10], our Saviour[[Luke 2:11||]] and our advocate[[1 John 2:1||]]; nay, He communicated Himself to us in other ways too: for by being born and living in the world He made Himself the companion of men[[Bar 3:38||]], at the Supper He gave Himself to us as food[[John 6:52||]][[Matt 26:26||]], by dying as the price of our deliverance, and in our heavenly home at last He gives Himself as the reward to be beheld, that makes us blessed. St Thomas touched on this briefly in his hymn on the Sacrament, saying: *Se nascens dedit socium, / Convescens, in edulium, / Se moriens, in pretium, / Se regnans dat in præmium* [“Being born, He gave Himself as our companion; / sitting at table, as our food; / dying, as our ransom; / reigning, He gives Himself as our reward”: from the hymn *Verbum supernum prodiens*]. Hence too He says to Abraham in Genesis: [[Gen 15:1|I am thy protector, and thy reward exceeding great|Ego protector tuus et merces tua magna nimis]]. Further, God is said to give Himself to those into whom He pours His charity and grace: for they have and possess God as the object of their love and of their occupation. And in this is shown full liberality, the highest condescension and the purest love of God for us: that in giving us His gifts He gives Himself as well, namely to be had, to be possessed, to be gazed upon, to be loved, to be enjoyed, to keep us, to help us, to defend us, to dwell with us for ever. For that is the most liberal love, by which one gives himself to another. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 15:5|The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup|Dominus pars hæreditatis meæ, et calicis mei]]. And in the book of Lamentations we read: [[Lam 3:24|The Lord is my portion, said my soul: therefore will I wait for him|Pars mea Dominus, dixit anima mea; propterea exspectabo eum]]. Here, however, in the literal sense, the words are about the giving by which the Only-begotten was given to us, in that He took our nature to accomplish our salvation. Hence we have in Isaias: [[Is 9:6|a CHILD IS BORN to us, and a son is given to us|Parvulus natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis]].

paras.t: Deinde ratio hujus subjungitur. Ut sine timore inordinato, carnali, sæculari, servili, de manu inimicorum nostrorum invisibilium seu visibilium, liberati per Christi adventum ac passionem, serviamus illi, scilicet vero Deo servitute latriæ, de qua in Deuteronomio habetur: Dominum Deum timebis et illi soli servies. Est latria virtus Deo cultum cæremoniamque impendens. In sanctitate, hoc est puritate mentali, omni terrena et carnali affectione exclusa, utpote in perfecta cordis conversione ad Deum, universis animæ affectibus reformatis, ordinatis, atque in Deum reductis. Sic nempe supersancto penitusque immensæ munditiæ Deo est obsequendum. Propter quod in Levitico loquitur: Nolite contaminare animas vestras: ego enim sum Dominus Deus vester; sancti estote, quoniam ego sanctus sum. In Deuteronomio quoque dicitur: Perfectus et absque macula eris cum Domino Deo tuo.
paras.en: Next the reason for this is added: [[1:74|without fear|Ut sine timore]], that is, without fear that is inordinate, carnal, worldly, servile; [[1:74|from the hand of our enemies|de manu inimicorum nostrorum]], invisible or visible, [[1:74|being delivered|liberati]] by the coming and passion of Christ, [[1:74|we may serve him|serviamus illi]], namely the true God, with the service of *latria*, of which we have in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 6:13|Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and shalt serve him only|Dominum Deum timebis et illi soli servies]]. *Latria* is the virtue that renders to God worship and ceremony [*latria*: the worship due to God alone]. [[1:75|In holiness|In sanctitate]], that is, in purity of mind, with every earthly and carnal affection shut out, namely in the perfect turning of the heart to God, with all the affections of the soul reformed, set in order and brought back to God. For so must God be served, who is more than holy and of wholly immeasurable cleanness. Wherefore He says in Leviticus: [[Lev 11:43|Do not defile your souls|Nolite contaminare animas vestras]]: [[Lev 11:44|For I am the Lord your God. Be holy because I am holy|ego enim sum Dominus Deus vester; sancti estote, quoniam ego sanctus sum]]. In Deuteronomy too it is said: [[Deut 18:13|Thou shalt be perfect, and without spot before the Lord thy God|Perfectus et absque macula eris cum Domino Deo tuo]].

paras.t: Porro quod ait, Sine timore, referri potest ad illud quod sequitur, Liberati, et ad verbum, Serviamus. Primo modo est sensus, quod sine nostro periculo ac timore Christus nos liberavit, quum tamen plures de hostium manibus non absque ingenti suo pavore atque periculo eruantur. Christus quoque absque sui ipsius inordinato timore nos liberavit. Quamvis passione instante, naturali timore concussus sit, hoc tamen sponte et potestative seu ex prævio rationis judicio contigit, et eumdem timorem, quum voluit, abjecit, atque intrepidus obviam profectus est hostibus. — Si autem referatur ad verbum hoc, Serviamus, iste est sensus, quod Christus ideo promisit daturum se nobis, ut liberati per ipsum ab hostibus, serviamus ei absque inordinato timore, in sanctitate: non quod nullos adversarios habeamus, quum omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo persecutionem patiantur; sed quod illos inordinate non metuamus, nec peccando subdi cogamur, nec dæmonum manus, ut antea, incidamus, nec inferni suppliciis deputemur, imo ab omni gloriæ obstaculo eruamur, merito dominicæ passionis, dummodo nos ipsi obicem non ponamus. Hæc est spiritualis securitas, internaque pax, et vera libertas militantis Ecclesiæ, quantum ad eos qui fide et opere Christiani consistunt: quæ in primitiva Ecclesia maxime abundabant, sicut in Actibus Apostolorum docetur. Unde apud Isaiam Dominus prænuntiavit: Sedebit, inquiens, populus meus in pulchritudine pacis, et in tabernaculis fiduciæ, et in requie opulenta. Et in Sophonia legitur: Lauda, filia Sion; exsulta in omni corde, filia Jerusalem: avertit Dominus inimicos tuos, non timebis malum ultra. Insuper, per Jeremiam quum Dominus protulisset, Suscitabo David germen justum, id est Christum filium David, ut omnes exponunt, mox subditur, In diebus illis salvabitur Juda, et Israel habitabit confidenter: quia videlicet conversi ad Christum, non timuerunt eos qui corpus occidunt, utpote parati mori pro fide et veritate ac Deo, eo quod essent repleti caritate et gratia Christi, per quam optimæ et invictissimæ fuerunt fiduciæ.
paras.en: Now the words *without fear* can be referred to what follows, *being delivered*, and to the word *we may serve*. In the first way the sense is that Christ delivered us without danger and fear on our part, whereas many are rescued from the hands of enemies only with great dread and danger to themselves. Christ, too, delivered us without inordinate fear on His own part. Although, as His passion drew near, He was shaken by natural fear[[Mark 14:33||]], this happened willingly and by His own power, or from the prior judgement of His reason; and He cast off that same fear when He willed, and went out fearless to meet His enemies[[Mark 14:42||]]. — But if it is referred to the word *we may serve*, the sense is this: that Christ promised to give Himself to us so that, delivered by Him from our enemies, we may serve Him without inordinate fear, in holiness: not that we have no adversaries, since [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution|omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo persecutionem patiantur]]; but that we do not fear them inordinately, nor are forced to submit to them by sinning, nor fall, as before, into the hands of the demons, nor are assigned to the torments of hell; nay, that by the merit of the Lord's passion we are rescued from every obstacle to glory, provided we ourselves put no hindrance in the way. This is the spiritual security, the inward peace and the true freedom of the Church militant, as regards those who are Christians in faith and deed: and these abounded above all in the primitive Church, as the Acts of the Apostles teach[[Acts 2:44||]][[Acts 4:32||]]. Hence the Lord foretold in Isaias: [[Is 32:18|my people shall sit in the beauty of peace, and in the tabernacles of confidence, and in wealthy rest|Sedebit, inquiens, populus meus in pulchritudine pacis, et in tabernaculis fiduciæ, et in requie opulenta]]. And we read in Sophonias: [[Soph 3:14|Give praise, O daughter of Sion|Lauda, filia Sion]] … [[Soph 3:14|rejoice with all thy heart, O daughter of Jerusalem|exsulta in omni corde, filia Jerusalem]]: [[Soph 3:15|he hath turned away thy enemies|avertit Dominus inimicos tuos]] … [[Soph 3:15|thou shalt fear evil no more|non timebis malum ultra]]. Moreover, when the Lord had said by Jeremias, [[Jer 23:5|I will raise up to David a just branch|Suscitabo David germen justum]], that is, Christ the son of David, as all expound it, there follows straightway: [[Jer 23:6|In those days shall Juda be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently|In diebus illis salvabitur Juda, et Israel habitabit confidenter]]: because, namely, being converted to Christ, they did not fear [[Matt 10:28|them that kill the body|eos qui corpus occidunt]], being ready to die for the faith, for the truth and for God, since they were filled with the charity and grace of Christ, through which they were of the best and most unconquerable confidence.

paras.t: Denique, ideo venit Christus, ut per ejus passionem redempti, serviamus ei secundum evangelicæ legis tenorem. Hæc autem est lex perfectionis. Propter quod ait apud Matthæum: Estote ergo et vos perfecti, sicut Pater vester cœlestis perfectus est. Ad quod exigitur, ut homo non solum habeat se reverenter et pure ad Dominum, sed etiam juste ad proximum, dando cuique quod suum est, et proximos suos ædificando in omnibus, juxta illud Apostoli: Quæ pacis sunt, sectemur, et quæ ædificationis sunt, in invicem custodiamus. Et rursus: Ne ponatis offendiculum fratri, vel scandalum; noli illum perdere pro quo Christus mortuus est. Ideo subditur: et justitia, id est actibus justitiæ tam distributivæ, quam commutativæ. Imo per justitiam intelligi potest quælibet virtus, secundum quod justitia dicitur omnis virtus, seu virtus communis. Omnis etenim virtus est quædam justitia, quia per eam debitum quoddam exsolvitur, seu Deo ut justum est ministratur: sicut per caritatem Deum diligimus ut tenemur, per misericordiam proximo subvenimus ut obligamur. Deo autem non solum in justitia quæ est virtus specialis, sed in omni virtute servire debemus, præsertim fide, spe et caritate, quibus directe colitur Deus, tanquam immediatum propriumque objectum illarum.
paras.en: Lastly, Christ came for this, that, redeemed by His passion, we may serve Him according to the tenor of the Gospel law. And this is the law of perfection. Wherefore He says in Matthew: [[Matt 5:48|Be you therefore perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect.|Estote ergo et vos perfecti, sicut Pater vester cœlestis perfectus est]] For this it is required that a man bear himself not only reverently and purely toward the Lord, but also justly toward his neighbour, giving each his own and edifying his neighbours in all things, according to that word of the Apostle: [[Rom 14:19|let us follow after the things that are of peace and keep the things that are of edification, one towards another|Quæ pacis sunt, sectemur, et quæ ædificationis sunt, in invicem custodiamus]]. And again: [[Rom 14:13|that you put not a stumblingblock or a scandal in your brother's way|Ne ponatis offendiculum fratri, vel scandalum]]; [[Rom 14:15|Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died|noli illum perdere pro quo Christus mortuus est]]. Therefore there follows: [[1:75|and justice|et justitia]], that is, in acts of justice, both distributive and commutative. Nay, by justice any virtue can be understood, in the sense in which every virtue is called justice, or general virtue. For every virtue is a kind of justice, since by it some debt is paid, or God is served as is just: as by charity we love God as we are bound, and by mercy we help our neighbour as we are obliged. And we must serve God not only in justice, which is a particular virtue, but in every virtue, above all in faith, hope and charity, by which God is worshipped directly, as their immediate and proper object.

paras.t: Coram ipso, hoc est recta intentione et cum attentione interna: ut in Dei præsentia nos constituamus, eumque ut regem ac judicem omnia intuentem pensemus; et ita ei soli finaliter placere optemus, ejus honorem et gloriam in omnibus exquiramus, timorate ac reverenter cuncta agentes, simplici corde, non velut hypocritæ coram hominibus bona agendo ob propriam utilitatem seu laudem: ut illud Psalmistæ veraciter dicere mereamur, Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo; et illud Eliæ, Vivit Dominus, in cujus conspectu sto hodie.
paras.en: [[1:75|before him|Coram ipso]], that is, with right intention and with inward attention: so that we set ourselves in God's presence and consider Him as king and judge who beholds all things; and so desire, as our final end, to please Him alone, and seek His honour and glory in all things, doing everything with fear and reverence, with a simple heart, not doing good before men like the hypocrites for our own profit or praise[[Matt 6:1||]]: that we may deserve to say truly that word of the Psalmist, [[Ps 118:168|I have kept thy commandments and thy testimonies: because all my ways are in thy sight.|Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo]], and that of Elias, [[3 Kings 17:1|As the Lord liveth, the God of Israel, in whose sight I stand|Vivit Dominus, in cujus conspectu sto]] this day [Denis adds *hodie*, “this day”, from 3 Kings 18:15].

paras.t: Itaque, Serviamus ei, non uno die, vel raro, aut modico tempore, sed incessanter et perseveranter, ut subditur: omnibus diebus nostris. Qui enim perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit. Ideo monet Apostolus: Bonum facientes, non deficiamus; tempore enim suo metemus non deficientes. Nihil demum tam stultum, quam tempus, non solum infructuose, sed etiam vitiose expendere. Jugiter igitur Deo altissimo obsequamur, semperque perfectius atque amorosius obsequi studeamus, pensantes quod scriptum est: Maledictus qui facit opus Dei negligenter.
paras.en: So let us serve Him, not for one day, or seldom, or for a short time, but unceasingly and perseveringly, as there follows: [[1:75|all our days|omnibus diebus nostris]]. For [[Matt 10:22|he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved|Qui enim perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit]]. Therefore the Apostle admonishes: [[Gal 6:9|in doing good, let us not fail. For in due time we shall reap, not failing|Bonum facientes, non deficiamus; tempore enim suo metemus non deficientes]]. In a word, nothing is so foolish as to spend one's time not only fruitlessly but even sinfully. Let us then serve the most high God continually, and strive always to serve Him more perfectly and more lovingly, weighing what is written: [[Jer 48:10|Cursed be he that doth the work of the Lord deceitfully|Maledictus qui facit opus Dei negligenter]] [Denis has *negligenter*, “negligently”, where the Vulgate has *fraudulenter*; the margin reads Jer. xvii, 10].

paras.t: Postremo, inquiritur quomodo per Christum liberatum sit genus humanum, quum tam pauci salventur, tamque multi pereant. Respondendum, quod Christus sua passione pro totius mundi seu populi satisfecit peccatis, quantum in ipso est: ita quod meritum suum tantum fuit, quod pro omnium peccatorum deletione sufficiens sit; sed non subvenit, nisi his quibus applicatur seu communicatur per fidem, caritatem, aut sacramenta. Sua quoque sanctissima conversatione ac passione meruit omnibus nobis gratiam copiosam: specialiter tamen pro originali peccato satisfecisse asseritur, quoniam propter reatum illius, a gloria totum genus differebatur humanum. Conversatio demum et passio Christi, ex tam perfectissima caritate ac obedientia orientes, tam acceptæ Deo Patri seu superbenedictæ Trinitati fuerunt, quod pro totius mundi liberatione et justificatione ita fuerunt idoneæ, meritoriæ et prædignæ, præsertim propter hypostaticam seu personalem unionem humanitatis Christi cum Verbo, ex qua infinitam quodammodo promerendi ac satisfaciendi idoneitatem efficaciamque sortita est.
paras.en: Lastly, it is asked how mankind has been delivered through Christ, when so few are saved and so many perish. The answer is that Christ by His passion made satisfaction for the sins of the whole world, or people, as far as lies in Him: so that His merit was so great as to be sufficient for blotting out all sins; but it avails only those to whom it is applied or communicated through faith, charity or the sacraments. By His most holy life and passion He also merited abundant grace for all of us: but He is said to have made satisfaction especially for original sin, since because of its guilt the whole human race was kept back from glory. Finally, the life and passion of Christ, springing from such most perfect charity and obedience, were so acceptable to God the Father, or to the more than blessed Trinity, that they were fit, meritorious and more than worthy for the deliverance and justification of the whole world; above all because of the hypostatic, or personal, union of Christ's humanity with the Word, from which it received a fitness and efficacy, in a manner infinite, for meriting and making satisfaction.

paras.t: Et tu, puer, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis. Secundum Origenem, Zacharias plenus Spiritu Sancto, duas prophetias generaliter nuntiat: primam de Christo, quæ se extendit hucusque; alteram de Joanne, quæ incipit hic, ubi prædicit quod gratia prophetiæ fuerit danda Joanni, ita quod erit atque vocabitur Propheta Christi, qui secundum Apostolum ad Romanos, est super omnia Deus benedictus in sæcula. Verumtamen apud Joannem legitur, iste Joannes interrogatus, Propheta es tu? respondisse, Non sum. Ad quod dupliciter respondetur: Primo, secundum Glossam ibidem, quod Judæi interrogantes, per Prophetam intellexerunt Eliseum: quod advertens Joannes, intentioni eorum rite respondit. Secundo, quod prophetam, id est prophetam dumtaxat, esse se negat, quia et plus quam propheta fuit, non solum denuntiando futura, sed et Christum demonstrans præsentem.
paras.en: [[1:76|And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest|Et tu, puer, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis]]. According to Origen, Zachary, full of the Holy Ghost, utters two prophecies in all: the first about Christ, which reaches as far as this; the other about John, which begins here, where he foretells that the grace of prophecy was to be given to John, so that he will be, and will be called, the Prophet of Christ, who, according to the Apostle to the Romans, [[Rom 9:5|is over all things, God blessed for ever|est super omnia Deus benedictus in sæcula]]. Yet we read in John that this John, when asked, [[John 1:21|Art thou the prophet?|Propheta es tu]], answered, I am not. To this a twofold answer is given. First, according to the Gloss on that place, that the Jews who asked meant Eliseus by *the Prophet*; and John, perceiving this, answered rightly to what they meant. Secondly, that he denies that he is a prophet, that is, a prophet only, since he was even more than a prophet[[Matt 11:9||]], not only foretelling things to come but also pointing out Christ present.

paras.t: Rursus inquiritur, cur Zacharias allocutus sit infantem octo dierum, in quo usus nondum exstitit rationis. Ad quod respondet Ambrosius, quod Zacharias agnovit infantem illum supernaturaliter intelligere sua verba, sicut in utero suæ Matris intellexit Filii Dei incarnationem atque præsentiam corporalem. Ait quippe Ambrosius: Potuit Joannes vocem patris sui natus audire, qui Mariæ salutationem, antequam nasceretur, audivit. Sciebat Zacharias alias esse aures Prophetæ, quæ spiritu Dei, non corporis ætate, reserantur. Habebat Joannes intelligendi sensum, qui exsultandi habebat affectum. Alii (sicut Beda) dicunt, quod non propter Joannis advertentiam, sed eorum qui aderant instructionem, ista prædixit: nam et inanimata et bruta alloquimur, ea ad Dei præconium invitando, non ut illa intelligant, sed ut nos ipsi ac audientes ad Dei laudem sic provocemur. Præterea multis nominibus invenitur Joannes appellatus. Dictus namque est amicus Sponsi, præcursor Christi, Baptista, angelus, lucerna ardens et lucens, propheta et plus quam propheta, atque Elias, propter gratiæ varia dona sibi collata.
paras.en: Again it is asked why Zachary spoke to an infant eight days old, in whom there was as yet no use of reason. To this Ambrose answers that Zachary knew that the infant understood his words supernaturally, just as in his Mother's womb he had understood the incarnation and bodily presence of the Son of God. For Ambrose says: John, once born, could hear his father's voice, who heard Mary's greeting before he was born. Zachary knew that a Prophet has other ears, which are opened by the Spirit of God, not by the age of the body. John had the sense to understand, who had the feeling to leap for joy. Others (as Bede) say that he foretold these things not for John's attention but for the instruction of those who were present: for we also address inanimate things and brute beasts, inviting them to the praise of God, not that they may understand, but that we ourselves and those who hear may so be stirred to the praise of God. Moreover, John is found called by many names. For he is called the friend of the Bridegroom[[John 3:29||]], the forerunner of Christ, the Baptist, an angel[[Mal 3:1||]], [[John 5:35|a burning and a shining light|lucerna ardens et lucens]], a prophet and more than a prophet[[Matt 11:9||]], and Elias[[Matt 11:14||]], because of the various gifts of grace bestowed on him.

paras.t: Præibis enim ante faciem Domini, id est ante corporalem ac manifestam præsentiam Christi, qui est Rex regum et Dominus dominantium. Joannes etenim natus est ante Christum; insuper orsus est prædicare et baptizare ante eumdem, præcessit etiam eum in limbum: idcirco præcursor vocatur. Quidam per faciem Domini intelligunt Christum Filium Patris, ut dicatur similitudo et facies Patris, quia per eum Pater cognoscitur. Per faciem enim notitia designatur: notitia autem in divinis Filio appropriatur, quemadmodum sapientia et veritas, quia per modum intellectualis emanationis procedit a Patre. Parare vias ejus, hoc est disponere homines ad Christi fidem, caritatem ac susceptionem: quod egit Joannes prædicando, monstrando et baptizando. Insuper, viæ Christi, id est viæ seu media per quæ Christus venit ad hominum corda, fuerunt prædicatio et baptismus Joannis, quæ ipse paravit, id est, sapienter exhibuit, sicut quis præparat mensam. Vel, viæ istæ sunt Baptismus et prædicatio Christi, ad quæ duo Joannes suo documento atque baptismate homines disponebat. Rursus, viæ istæ sunt opera virtuosa, seu præceptorum custodiæ, ad quæ homines Joannes induxit, vitia exstirpando, ac virtutes dispositive seu instrumentaliter inducendo. Propter quod per Malachiam Dominus loquitur de Joanne: Ecce ego, inquiens, mitto angelum meum, et præparabit viam ante faciem meam. Rursus, viæ istæ sunt misericordia qua Deus venit ad nos, et pœnitentia qua imus ad eum. Ad primam paravit Joannes, Christi gratiam et Baptismum insinuando; ad secundam, pœnitentiam exhortando, et rigorose vivendo. — Præterea, secundum Chrysostomum, quemadmodum reges quosdam habent qui eminus seu longe eos præcedunt, et item commilitones qui de propinquo præcedunt; sic Christus habuit Prophetas alios, eum longe ante prænuntiantes et præcedentes, Joannem vero eum de proximo præcedentem ac præsentem, deinde monstrantem.
paras.en: [[1:76|for thou shalt, go before the face of the Lord|Præibis enim ante faciem Domini]], that is, before the bodily and manifest presence of Christ, who is [[Apoc 19:16|KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS|Rex regum et Dominus dominantium]]. For John was born before Christ; besides, he began to preach and baptize before Him, and he went before Him also into limbo: therefore he is called the forerunner. Some understand by *the face of the Lord* Christ, the Son of the Father, so that He is called the likeness and face of the Father, because through Him the Father is known[[John 14:9||]] [the margin gives Joann. xiv, 6–10]. For by the face, knowledge is signified: and knowledge, in divine things, is appropriated to the Son [that is, attributed to one Person by a certain fittingness, though common to all three], as are wisdom and truth, because He proceeds from the Father by way of intellectual emanation. [[1:76|to prepare his ways|parare vias ejus]], that is, to dispose men to the faith, love and reception of Christ: which John did by preaching, pointing out and baptizing. Further, *the ways of Christ*, that is, the ways or means by which Christ came to the hearts of men, were the preaching and baptism of John, which he prepared, that is, wisely set forth, as one prepares a table. Or these ways are the Baptism and preaching of Christ, to which two John disposed men by his teaching and his baptism. Again, these ways are virtuous works, or the keeping of the commandments, to which John led men, rooting out vices and bringing in virtues dispositively or instrumentally [that is, preparing for them, as an instrument of God, not causing them himself]. Wherefore the Lord speaks of John through Malachias, saying: [[Mal 3:1|Behold I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face|Ecce ego … mitto angelum meum … ante faciem meam]][[Matt 11:10||]]. Again, these ways are the mercy by which God comes to us, and the penance by which we go to Him. For the first John prepared by making known the grace and Baptism of Christ; for the second, by exhorting to penance and living austerely. — Moreover, according to Chrysostom, as kings have some who go before them at a distance, far off, and also companions in arms who go before them close at hand, so Christ had other Prophets, who foretold Him and went before Him long beforehand, but John going before Him close at hand and present, and then pointing Him out.

paras.t: Deinde, secundum Theophilum, Zacharias exponit quomodo Joannes viam Domini præparavit, puta docendo. Ad dandam scientiam salutis plebi ejus, hoc est ad exhibendum seu prædicandum populo Judæorum notitiam qua ad veram felicitatem pertingitur, seu notitiam Christi, qui est salus nostra. Hæc est scientia salutaris, doctrina moralis, declaratio adventus mysteriorumque Christi, et sacramentorum Ecclesiæ. Itaque non ait, Ad dandam salutem, sed, Scientiam salutis, quia Joannes salutem non dedit, sed prædicavit. Propter quod apud Joannem habetur: Non erat ille lux, sed ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine. Hanc scientiam cœpit Joannes dare, quam Christus et Apostoli postea plenius contulerunt: de qua ad Philippenses ait Apostolus, Existimo omnia detrimentum esse propter eminentem scientiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Hanc autem scientiam dedit, In remissionem peccatorum eorum, videlicet plebis suæ, puta credentium. Hæc autem scientia dispositive ac incitative valuit ad diluenda peccata, quia per eam ad pœnitentiam Christique fidem explicitam populus inducebatur. Solus autem Deus dimittit peccata effective, secundum illud: Quis potest dimittere peccata, nisi solus Deus? Passio Christi [hoc facit] meritorie, juxta quod in Apocalypsi habetur: Christus dilexit nos, et lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo. Fides autem formata hoc agit formaliter, prout in Actibus dicitur: Fide purificans corda eorum. Opera vero pœnitentiæ hoc faciunt satisfactorie.
paras.en: Next, according to Theophilus [Theophylact], Zachary explains how John prepared the way of the Lord, namely by teaching: [[1:77|To give knowledge of salvation to his people|Ad dandam scientiam salutis plebi ejus]], that is, to set forth or preach to the people of the Jews the knowledge by which true happiness is reached, or the knowledge of Christ, who is our salvation[[Acts 4:12||]]. This is the saving knowledge: moral teaching, the declaring of the coming and mysteries of Christ, and of the sacraments of the Church. So he does not say *to give salvation*, but *knowledge of salvation*, because John did not give salvation but preached it. Wherefore we have it in John: [[John 1:8|He was not the light, but was to give testimony of the light.|Non erat ille lux, sed ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine.]] This knowledge John began to give, which Christ and the Apostles afterwards bestowed more fully: of which the Apostle says to the Philippians: [[Phil 3:8|I count all things to be but loss for the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ, my Lord|Existimo omnia detrimentum esse propter eminentem scientiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi]]. And he gave this knowledge [[1:77|unto the remission of their sins|In remissionem peccatorum eorum]], that is, of His people, namely of those who believe. This knowledge availed for washing away sins dispositively and by stirring men up, because by it the people were led to penance and to explicit faith in Christ. But God alone forgives sins effectively, according to the words: [[Mark 2:7|Who can forgive sins, but God only?|Quis potest dimittere peccata, nisi solus Deus?]] The passion of Christ [does this] meritoriously, according to what we have in the Apocalypse: Christ [[Apoc 1:5|hath loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood|dilexit nos, et lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo]]. Formed faith [that is, faith given its form by charity] does this formally, as is said in the Acts: [[Acts 15:9|purifying their hearts by faith|Fide purificans corda eorum]]. And the works of penance do it by way of satisfaction.

paras.t: Per viscera misericordiæ, id est intimam, secretam, viscerosam, seu amorosam misericordiam, Dei nostri unigeniti, scilicet propter nos incarnati, in quibus visceribus misericordiæ visitavit nos, id est, per incarnationem ad nos descendit, et nostram sibi conjunxit naturam, nos quoque ægrotos velut medicus pius nunc accessit. Itaque viscera in Deo, spiritualiter et metaphorice appellantur caritas et misericordia ejus, quibus inductus est succurrere nobis, sicut de Christo ait Apostolus: Qui dilexit me, et tradidit semetipsum pro me. Rursus quoque de Patre: Propter nimiam (inquit) caritatem qua dilexit nos Pater, Filium suum misit. Itaque, quia non propter merita nostra, sed ob suam pietatem et caritatem Deus hæc beneficia nobis largitus est, recte ait: Per viscera misericordiæ Dei nostri, in quibus visitavit nos. Unde in epistola Joannis legitur: In hoc est caritas, non quasi nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos. Hæc viscera Dei olim quasi latebant, juxta illud Isaiæ: Multitudo viscerum tuorum et miserationum tuarum super me continuerunt se.
paras.en: [[1:78|Through the bowels of the mercy of our God|Per viscera misericordiæ]], that is, through the inmost, secret, heartfelt or loving mercy [*viscera*, “bowels”, the seat of tender feeling] of our God, the Only-begotten, namely made flesh for us, [[1:78|in which|in quibus]] bowels of mercy [[1:78|hath visited us|visitavit nos]], that is, came down to us by the incarnation and joined our nature to Himself, and now came to us, who were sick, like a loving physician. So in God the *bowels* are, spiritually and metaphorically, His charity and mercy, by which He was moved to come to our help, as the Apostle says of Christ: [[Gal 2:20|who loved me and delivered himself for me|Qui dilexit me, et tradidit semetipsum pro me]]. And again of the Father: [[Eph 2:4|for his exceeding charity wherewith he loved us|Propter nimiam (inquit) caritatem qua dilexit nos]] the Father sent His Son. So, since God bestowed these benefits on us not for our merits but out of His loving-kindness and charity, he rightly says: *Through the bowels of the mercy of our God, in which He hath visited us*. Hence we read in the epistle of John: [[1 John 4:10|In this is charity: not as though we had loved God, but because he hath first loved us|In hoc est caritas, non quasi nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos]]. These bowels of God were once as it were hidden, according to the words of Isaias: [[Is 63:15|the multitude of thy bowels, and of thy mercies? they have held back themselves from me|Multitudo viscerum tuorum et miserationum tuarum super me continuerunt se]].

paras.t: Itaque, Visitavit nos oriens ex alto, hoc est, de summo cœlo ad terram descendens, de sinu Patris, imo de corde Patris in uterum Virginis veniens, ab altitudine suæ habitationis, qua inaccessibilem lucem inhabitat, ad peregrinos et exsules se inclinans, quemadmodum scriptum est: A summo cœlo egressio ejus. Christus quoque Oriens nuncupatur: qui candor est lucis æternæ, et gloriæ splendor paternæ, ex supersplendidissimo Dei Patris corde æternaliter oriens et emanans, deinde per humanitatem assumptam hominibus innotescens atque resplendens. Qui in Ecclesiastico testatur: Ego, inquiens, in altissimis habitavi; et rursus, Ego feci in cœlis, ut oriretur lumen indeficiens. De quo secundum formam servi, Deus Pater per Zachariam ait: Ecce ego adducam servum meum Orientem. De quo per eumdem Zachariam: Ecce vir, Oriens nomen ejus. At vero, sicut a parte cœli orientali, qua […] ita a Christo lux gratiæ nobis profluxit […] Solque sapientiæ, Deus unus et trinus, per ejus humanitatem nos illustravit.
paras.en: So, [[1:78|the Orient from on high hath visited us|Visitavit nos oriens ex alto]], that is, coming down from the height of heaven to earth, from the bosom of the Father, nay, from the heart of the Father into the womb of the Virgin; from the height of His dwelling, in which He inhabits light inaccessible[[1 Tim 6:16||]], bending down to pilgrims and exiles, as it is written: [[Ps 18:7|His going out is from the end of heaven|A summo cœlo egressio ejus]]. Christ is also called *the Orient* [*Oriens*, “the rising”, the dayspring]: who is [[Wis 7:26|the brightness of eternal light|candor est lucis æternæ]], and the splendour of the Father's glory[[Heb 1:3||]], rising and flowing forth eternally from the most resplendent heart of God the Father, and then, through the humanity He took, becoming known and shining out to men. He testifies in Ecclesiasticus, saying: [[Ecclus 24:7|I dwelt in the highest places|Ego, inquiens, in altissimis habitavi]]; and again: [[Ecclus 24:6|I made that in the heavens there should rise light that never faileth|Ego feci in cœlis, ut oriretur lumen indeficiens]]. Of whom, according to the form of a servant, God the Father says through Zachary: [[Zach 3:8|I WILL BRING MY SERVANT THE ORIENT|Ecce ego adducam servum meum Orientem]]. Of whom again through the same Zachary: [[Zach 6:12|BEHOLD A MAN, THE ORIENT IS HIS NAME|Ecce vir, Oriens nomen ejus]]. But, as from the eastern part of the sky, where […], so from Christ the light of grace has flowed forth to us […]; and the Sun of wisdom, God one and three, has enlightened us through His humanity. [the foot of the left column of PDF 428 (p. 408) is unreadable in the OCR: some two lines are lost after *qua* and one or two after *profluxit*]

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Illuminare his, hoc est ad illuminandum eos, qui in tenebris ignorantiæ et erroris seu infidelitatis, et in umbra mortis sedent, id est in vita impia: quæ umbra mortis vocatur, quia a Deo separat mentem, sicut mors naturalis seu corporalis a corpore segregat animam, juxta illud Isaiæ: Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter vos et Deum vestrum. Vel umbra mortis, est sæculum præsens, quod quum sit vallis lacrimarum, peregrinatio et exsilium, umbra et similitudo mortis respectu patriæ nominatur; imo et vita præsens, umbra mortis vocatur, dicente Gregorio: Vita temporalis æternæ vitæ comparata, mors est potius dicenda, quam vita. Quidam per umbram mortis, oblivionem intelligunt, quia sicut mors tollit ab exsistentia in natura, sic oblivio ab exsistentia in memoria. Insuper aliqui per sedentes in tenebris, accipiunt patres in limbo detentos, qui fuerunt in tenebris, hoc est carentia lucis gloriæ, et loco obscuro: ad quorum illuminationem Christus post mortem in cruce statim descendit, eosque mox ibi lumine gloriæ illustravit, ita quod tunc Deum per speciem videre cœperunt, secundum doctores. Tunc namque pro originalis peccati reatu fuerat satisfactum, pretiumque redemptionis solutum, pro quo reatu dumtaxat sancti illi differebantur a gloria. Per sedentes vero in umbra mortis, intelligunt viatores et peccatores. — Proprie quoque per sedentes in tenebris, intelliguntur gentiles idololatræ, ad quorum illuminationem Christus descendit, sicut apud Joannem loquitur: Alias oves habeo, quæ non sunt ex hoc ovili, et illas oportet me adducere. De hac re multa in Isaia leguntur, ut est illud: Populus qui ambulabat in tenebris, vidit lucem magnam; habitantibus in regione umbræ mortis, lux orta est eis. Rursus per Isaiam prophetam Pater loquitur Christo: Dedi te in lucem gentium, ut aperires oculos cæcorum, et educeres de conclusione vinctum, de domo carceris sedentes in tenebris. Sed et per Isaiam Christus de Patre testatur: Glorificatus sum in oculis Domini, et dixit: Parum est ut sis mihi ad suscitandas tribus Jacob, et ad fæces Israel convertendas; dedi te in lucem gentium, ut sis salus mea usque ad ultimum terræ. Hinc quoque Joannes de ipso ait: Erat lux vera quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum.
paras.en: Hence there follows: [[1:79|To enlighten them|Illuminare his]], that is, to enlighten those [[1:79|that sit in darkness|qui in tenebris]] of ignorance and error or unbelief, [[1:79|and in the shadow of death|et in umbra mortis sedent]], that is, in an ungodly life: which is called the shadow of death because it separates the mind from God, as natural or bodily death separates the soul from the body; according to the words of Isaias: [[Is 59:2|your iniquities have divided between you and your God|Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter vos et Deum vestrum]]. Or the shadow of death is the present world, which, since it is a vale of tears, a pilgrimage and an exile, is called a shadow and likeness of death in comparison with our fatherland; nay, the present life too is called the shadow of death, as Gregory says: Temporal life, compared with eternal life, should rather be called death than life. Some understand by the shadow of death forgetfulness, because as death takes away from existence in nature, so forgetfulness takes away from existence in the memory. Moreover some take *those that sit in darkness* to be the fathers held in limbo, who were in darkness, that is, in the want of the light of glory, and in an obscure place: to enlighten whom Christ, after His death on the cross, at once went down, and there forthwith enlightened them with the light of glory, so that they then began to see God face to face, according to the doctors. For then satisfaction had been made for the guilt of original sin, and the price of redemption paid; and it was for that guilt alone that those saints were held back from glory. By *those that sit in the shadow of death* they understand wayfarers and sinners. — Properly, too, *those that sit in darkness* are understood as the idolatrous Gentiles, to enlighten whom Christ came down, as He says in John: [[John 10:16|other sheep I have that are not of this fold: them also I must bring|Alias oves habeo, quæ non sunt ex hoc ovili, et illas oportet me adducere]]. Many things are read of this in Isaias, as that: [[Is 9:2|The people that walked in darkness, have seen a great light: to them that dwelt in the region of the shadow of death, light is risen|Populus qui ambulabat in tenebris, vidit lucem magnam; habitantibus in regione umbræ mortis, lux orta est eis]]. Again, through the prophet Isaias the Father says to Christ: [[Is 42:6|for a light of the Gentiles|in lucem gentium]], [[Is 42:7|That thou mightest open the eyes of the blind, and bring forth the prisoner out of prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house.|ut aperires oculos cæcorum, et educeres de conclusione vinctum, de domo carceris sedentes in tenebris.]] [the line *rires oculos cæcorum, et educeres de con-* is garbled in the OCR (foot of the right column of PDF 428) and is supplied from the verse, which the margin gives]. And through Isaias Christ testifies of the Father: [[Is 49:5|I am glorified in the eyes of the Lord|Glorificatus sum in oculis Domini]], and He said: [[Is 49:6|It is a small thing that thou shouldst be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to convert the dregs of Israel. Behold, I have given thee to be the light of the Gentiles, that thou mayst be my salvation even to the farthest part of the earth|Parum est ut sis mihi ad suscitandas tribus Jacob, et ad fæces Israel convertendas; dedi te in lucem gentium, ut sis salus mea usque ad ultimum terræ]]. Hence John too says of Him: [[John 1:9|That was the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world.|Erat lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum.]]

paras.t: Ad dirigendos pedes nostros, hoc est affectus: de quibus cantamus, Statuit supra petram pedes meos; et in Canticis loquitur Sponsa, Lavi pedes meos; In viam pacis, hoc est ad conversationem justam ac virtuosam, quæ est iter ad pacem pectoris in præsenti, atque ad pacem æternitatis in futuro. Ad hanc duplicem pacem præstandam, Christus potissimum venit et passus est. Propter quod testabatur Apostolis: Pacem, inquiens, relinquo vobis, pacem meam do vobis. Hinc de Christo ait Apostolus: Veniens evangelizavit pacem his qui longe, et his qui prope, hoc est gentilibus ac Judæis: quæ verba ex Isaia accepta sunt.
paras.en: [[1:79|to direct our feet|Ad dirigendos pedes nostros]], that is, our affections: of which we sing: [[Ps 39:3|he set my feet upon a rock|Statuit supra petram pedes meos]]; and in the Canticles the Bride says: [[Cant 5:3|I have washed my feet|Lavi pedes meos]]; [[1:79|into the way of peace|In viam pacis]], that is, to a just and virtuous manner of life, which is the road to peace of heart in the present, and to the peace of eternity in the future. To bestow this twofold peace above all Christ came and suffered. Wherefore He testified to the Apostles, saying: [[John 14:27|Peace I leave with you: my peace I give unto you|Pacem, inquiens, relinquo vobis, pacem meam do vobis]]. Hence the Apostle says of Christ: [[Eph 2:17|coming, he preached peace to you that were afar off: and peace to them that were nigh|Veniens evangelizavit pacem his qui longe, et his qui prope]], that is, to Gentiles and Jews: which words are taken from Isaias[[Is 57:19||]].

paras.t: Denique, quum pax ista spiritualis ac vera, fructusque Spiritus, secundum Apostolum ad Galatas, sit quies, tranquillitas seu quietatio mentis in Deo, seu gaudium imperturbatum in eo; certum est quod per conversationem virtuosam homo ad pacem pertingat, vitiorum ac passionum tumultus inquietudinesque sedando et exstirpando. Præcipue tamen pax a caritate procedit, quasi efficienter. Caritas namque unionem et concordiam parit, quietem quoque et gaudium in amato, dum ei conjungitur, designat. Hinc ait Psalmista: Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam. Ex justitia vero procedere dicitur, quasi a prohibens removente, quia justitia impedimenta pacis aufert et perimit, juxta illud Isaiæ: Erit opus justitiæ pax. Rursus, pax ponitur effectus prudentiæ, tanquam virtutis dirigentis ad pacem per veram discretionem, qua quis ordinate se habet: unde nec perturbatur. Ideo ad Romanos ait Apostolus: Prudentia spiritus, vita et pax. Hanc itaque pacem amemus, hanc exquiramus et conservemus, quum dicat Salvator: Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur.
paras.en: Lastly, since this spiritual and true peace, a fruit of the Spirit according to the Apostle to the Galatians[[Gal 5:22||]], is the rest, tranquillity or quieting of the mind in God, or undisturbed joy in Him, it is certain that a man reaches peace by a virtuous manner of life, calming and rooting out the tumults and disquiet of vices and passions. Yet peace proceeds chiefly from charity, as from its efficient cause. For charity brings forth union and concord, and betokens rest and joy in the one loved, when one is joined to him. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]. And it is said to proceed from justice as from that which removes what hinders it, because justice takes away and destroys the hindrances to peace, according to the words of Isaias: [[Is 32:17|the work of justice shall be peace|Erit opus justitiæ pax]]. Again, peace is set down as an effect of prudence, as the virtue that directs to peace through true discernment, by which one bears oneself in an orderly way, and so is not disturbed. Therefore the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 8:6|the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace|Prudentia spiritus, vita et pax]]. Let us then love this peace, seek it out and keep it, since the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:9|Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.|Beati pacifici: quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur.]]

paras.t: Postremo, canticum istud sententiosum ac dulce devotissime concinamus, grata et affectuosa mente ineffabilia Dei beneficia, præsertim Verbi æterni incarnationem, intime recolentes, et grates Deo innumerabiles præcordialissime referentes.
paras.en: Lastly, let us sing this sweet canticle, so full of meaning, most devoutly, with a grateful and loving mind inwardly recalling the unspeakable benefits of God, above all the incarnation of the eternal Word, and giving God countless thanks from the depths of our hearts.

paras.t: Puer autem, puta Joannes, crescebat mente et corpore, sed multo plus mente, proficiendo ineffabiliter omni charismate gratiarum, ab eo tempore quo ratione uti continue cœpit; et confortabatur spiritu, hoc est a Spiritu Sancto, seu donis et gratia ejus; vel, Spiritu, id est in anima sua seu spiritu rationali, sicut ait Apostolus: Optimum est gratia stabiliri cor. Et erat in desertis, hoc est eremi et solitudinis locis, ut ibi Deo per contemplationem et fervidam dilectionem liberius frequentiusque vacaret, quotidiana peccata, quæ ex humana cohabitatione sæpe contingunt, magis vitaret, solis supernis intenderet, vitam rigorosiorem exemplarioremque duceret, atque per hoc magis idoneus fieret Christi testis, ac pœnitentiæ exhortator. Hinc asserit Beda: Prædicator pœnitentiæ futurus, ut liberius auditores suos a mundi illecebris avertat, primævam in desertis peragit vitam. Et Origenes: Erat, inquit, in desertis, ubi purior aer est, cœlum apertius, ac familiarior Deus: ut quia nondum baptismi et prædicationis tempus advenit, vacaret orationibus, et cum angelis conversaretur, appellaret Dominum, et illum audiret dicentem, Ecce adsum. Denique in Hymno cantatur: Antra deserti teneris sub annis, civium turmas fugiens petisti, etc. Usque in diem ostensionis suæ ad Israel, hoc est, quousque Deo jubente venit, et manifestavit se populo Israelitico, prædicans et baptizans circa Jordanem. Quo autem tempore facta sit illa ostensio, infra capitulo tertio dicitur: Anno quintodecimo imperii Tiberii Cæsaris. Itaque cœpit Joannes facere et docere, sicut et Christus, tanquam verus ejus præcursor, præco, servus, amicus, discipulus.
paras.en: [[1:80|And the child grew|Puer autem, puta Joannes, crescebat]], namely John, in mind and body, but much more in mind, advancing unspeakably in every gift of grace from the time when he began to use his reason continuously; [[1:80|and was strengthened in spirit|et confortabatur spiritu]], that is, by the Holy Spirit, or by His gifts and grace; or *in spirit*, that is, in his soul or rational spirit, as the Apostle says: [[Heb 13:9|it is best that the heart be established with grace|Optimum est gratia stabiliri cor]]. [[1:80|and was in the deserts|Et erat in desertis]], that is, in places of wilderness and solitude, so that there he might give himself to God more freely and more often by contemplation and fervent love; might better avoid the daily sins that often arise from living among men; might attend to heavenly things alone; might lead a stricter and more exemplary life; and so might become a fitter witness of Christ and preacher of penance. Hence Bede declares: Being about to be a preacher of penance, he spends his early life in the deserts, so that he might the more freely turn his hearers from the allurements of the world. And Origen says: He was in the deserts, where the air is purer, the sky more open, and God more familiar: so that, since the time of baptism and preaching had not yet come, he might give himself to prayer, converse with the angels, call upon the Lord and hear Him saying, Behold, I am here. And in the Hymn we sing: *Antra deserti teneris sub annis, civium turmas fugiens petisti*, etc. [“In tender years, fleeing the crowds of the city, thou didst seek the caves of the desert”: from the hymn *Ut queant laxis* for St John's day]. [[1:80|until the day of his manifestation to Israel|Usque in diem ostensionis suæ ad Israel]], that is, until at God's bidding he came and showed himself to the people of Israel, preaching and baptizing about the Jordan. At what time that manifestation took place is said below, in the third chapter: [[Luke 3:1|in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar|Anno quintodecimo imperii Tiberii Cæsaris]]. So John began to do and to teach[[Acts 1:1||]], as Christ did too, as His true forerunner, herald, servant, friend and disciple.
